items.description: In `a2a_generate_card_with_agent_validator::validate_args_impl`, only the input `path` is canonicalized/validated for read access. The `output_path` parameter is copied verbatim into `args_.output_path` with no `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(parsed.output_path, agentlib::access_type::write, ...)` check, unlike the analogous `security_review_with_agent_security.cpp` and `html_extract_tables_validator.cpp` which both validate output paths under write access. This output path is later embedded into the subagent task prompt (used to derive the write destination), so an untrusted caller can direct the downstream subagent to write/overwrite arbitrary files within the sandbox write scope without authorization checks.
items.proposed_fix: Validate `parsed.output_path` with `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(parsed.output_path, agentlib::access_type::write, canonical_output_path, out_error)` when non-empty and reject on failure, mirroring `security_review_with_agent_validator`. Store the canonical output path (and a canonical default sidecar path derived from `safe_path`) in the args for use by the tool.
items.summary: a2a_generate_card_with_agent: output_path is never write-access-validated

items.description: When `output_path` is empty, `execute()` derives the default destination card path from `args_.requested_path` — the raw, un-normalized user-supplied string — rather than from the already-validated canonical `args_.safe_path`. Because `requested_path` is the original untrusted input (which may contain `..`, symlinks, or alternate directory forms), the sidecar card path computed via `substr(0, len-3)+".card.json"` can resolve to a location different from the intended one, re-introducing path-traversal / normalization issues after input validation was already performed on `safe_path`.
items.proposed_fix: Derive the default destination from the canonicalized `args_.safe_path` (compute the `.card.json` sidecar against the canonical path), so the effective write destination reflects the same path that passed read-access validation. Optionally validate the resulting write destination for write access as well.
items.summary: a2a_generate_card_with_agent: derived default output path is built from un-canonicalized requested_path

items.description: In `a2a_generate_card_with_agent_tool::execute()`, the tool only looks up the subagent definition via `find_subagent_by_name("a2acardgenerator")`, builds a task prompt string, calls `set_success()`, and returns a "dispatched" message. It never actually spawns the subagent (`spawn_subagent`), never calls `submit_prompt`, and never `wait_until_idle()`. The tool reports success to the caller implying the card was synthesized and written, but that work is deferred to a separate, separately-triggered subagent invocation and has no `set_allowed_write_file` gate (unlike `security_review_with_agent_tool`). The tool's `is_pure()` returns false, correctly flagging side effects, yet no side effect actually occurs here, and the unvalidated `dest_card_path` is handed off as a prompt string for some later run to act upon. This both misrepresents completion and delegates a security-sensitive file write to an un-validated path.
items.proposed_fix: Either actually spawn/execute the a2acardgenerator subagent in-process and gate its writes with `set_allowed_write_file(canonical_output_path)` before reporting success, or, if this tool is intended only to queue/emit a directive, rename it/clarify semantics and ensure the eventual writer validates the output path for write access. Do not set `set_success` before the write is authorized and performed.
items.summary: a2a_generate_card_with_agent: reports success without actually spawning/running the subagent or gating the write

items.description: The task prompt embeds `args_.requested_path` and `dest_card_path` — both derived from untrusted agent/user input (the latter not write-validated, see related finding) — directly into a prompt string that is later consumed by the `a2acardgenerator` LLM subagent: `std::format("Please read the agent definition file at `{}` ...Write the validated card to `{}`...", args_.requested_path, dest_card_path)`. Untrusted values reflected into a downstream LLM prompt are a classic prompt-injection vector: a specially crafted `path` value could inject additional directives causing the downstream subagent to read or write unintended files or reveal content. The reflected value is also used in the returned markdown report without escaping/UI-safety checking.
items.line_content:
std::string task_prompt = std::format(
	    "Please read the agent definition file at `{}` and synthesize an A2A Agent Card JSON file.\n"
items.proposed_fix: Treat `requested_path` and the resolved destination as untrusted. Sanitize/validate both (e.g., reject control characters and ensure they contain no embedded instruction framing), pass the canonical validated paths rather than raw user strings, and escape reflected values in the returned report (consistent with `fs_utils::is_safe_for_ui` / `strip_ansi` protections used elsewhere).
items.summary: a2a_generate_card_with_agent: unvalidated/raw paths reflected into a subagent prompt (prompt-injection amplification)

items.description: In `a2a_validate_card_tool::execute()`, the VFS branch reads the card file via `vfs->read_file(args_.safe_path)` and assigns `view_opt.value()->view()` to `json_str` with no size cap, and the non-VFS branch reads the whole file via `std::ifstream`. There is no upper bound on the amount of data read or fed into `nlohmann::json::parse`. An attacker controlling the card file or `card_data` could supply an extremely large document, causing unbounded memory consumption before parsing (resource exhaustion / DoS).
items.proposed_fix: Enforce a maximum input size (e.g., reject card files/`card_data` over a configured byte limit) before reading/parsing, and consider using `nlohmann::json::parse` with size- or depth-limited options (e.g., a max depth / SAX parser) to bound resource usage.
items.summary: a2a_validate_card: no size limit on card file/VFS data or card_data before full read+JSON parse (resource exhaustion)

items.description: The generated validation report interpolates untrusted card content directly into the output without sanitization: `agent_name = card.value("name", ...)`, `agent_desc`, `agent_ver`, and each skill string are concatenated into the returned Markdown (`std::format` and `report += "`" + s.get<std::string>() + "`"`). These values originate from an untrusted (user/network-provided) card. The validator only checks that `name`/`description` are non-empty strings and `version` is a string — it does not reject control characters or ANSI escape sequences. A malicious card could inject terminal escape sequences / ANSI control characters into the editor output (terminal injection, UI spoofing / log forging). The rest of the codebase uses protections like `fs_utils::is_safe_for_ui` and `strip_ansi` elsewhere; this path lacks them.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize all reflected card-derived strings (name, description, version, skills) before embedding them into the report — reject or strip control characters / ANSI escapes (using `fs_utils::is_safe_for_ui` or an equivalent `strip_ansi` filter) — to prevent terminal/console injection from untrusted card content.
items.summary: a2a_validate_card: unsanitized card content (name/desc/version/skills) reflected into report — terminal injection

items.description: In `a2a_validate_card_validator::validate_args_impl`, the `card_data` argument is accepted with no length limit and passed straight through to `args_.card_data`. There is no cap on the size of the raw JSON string a caller may submit, consistent with the unbounded read in the tool (see related finding). Combined, an untrusted caller can submit an arbitrarily large `card_data` string to be held in memory and parsed, enabling resource exhaustion.
items.proposed_fix: Reject `card_data` strings exceeding a maximum configured length in the validator (e.g., a few MB), bounding memory usage before the JSON is parsed.
items.summary: a2a_validate_card validator: no length cap on card_data argument

items.description: The `a2acardgenerator` subagent (registered in `plugin_run`) has `read_only: true` per its definition (a2acardgenerator.md frontmatter), yet its system prompt instructs it to "Write Output File ... using `fs_write_file`" (step 4). A `read_only: true` subagent cannot perform file writes, so the intended card write either silently fails or is inconsistent with the read-only contract. Additionally, `plugin_run` does not set any `set_allowed_write_file` for the generated card destination, and `a2a_generate_card_with_agent_tool::execute` never sets one either — leaving the write path unauthorized/ungoverned if it is actually permitted. This indicates the card write flow is not properly sandboxed/authorized.
items.proposed_fix: Reconcile the a2acardgenerator subagent's read_only flag with the fact that it must write the card file. Either mark it as non-read-only and scope its write permission to the validated canonical output path (via `set_allowed_write_file`), or change the design so writes are performed by the calling tool under an authorized write path. Ensure the card write destination is always write-access validated before any write.
items.summary: a2acardgenerator subagent flagged read_only=true but instructed to fs_write_file; write path not authorized/gated

items.description:
Both `resolve_input_file` (line 146-153) and the local-disk branch of `resolve_input_data` (line 75-90) read arbitrary local filesystem paths using `fs_utils::safe_absolute(...)` and `std::filesystem::exists(...)` WITHOUT ever invoking `ctx.fs_security.validate_access`. The project has an explicit sandbox mechanism (`file_security_manager::validate_access`) and a base class (`single_file_tool_validator`) whose entire purpose is to canonicalize and authorize path arguments against the allowlist/ignore/working-directory policy before a tool touches the file. These tools entirely bypass it.

The JSON schemas advertise `path` as a "Relative path under the project workspace", but since an absolute path (or `../../` traversal that resolves to any absolute path) is accepted directly, a prompt-injected/compromised LLM could read ANY file the editor process can read (e.g. /etc/passwd, ~/.ssh/keys, project-ignored secrets). This is a sandbox escape / arbitrary-file-read vulnerability. Both `data_compress_tool::execute` (line 21) and `data_decompress_tool::execute` (line 21) funnel attacker-controlled path arguments into these functions, so the bypass is reachable from both tools.

Fix: route path arguments through `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(path, access_type::read, resolved, err)` (ideally by deriving from `single_file_tool_validator` or `single_string_tool_validator`) and only read the resolved, authorized path.
items.proposed_fix: Before reading any local path, canonicalize and authorize it via ctx.fs_security.validate_access(path, access_type::read, resolved_path, error) and read only the returned resolved path. Prefer deriving the validators from single_file_tool_validator so the security manager check is applied centrally. Refuse reading paths at or above the working directory root / allowlist unless explicitly allowed.
items.summary: Sandbox bypass: input path resolution never validates against file_security_manager (arbitrary file read)

items.description:
`decompress_data` performs decompression with NO limit on the decompressed output size, enabling classic decompression-bomb (zip-bomb) memory exhaustion when an AI agent decompresses attacker-controlled data from the repo or network:

- zstd path (lines 458-466): `rSize = ZSTD_getFrameContentSize(...)` is taken directly from the untrusted frame header and `std::vector<uint8_t> result(rSize)` is allocated up-front with zero upper-bound validation. A tiny malicious frame header declaring a multi-GB content size causes an immediate huge allocation / OOM crash of the editor process without even needing the payload to be large.
- zlib/gzip path (lines 424-455): the `inflate` loop grows `result` via repeated `result.insert(...)` with no cap on `zs.total_out`.
- lzw (line 378), ascii85 (line 257), runlength (line 274/282) decoders likewise grow `output` with no bound.

Because compressed input originates from untrusted/variable sources (files in the workspace, remote data fetched by the agent), an attacker-controlled tiny payload can expand to gigabytes, exhausting memory. These tools are invoked by the LLM (subject to prompt injection), so this is a reachable, high-impact DoS.

Fix: enforce a configurable maximum decompressed size (e.g. a constant like MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES, default ~100MB) checked BEFORE the zstd allocation (reject rSize > limit) and enforced incrementally in the streaming paths; abort and throw when exceeded.
items.line_content:
std::vector<uint8_t> result(rSize);
        size_t dSize = ZSTD_decompress(result.data(), rSize, input.data(), input.size());
items.proposed_fix: Add a maximum decompressed-size limit. For zstd, reject `rSize > max` before allocating. For zlib/gzip, stop the inflate loop and throw once `zs.total_out > max`. Guard lzw/ascii85/runlength output growth the same way. Return a clear error ("decompressed data exceeds maximum allowed size") instead of allocating unbounded memory.
items.summary: Decompression bomb: no output-size cap in decompress_data (zstd allocates frame-declared size directly)

items.description:
In `format_binary_output` (line 492), the function constructs a **brand-new** `agentlib::virtual_file_system vfs;` from scratch and calls `vfs.write_file(uri, ...)`. This new VFS is completely separate from the caller's `tool_context` VFS (`ctx.fs_security.get_vfs()`), so it has none of the context's mounted buffers or configured providers. Consequences:

1. Sandbox/security mismatch: the write path is not checked by `ctx.fs_security`. While the project-rooted `file://` provider has a directory-traversal guard (in `file_vfs_provider::create_file`), the default scheme handled by `memory_vfs_provider` for `tmp://`/`agent://` etc. is NOT routed through the security manager's write policy (allowlist, ignore patterns such as .agentignore, read-only scheme enforcement). Moreover the write_file result string is returned directly to the AI agent, leaking the on-disk path.
2. Correctness bug: when `output_format != "text"` AND `output_file` is empty (the normal return-as-string path), `format_binary_output` still runs `mime::detect_buffer_type` on the data and calls `fs_utils::format_binary_output(data, output_format, mime_type)` (line 510-511) — it never uses the passed `output_file` at all in that branch, so the "output_file" is ignored whenever it is "" which is fine, but the bigger issue is the write path uses the wrong VFS instance.

The intent of the tool is to write the decompressed/compressed result to a contextual VFS URI (e.g. tmp://). Using a fresh VFS defeats the shared in-memory VFS namespace the host uses to expose results to the user and other tools, so written files won't be visible under the expected URI and may silently go to a different backing store.

Fix: pass the context VFS down into format_binary_output (or write via ctx.fs_security.get_vfs()), and validate the output path with validate_access(write) before writing.
items.line_content:
agentlib::virtual_file_system vfs;
        std::string result = vfs.write_file(uri, data.data(), data.size());
items.proposed_fix: Have format_binary_output take an `agentlib::virtual_file_system* vfs` (from the tool_context) and use it for the write, and validate the output path via ctx.fs_security.validate_access(path, access_type::write, ...) before writing. Do not construct a throwaway VFS.
items.summary: format_binary_output constructs a throwaway VFS instead of using the context VFS (write path bypasses contextual sandbox + wrong backing store)

items.description:
The `data_compress_validator::validate_args_impl` (and the decompress equivalent) reads `offset`/`size` (decompress only has offset/size) and the path but does a fundamentally shallow validation:

- It does no type checking on `offset`/`size` — `raw_json.value("offset", 0)` will throw on a non-integer, which is caught, but a huge `size` (e.g. INT64... or a negative other than -1) and a huge `offset` are accepted. `resolve_input_data` then does `length = decoded.size() - offset` which for `offset > size` underflows size_t (wraps to a huge number) leading to a huge `actual_len` and a vector copy attempt / potential hang or memory spike reading an entire multi-GB file. Specifically when `length < 0` is entered with `decoded.size() < offset`, `size_t` arithmetic underflows.
- More importantly, no numeric bounds (e.g. size limit on `input_data`, max offset/size) are enforced, and there is no rejection of absolute paths / traversal as noted in the sandbox finding.

The validator is the natural place to reject dangerous inputs early (project rule: 'Validate untrusted input as early as possible'), but currently it only checks mutual exclusivity of path/input_data. Add checks that offset >= 0, offset <= data size once resolved, and size within a sane bound; reject non-numeric gracefully; and reject outright-absolute or traversal path arguments before creating the tool.
items.proposed_fix: Validate offset >= 0 and size within a reasonable maximum; reject negative size values other than -1; reject absolute/traversal paths (force validate_access at validation time via single_file_tool_validator); enforce a maximum input_data string length to bound base64/hex decode memory.
items.summary: Shallow arg validation: offset/size not type- or range-checked -> size_t underflow and unbounded reads

items.description:
`LZWBitReader::read_bits` (lines 296-321) has two related unsafe behaviors:

1. Out-of-bounds read: `if (byte_idx_ >= data_.size()) return 257;` checks the bounds at the START of the loop, but if `bit_idx_ != 0` and a read straddles a byte boundary (line 296-320), it first consumes the remaining bits of the current (last) byte, then sets `byte_idx_++` and `bit_idx_ = 0`, and loops again. On that next iteration `byte_idx_ >= data_.size()` is caught before dereferencing — but only if the check re-runs. It does re-run at the top of the while loop, so the raw `data_[byte_idx_]` access itself is protected. However, the deeper issue: the failure mode returns the magic value `257` (EOD) mid-stream, which the caller treats as a clean end-of-data signal. When a malformed/truncated LZW stream causes an early `return 257`, `lzw_decode` silently stops producing output rather than reporting an error, so truncated/malicious data yields a partially-decoded buffer without raising an exception. This is a correctness/robustness gap rather than memory corruption, but combined with the next point it matters.

2. `(1 << bits_to_take)` at line 307 when `bits_to_take == 8`: `1 << 8` is fine (256). But `(1 << bits_to_take) - 1` where bits_to_take can be up to 8 only produces an 8-bit mask correctly (byte shift of uint8_t mask; `mask = (1 << 8) - 1 = 255`). bits_to_take is `std::min(bits_needed, bits_available)` and bits_available <= 8, so 8 is the max — OK. The `val = (val << bits_to_take)` uses uint32_t, and read_bits is only ever called with code_size up to 12, so no overflow. Net: no memory corruption found, but the EOD-return-257 mid-stream silent truncation is a robustness/security-adjacent issue worth flagging as low, plus the use of a magic constant for end-of-data colliding with the LZW 'clear'/EOD code space is fragile.
items.proposed_fix: Return a separate error signal (exception/thrown on truncated stream) instead of the magic constant 257 when data is exhausted mid-request; validate remaining input before the loop so truncated LZW streams produce an error rather than a silent, possibly partial decode. Use an enum for EOD/CLEAR rather than magic numbers.
items.summary: LZWBitReader returns magic 257 (EOD) on truncated input, silently truncating malformed LZW decode

items.description:
The zlib decompression fallback block (lines 433-454) contains fragile/dangerous logic:

1. On the first inflate pass failing to reach Z_STREAM_END, if `fmt == "zlib"`, it calls `inflateInit2(&zs, -15)` again on the SAME z_stream (`zs`) that was already passed to `inflateEnd(&zs)` at line 432. Re-using the same z_stream struct for a second inflateInit2 after deflateEnd is documented as valid (inflateInit2 re-initializes the stream), BUT the code does `memset(&zs, 0, sizeof(zs))` first (line 435) which is correct before the second init. OK. However, if this second attempt ALSO fails, `inflateEnd(&zs)` is called on line 448 inside that block — fine. But if `inflateInit2(&zs, -15)` at line 436 returns NOT Z_OK (allocation failure), the code does NOT call inflateEnd (nothing initialized) — acceptable. Net: no leak here.

2. Real issue: `inflate(&zs, 0)` with `Z_NO_FLUSH` on a stream where `avail_out` becomes 0 without reaching Z_STREAM_END returns Z_BUF_ERROR, NOT Z_OK, so the `do/while(ret==Z_OK)` loop exits on Z_BUF_ERROR with a partially-produced `result` that is then returned as if it were a valid full decompression (because the code only throws when `result.empty()`). A truncated/corrupt gzip/zlib payload therefore returns a silent partial decompression to the AI agent with no error, which the agent may then treat as authoritative content. This is a correctness issue with security implications (agent acting on truncated data).

3. The `windowBits = format == "gzip" ? 15+16 : 15` combined with a second brute-force attempt with `-15` (raw deflate) means it silently tries multiple interpretations; combined with "auto" detection using only the first magic byte `0x78` for zlib, a raw-deflate stream starting with 0x78 will be misrouted. Fragile format handling overall.

Recommendation: check `ret` for Z_BUF_ERROR/Z_DATA_ERROR in decompression loops and throw on incomplete streams; only accept Z_STREAM_END as success for zlib/gzip.
items.proposed_fix: Distinguish Z_OK/Z_STREAM_END from Z_BUF_ERROR/Z_DATA_ERROR in the inflate loop; throw an error when the stream does not reach Z_STREAM_END instead of returning a partial buffer. Remove the ambiguous double-inflate-with-different-windowBits fallback or gate it behind an explicit format flag.
items.summary: inflate loop returns silent partial decompression on truncated/corrupt zlib/gzip streams (Z_BUF_ERROR treated as success)

items.description: In elf_hex_highlighter::parse(), the section symbol-table loop bounds-checks each entry with `if (sym_start + symtab_entsize > data.size()) break;` (line 494) and then only calls bounds-checked read_u32/read_u64 helpers. However, the lines `st_info = data[sym_start + 4];` (64-bit, line 505) and `st_info = data[sym_start + 12];` / `read_u16(data, sym_start + 14)` (32-bit, lines 513-514) access the buffer DIRECTLY with no bounds check. Because `symtab_entsize` is attacker-controlled (read from the ELF section header) and can be smaller than the real record size (24 for 64-bit, 16 for 32-bit), a crafted ELF can set entsize so that `sym_start + symtab_entsize <= data.size()` passes while `data[sym_start + 12]` lies past the end of the buffer, producing a heap out-of-bounds read. This parser is fed raw, untrusted ELF bytes by elf_list_symbols_tool::execute() (elf_list_symbols_entry.cpp line 48) and elf_list_sections_tool::execute(), so this is reachable from the agent toolcall surface. Fix: use bounds-checked reads (read_u16/read_u32/read_u64) for ALL field accesses, and tighten the guard to require `sym_start + (is_64 ? 24 : 16) <= data.size()`.
items.proposed_fix: Replace direct data[] access with a bounds-checked helper, and strengthen the loop guard to `if (sym_start + (header_.is_64 ? 24 : 16) > data.size()) break;` so all field accesses remain within the buffer regardless of symtab_entsize.
items.summary: Out-of-bounds byte read in ELF symbol parser reachable from elf_list_symbols tool with crafted ELF

items.description: Temporary .s/.o/.bin files are named using only `std::random_device` + `mt19937` over a 6-digit uniform_int_distribution (100000-999999, ~900k possibilities) and are written directly into project_root/build (or '.') with `std::ofstream out(s_file)`. This is not a cryptographically strong name and does not use exclusive/open-with-O_EXCL creation, so it is vulnerable to symlink attacks and TOCTOU races: a concurrent process (or another agent/worker sharing the build dir) could pre-create a symlink or matching file at the predicted path to hijack the write or swap the file before it is passed to `as`/`objcopy`. Additionally, files are only cleaned up on a few success/error paths; because cleanup is not exception-safe (RAII), an exception (e.g. bad_alloc) or an early failure leaks the files. Recommend creating temp files via a secure temp facility (std::filesystem::temp_directory_path + unique random names, or open with O_EXCL), and use an RAII guard (scope_guard/destructor) to guarantee cleanup on all exit paths.
items.proposed_fix: Generate temp paths with high-entropy/secure randomness and exclusive creation (O_EXCL), place them in an isolated per-invocation temp directory, and wrap cleanup in an RAII guard that removes all temp files on every exit path.
items.summary: x86_assemble uses predictable 6-digit random temp filenames created directly in the project build dir (symlink/TOCTOU, no secure temp, no RAII cleanup)

items.description: The commands `as {} -o {} {}` and `objcopy -O binary -j .text {} {}` are built with std::format and passed to fs_utils::execute_command_sync(), which executes the string via a shell (popen + ` 2>&1`). The project provides a SECURE-BY-DESIGN formatted execution path (command_runner::execute / execute_and_get_output + fs_utils::format_command / escape_arg / escape_shell_arg) that automatically shell-escapes placeholder args to prevent command injection, but this tool bypasses it and hand-concatenates. Today the interpolated values (as_flag, o_file, s_file, bin_file) are internally derived and not directly user-controlled, so there is no immediate injection; however this is a fragile anti-pattern: any future refactor that interpolates a user/LLM-derived value (e.g. a filename or flag) here silently becomes a command-injection hole. Recommend building the command with the escaping-aware execute() override (pass args as placeholders) or, better, invoking as/objcopy exec-style without a shell.
items.line_content: std::string as_cmd = std::format("as {} -o {} {}", as_flag, o_file, s_file);
items.proposed_fix: Use the shell-escaping formatted execute() overload (``execute("as {} -o {} {}", as_flag, o_file, s_file)``) or invoke the assembler via exec-family without a shell, so interpolated values can never introduce shell metacharacters.
items.summary: x86_assemble builds shell commands via std::format string interpolation and runs them through popen without the project's shell-escaping mechanism

items.description: In both elf_list_sections_entry.cpp (sec.name, line 65) and elf_list_symbols_entry.cpp (sym.name, line 76), untrusted strings read from the parsed ELF file are concatenated directly into markdown table rows without escaping `|` or newlines. A crafted ELF with symbol/section names containing `|`, newlines, or other markdown metacharacters can break the table structure or inject arbitrary markdown/rows into the tool result that is fed back to the LLM (prompt/context injection). The requested_path argument is likewise echoed unescaped into the result header and into set_success/set_failure messages. Note the x86_disassemble tool already escapes `|` (escaped_instr), so this is an inconsistency that indicates escaping is the intended practice. Fix: escape `|`, newlines, and backslashes for all file-derived and argument-derived strings before embedding them in table output, and sanitize the path echoed into messages.
items.proposed_fix: Apply a table-escaping helper (escape `|`, `\n`, `\r`, `\`) to sec.name / sym.name and to the echoed requested_path before interpolating into output, mirroring the escaping already present in x86_disassemble.
items.summary: File-derived section/symbol names and the requested path are echoed into markdown tables without escaping (table/markdown injection into agent context)

items.description:
Several resource-safety issues in the input-resolution layer:

1. Unbounded memory amplification on `input_data`: `resolve_input_data` decodes base64 (`fs_utils::base64_decode`, lines 53 and 116) and hex (lines 104-107) fields into full vectors with no size limit. `input_data` is an attacker/agent-controlled string from the JSON tool args; a large `input_data` (e.g. multi-MB hex/base64 in a single tool call) forces multi-MB allocations before any decompression even starts. Combined with the decompression-bomb finding, this multiplies the OOM surface. There is no cap on `input_data` length in either validator.

2. `read_file` (lines 30-46) with `length < 0` computes `length = file.tellg() - offset` and then allocates `std::vector<uint8_t> data(length)` (line 42), reading an ENTIRE file into memory with no size cap. A tool call referencing a large binary file (or an absolute path via the sandbox bypass) reads the whole file into RAM. No maximum-file-size guard exists.

3. Exception swallowing: `resolve_input_data` catches all exceptions with `catch (...) {}` (lines 90, 121) and silently falls through to the next interpretation attempt. This means a partially-decoded or failed base64/hex attempt silently degrades to treating the raw string as a literal (line 124), which can mis-handle data gracefully but also can mask real errors. More importantly it makes it harder to force-catch invalid binary payloads.

Recommendation: cap `input_data` length in the validators, cap decoded/read buffer sizes in resolve functions, and return/throw explicit errors instead of bare `catch(...){}`.
items.proposed_fix: Add maximum length limits for input_data (validator) and for read/decode buffer sizes in resolve_*; avoid bare catch(...){} — catch and rethrow descriptive errors; prevent reading arbitrarily large files (cap by a max-bytes constant or stream incrementally).
items.summary: Unbounded input_data decode and whole-file read allocations; silent catch(...){} masks errors

items.description: Both `data_compress_tool::execute` (lines 18-35) and `data_decompress_tool::execute` (lines 16-36) catch `std::exception` and return the raw `e.what()` string to the agent/user. Because the decompression/format parsers accept attacker-controlled input, `e.what()` may embed the untrusted input (e.g. `""` + path in resolve_input_file's error: `"Could not find or read input file: " + input_file`, and `"Unsupported or unavailable decompression format: " + format`, and ASCII85 invalid-character exceptions). This reflects attacker-controlled data back to the LLM/user and could carry control characters or be used to confuse prompt routing. Severity low, but worth sanitizing. Also, `set_failure` is called but the code then returns a separate string (rather than a structured failure JSON), so callers may not reliably see the failure state. This is minor UX/robustness, not memory safety.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize/limit error strings before returning them; return a structured failure result instead of the raw exception message; avoid embedding untrusted input verbatim in error messages.
items.summary: Raw exception messages (may embed attacker-controlled input) returned to agent; failure state not structured

items.description: In elf_list_sections_entry.cpp, elf_list_symbols_entry.cpp (and elf.cpp parse), the whole file is slurped into an in-memory std::vector<uint8_t> with `std::vector<uint8_t> bytes(size)` after `tellg()`, with no upper bound on size. An attacker targeting the tool could cause a nominally small file to be expanded (or pass a file whose reported size is enormous), forcing a huge contiguous allocation and wasting memory. More importantly, the entry/security wrappers permit the LLM agent to pass an arbitrary `path` (validated only for read access against the fs_security manager); if the pipeline is pointed at a mount point or special file (e.g. /proc/..., a sparse file, or FUSE/network filesystem), this can cause pathological memory usage or blocking reads. There is no size cap (e.g. reject files > a few MB) and no low-memory handling. Recommend imposing an explicit maximum input size before allocating, and handling the partial/failed read robustly (note the code already guards `size > 0` for the read but still allocates `size` bytes).
items.proposed_fix: Cap the number of bytes read to a bounded maximum (e.g. 64 MB) before allocation, and fail cleanly when the file exceeds the limit, rather than allocating unbounded vector of file size.
items.summary: ELF tools allocate unbounded memory sized by file length with no size cap or file-type guard

items.description: elf_list_symbols accepts a user/LLM-supplied `pattern` and compiles it as a regular expression via re2::RE2 (elf_list_symbols_entry.cpp line 58). Although RE2 is safe against catastrophic backtracking/ReDoS by design (linear time, no backreferences), the input is a full regex accepted without any length or complexity limit, and it is applied as a PartialMatch to every symbol name in the table up to 200 matches. A pathological pattern combined with a large symbol table could still be wasteful, and the validator does not pre-validate the regex (invalid patterns are only detected at execute time). Recommend validating/compiling the pattern in the validator (or limiting pattern length / applying a whitelist to plain-substring mode) and documenting that the pattern is a regex. Low severity because RE2 is ReDoS-safe.
items.proposed_fix: Validate/compile the regex during arg validation (report errors early) and impose a max pattern length; optionally add a 'substring' (literal) mode to avoid treating the pattern as a full regex when not intended.
items.summary: Unbounded user regex pattern in elf_list_symbols is only validated at execute time (RE2 is ReDoS-safe, so low severity)

items.description: x86_assemble writes the raw `args_.instruction` string directly into the temporary .s source file (line 59) which is then piped to the system `as` assembler. `as` is not a shell, and instruction content cannot escape into shell execution by itself; however the tool relies on `as`'s text input for security. Since this runs on a real host toolchain via the sandboxed command runner, the risk is primarily that a malicious instruction string could produce unexpected assembler directives/behaviors, and that there is no length limit on `instruction` (a huge instruction string will be written to disk and processed). Also, the temporary .o/.bin files are produced inside the project build directory; combined with the predictable temp filename this lets a local actor influence the files consumed by `as`/`objcopy`. Recommend limiting the instruction length and asserting the instruction only contains assembly-language characters (rejecting metacharacters) before writing it to the temp source.
items.proposed_fix: Bound the instruction length and reject instruction strings containing non-assembly characters (e.g. `|`, `;`, newlines) before writing to the temp .s file.
items.summary: Unbounded/unfiltered assembly instruction string written to temp source and fed to the system assembler

items.description: In elf_list_sections_tool::execute (line 65), `sec.name` is read from the untrusted ELF file and concatenated into a markdown table row without escaping `|`, newlines, or backslashes (the same issue recorded for elf_list_symbols at line 76). A crafted ELF can place a malicious section name containing `|`, `\n`, or other markdown metacharacters into the section header string table, breaking the table or injecting arbitrary markdown/rows into the tool result returned to the LLM (prompt/context injection). The `requested_path` is also echoed unescaped. Recommend escaping table cell delimiters and control characters for all file-derived strings before formatting them into output.
items.line_content: result += std::format("| {} | {} | 0x{:X} | 0x{:X} | {} |\n", sec.index, sec.name, sec.offset, sec.size, sem_desc);
items.proposed_fix: Escape `|`, `\n`, `\r`, and `\` in sec.name (and requested_path) before interpolating into the markdown table, using a shared escaping helper consistent with the one already present in x86_disassemble.
items.summary: ELF section names embedded unescaped in markdown table (table/markdown injection into agent context)

items.description: In x86_disassemble_tool::execute (line 153-191), the disassembly loop only checks `length` after a successful Zydis decode; on the failure path it forces `length = 1`, which guarantees forward progress. This is mostly safe because a `ZYAN_SUCCESS` Zydis decode always reports a non-zero instruction length. However, there is no defensive assertion that a successful decode produced `length >= 1`; if Zydis ever returned 0 (e.g. an odd decoder state or a future version regression), the loop would fail to advance `offset` and spin forever, exhausting the agent's context/CPU with no cap on bytes. Recommend adding a defensive `if (length == 0) length = 1;` (or a `break`) guard after decoding to guarantee forward progress, and optionally capping the total number of instructions.
items.proposed_fix: After a successful Zydis decode, guard `if (length == 0) length = 1;` to guarantee the offset always advances and the loop cannot spin indefinitely.
items.summary: No defensive guard against zero-length disassembly preventing potential infinite loop

items.description: Several DOM traversal functions recurse over the entire document tree with no depth limit: walk_node (line 254), collect_rows (58), collect_cells (76), find_tables_local (543), and return/child recursion throughout. The same unbounded recursion pattern exists in html_extract_tables_tool.cpp traverse_dom (157), html_list_links_tool.cpp find_links (39), and html_list_images_tool.cpp find_images (39). These are reachable from two untrusted paths: (1) the extract/list tools read arbitrary files supplied to the agent, and (2) the html_to_markdown / html_extract_tables filters applied directly to content fetched from the network via web_fetch (web_fetch_security.cpp applies the html_to_markdown filter). A maliciously crafted, deeply nested HTML document (e.g. millions of nested <div> elements) will drive the recursive call stack past its limit and crash the process — a denial of service. Recommended fix: impose an explicit traversal depth/iteration budget (cap on recursion depth and total visited nodes), bail out gracefully once exceeded, and reject or truncate pathological inputs.
items.line_content: void walk_node(lxb_html_document_t *document, lxb_dom_node_t *node, std::string &out, bool rich, int &list_depth,
items.proposed_fix: Add a depth counter (e.g. int depth, max ~512) and a total-node/iteration budget to all recursive walkers; return early without recursive descent once the limit is reached. Alternatively convert to an explicit iterative traversal with a bounded work queue. Apply the same guard to the filter-registered convert_to_markdown/extract_tables paths since they accept untrusted network content.
items.summary: Unbounded recursion in DOM traversal can cause stack exhaustion (DoS) on untrusted HTML

items.description: plugin.cpp registers three content filters (html_to_markdown, html_to_markdown_plain, html_extract_tables) that take an arbitrary std::string input and return a Markdown string with NO size limit on either the input or the produced output. These filters are applied to network-fetched content (see web_fetch_security.cpp which references the html_to_markdown filter), so a large or repetitive remote document (tables, links, text) can produce a multi-megabyte block injected straight into the model's context window, exhausting context and wasting tokens/compute. The 5MB input guard that exists in the four *_validator.cpp tools does NOT apply to this filter path at all, so the filter path is entirely unguarded. Even the tool path only caps input size (5MB) but returns the fully expanded Markdown with no output cap. Recommend capping both filter input size and the size of the returned Markdown, and truncating with a clear notice when exceeded.
items.proposed_fix: Enforce an input size limit (consistent with the 5MB tool limit) and an output byte/token cap inside convert_to_markdown/extract_tables (or at the filter-registration wrapper), truncating the result and appending a '...[truncated at N bytes]' marker rather than returning unbounded content into the model context.
items.summary: No output/context size cap: filters and tools can flood the LLM context with unbounded conversion results

items.description: convert_to_markdown reads the entire input file into memory with no size guard at parse time and no cap on the produced output. The tool validators do enforce a 5MB input cap upstream (html_extract_text_validator), but the html_to_markdown / html_extract_tables FILTER path registered in plugin.cpp bypasses those validators entirely: editor.cpp auto-applies the html_to_markdown filter to any fetched document detected as HTML (likely originating from network/web_fetch), and web_fetch_security.cpp references the html_to_markdown filter for returned content. A very large or deeply nested remote document can cause multi-hundred-MB allocations in the recursive walkers (e.g. repeated list indentation / heading strings), risking OOM. Recommend validating/capping input size at the parse boundary in convert_to_markdown/extract_tables and bounding the amount of output produced, rather than relying only on the separate tool validators.
items.proposed_fix: Add an input-size guard at the top of convert_to_markdown() and extract_tables() (reject/truncate above a cap, same as the 5MB tool limit) and enforce a total-output byte budget during traversal so adversarial documents cannot trigger oversized allocations in the recursive walkers.
items.summary: Unbounded memory consumption on large/long-tail documents via the filter path (bypasses 5MB tool-limit guard)

items.description: In the link rendering path (html_extract_text_tool.cpp), href values are inserted into the output Markdown as '[' + link_text + '](' + href + ')' with no sanitization/validation of the URL aside from prepending 'https:' for protocol-relative URLs. Raw attribute bytes (which are untrusted, coming from the document being parsed) are copied verbatim into the returned string. This can inject arbitrary characters into the Markdown/tool output that is fed to the model and the rest of the system: crafted href values (e.g. containing ')', newlines, backticks, or ']'/'[' sequences) can break out of the link syntax, produce malformed/confusing output, or smuggle content that misleads the model (context/prompt-injection vector via link text or URLs). Additionally, there is no scheme allow-listing: javascript:, data:, vbscript:, file: links are passed through as-is, and URLs starting with '/' are silently prefixed with base_url, which itself comes from an untrusted <base href> element in the document (extract_base_url reads it directly). A malicious document can set <base href> to an attacker-controlled host and rewrite all relative links to point there. Recommend validating/normalizing the scheme, stripping control characters, escaping Markdown-special characters in href and link text, and not trusting <base href> from untrusted documents.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize href and link_text before embedding (strip NUL/control chars, escape Markdown specials), reject or neutralize dangerous schemes (javascript:, data:, vbscript:, file:), and disregard <base href> values from untrusted documents (or only honor it when the document's own scheme/host is known and trusted).
items.summary: Unsantized href/link output allows Markdown break-out and malicious scheme/URL injection

items.description: extract_base_url (line 191) runs a full-document lxb_dom_elements_by_tag_name() search for 'base' then, on miss, a second full-document search for 'link' elements, iterating every matched node. Combined with the unbounded, recursion-heavy walkers in the same tool (see separate finding), a large document triggers O(num_nodes) collection allocations plus O(num_nodes) text-content extraction for every table/cell, on top of the memory already held by the lexbor DOM. Since this runs on untrusted content (files or network-fetched docs via the filter path), this contributes to CPU/allocator resource exhaustion. Recommend capping the document size before parsing and bounding per-document node processing rather than unbounded full-tree searches.
items.proposed_fix: Guard document size prior to parsing (reject oversized inputs) and limit the number of nodes touched in extract_base_url and the walkers so pathological documents fail fast instead of exhausting CPU/memory.
items.summary: Full-tree ::elements_by_tag_name searches and per-node allocation on untrusted documents add CPU/allocation pressure (resource-exhaustion amplification)

items.description: The primary claim — that the forward-declared register/unregister_* symbols lack a linkage guarantee and could be missing from the build — is incorrect. src/plugins/meson.build (lines 73-83) lists all four *_validator.cpp files (html_extract_tables_validator.cpp, html_list_links_validator.cpp, html_list_images_validator.cpp, html_extract_text_validator.cpp) in the html_plugin shared_module target, and each defines its corresponding register_*/unregister_* symbol. So the symbols are reliably compiled and linked into the plugin binary; there is no missing/renamed symbol risk in the current build. The secondary observation about registration-failure handling (plugin_run() does not check return values of register_* / register_filter calls and could fail silently) is a valid but minor robustness/maintainability point, not a defect in the current linkage.
items.proposed_fix: Ensure all six register/unregister_* symbols are compiled and linked (add *_validator.cpp files to the plugin target in meson.build / src/meson.build as needed), and have plugin_run() verify each tool/filter registration succeeded, surfacing a clear error on failure rather than failing silently.
items.summary: plugin.cpp relies on forward-declared register/unregister symbols with no linkage guarantee or registration-failure handling

items.description: `image_rotate` reads `args_.safe_path` directly into `Magick::Image img(args_.safe_path)` and fully trusts it. `safe_path` is produced by `image_rotate_validator::resolve_image_uri()` which passes the user-controlled `name` argument straight into `image_manager::resolve_uri()`. That resolver takes the URI substring after `images://by-sha256/` verbatim (no check that it is a 64-char lowercase hex SHA-256) and joins it with the cache dir: `std::filesystem::path(get_cache_dir()) / target_hash`. A crafted name such as `images://by-sha256/../../../../etc/passwd` (or similar `..` traversal) escapes the image cache directory and can point ImageMagick at arbitrary readable files on disk, which are then decoded. This completely bypasses the `ctx.fs_security.validate_access()` allowlist/ignore controls that the image_import and image_export tools DO use, so the agent (or a malicious prompt) can read arbitrary local files. Mitigation: validate that the `images://by-sha256/` hash component is exactly `[0-9a-f]{64}` before joining; reject any `..` or non-hex components; and/or re-run the resolved path through `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(..., access_type::read, ...)`.
items.proposed_fix: In `image_manager::resolve_uri()` (and/or the rotate/threshold validators), strictly validate the `by-sha256/<hash>` component is a 64-char lowercase hex string and reject any path containing `..` or path separators. Additionally, have the tool re-validate the resolved path with `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(safe_path, agentlib::access_type::read, resolved, out_error)` before opening it with ImageMagick.
items.summary: Path traversal / arbitrary file read: rotate tool reads untrusted resolved path via user-controlled 'name' without sandbox validation

items.description: Same issue as image_rotate: `image_threshold_tool::execute` reads `args_.safe_path` into `Magick::Image img(args_.safe_path)` trusting a path derived from the user-controlled `name` parameter through `image_manager::resolve_uri()`. `resolve_uri` concatenates the raw substring after `images://by-sha256/` onto the cache directory with no verification that it is a 64-char hex hash, so `..` traversal can escape the cache and point ImageMagick at arbitrary readable files. This bypasses the `fs_security.validate_access` allowlist used by import/export. Fix by validating the hash component (exactly `[0-9a-f]{64}`, no path separators / `..`) and/or re-checking the resolved path through `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(..., access_type::read, ...)`.
items.proposed_fix: Validate the `images://by-sha256/<hash>` URI form strictly (64-char lowercase hex, reject `..` and separators) in `resolve_uri`/validators, and re-validate the resolved `safe_path` via `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(..., access_type::read, ...)` before opening with ImageMagick.
items.summary: Path traversal / arbitrary file read: threshold tool reads untrusted resolved path without sandbox validation

items.description: `generate_image_thumbnail_json` reads an arbitrary user-supplied `path` directly into `image.read(path)` with no sandbox validation and no handling of `ctx.fs_security`. The `path` comes straight from the attacker/agent-controlled JSON. There is no check that the path is within the allowed workspace, no ignore-list enforcement, and no `fs_security.validate_access(...)` call. The image_thumbnail filter is registered for the "image" family and can be triggered with any path, enabling arbitrary file reads on the host (decoded/exfiltrated via the returned thumbnail JSON). Even though the function returns "{}" on exception, the file is still read and decoded by ImageMagick before that. The `image` family tools should go through the same `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(..., access_type::read, ...)` gate used by image_import. Mitigation: pass the tool_context into the filter callback (or otherwise register it with the seccomp/sandbox enforcement) and validate the path before opening.
items.proposed_fix: Validate `path` through the sandbox/allowlist (e.g. `ctx.fs_security.validate_access`) before calling `image.read(path)`, so only paths inside the allowed workspace can be read. Reject absolute/escaping paths, and reject non-existent or ignored files.
items.summary: Arbitrary file read: image_thumbnail filter reads user-supplied 'path' with no sandbox validation

items.description: In `generate_image_thumbnail_json`, `width` and `height` are taken directly from the user JSON with no upper bound, only a `<= 0` check. The function then allocates `pixeldata(req_height, std::vector<temp_pixel_data>(req_width))` where `req_width = width*2` and `req_height = height*2`. A malicious or accidental request for very large dimensions (e.g. width=100000, height=100000 => 4e10 temp_pixel_data cells, each 32 bytes => ~1.28 TB) causes an unbounded heap allocation → memory exhaustion / DoS. Additionally, `image.read(path)` decodes the full source image with no bandwidth/pixel/resource limits configured, so a crafted decompression-bomb image (e.g. a small PNG that expands to enormous pixel dimensions, or a malicious MJPG/compressed format) inflates into unbounded memory/CPU. Both are decompression-bomb style resource exhaustion. Mitigation: impose a hard upper bound on width/height (e.g. reject anything above a sane NxN), cap the resulting pixeldata allocation, and configure ImageMagick resource limits (magick_resource_limit / pixel cache, image width/height, area, timeout) before decoding.
items.proposed_fix: Add upper-bound validation: reject width/height above a configurable cap (e.g. 4096) before allocation, guard the size of `pixeldata` (`req_width * req_height * sizeof(temp_pixel_data)`), and set ImageMagick resource limits (e.g. `Magick::ResourceLimits::width/height/area/memory/time`) before decoding the image to defeat decompression bombs.
items.summary: Unbounded allocation / decompression bomb in image_thumbnail (no dimension cap, no ImageMagick resource limits)

items.description: The extracted href (links tool) and src (images tool) values are inserted into Markdown output raw, only passing through sanitize_value() which escapes pipe `|` and normalizes whitespace. It does NOT escape/close the Markdown table cell structure, escape backticks, `[]()`, or newline-derived cell injection. A malicious HTML file can craft an `href`/`src` attribute (or `alt` text) containing `|` already escaped but more importantly content designed to break out of the table or inject Markdown/HTML such as `[](javascript:)` or raw HTML tokens. Because these tools are AI-agent toolcalls whose output is fed into LLM context, this allows prompt/context injection: an attacker-controlled HTML file can embed instructions that get interpreted by the LLM as new directives. The same sanitize_cell weakness exists in html_extract_tables_tool.cpp and html_extract_text_tool.cpp (process_table).
items.proposed_fix: Escape Markdown control characters (backslash, backtick, `[`, `]`, `(`, `)`, `*`, `_`, `<`, `>`) in cell/href/src content in addition to `|`, and strip or reject `javascript:`/`data:`/`vbscript:` URLs. Consider using a shared HTML-sanitizer utility across all four plugins rather than duplicate per-file functions.
items.summary: Markdown injection via href/src cell content (table/links/images list)

items.description: No validation/filtering is applied to href/src values to block dangerous URL schemes. A malicious HTML page can contain href="javascript:alert(1)" or data:text/html,... or file:// links. While these tools only read files and don't fetch URLs directly, the extracted URLs are returned as tool output that is fed back into the LLM agent prompt. If a downstream tool (or the LLM) is instructed by injected content to navigate/visit these URLs, it could lead to script execution, SSRF, or exfiltration. The link text and URL content originate from untrusted HTML files and should be treated as untrusted input throughout.
items.proposed_fix: Add a URL-scheme allowlist (https/http only, optionally mailto) when emitting links/images, and neutralize or omit javascript:, data:, vbscript:, file: URLs. Apply consistently across list_links, list_images, and extract_text (which also emits hyperlinks).
items.summary: Unrestricted URL scheme injection (javascript:/data:) into LLM context

items.description: Both `image_rotate_tool::execute` and `image_threshold_tool::execute` decode the source image via `Magick::Image img(args_.safe_path)` with no ImageMagick resource limits configured (no pixel cache width/height/area limit, no maximum pixel count, no decode timeout). A malicious/crafted image stored in the VFS (e.g. imported from a URL or local file) could be a decompression bomb (small compressed bytes expanding to enormous pixel dimensions) that exhausts memory and CPU during decode, then again during rotate/adaptiveThreshold. Unlike `image_getdata_tool` (which enforces a byte-size limit), these tools have no resource guard. Mitigation: set `Magick::ResourceLimits` (width, height, area, memory, disk, list-length, timeout) before decoding, and/or enforce a maximum decoded-pixel count.
items.proposed_fix: Before loading, configure ImageMagick resource limits (e.g. `Magick::ResourceLimits::width()`, `height()`, `area()`, `memory()`, `disk()`, `time()`) and reject images whose decoded dimensions exceed a cap, so decompression bombs cannot exhaust memory/CPU during decode or rotate.
items.summary: Decompression-bomb DoS: rotate tool decodes image with no ImageMagick resource limits

items.description: In `image_threshold_tool::execute`, the result message computes `100 - white_pct`. Because `white_pct` is derived from integer rounded counts, `white_pct + (100 - white_pct)` is always 100, which is fine, but the "% white / % black" split can be misleading. More importantly, `static_cast<size_t>(img_w) * static_cast<size_t>(img_h)` for `total_pixels` is computed in size_t after the image is already decoded — but the same decompression-bomb concern applies here as to rotate: `img` is decoded with no resource limits. Additionally, the `(static_cast<double>(row[x].red) / MaxRGB)` conversion per pixel for counting white pixels is O(N) re-scan on top of decode with no cap on image dimensions. Recommend setting ImageMagick resource limits before `img.threshold`/`adaptiveThreshold` acting on a potentially huge image.
items.proposed_fix: Configure ImageMagick decode resource limits (width/height/area/time) before loading the image and cap the decoded pixel count to defeat decompression-bomb memory/CPU exhaustion.
items.summary: Decompression-bomb DoS: threshold tool decodes/processes image with no resource limits

items.description: The size limit is enforced only in the validator (validate_args_impl reads file_size and rejects >5MB). However, the text extraction walk_node function performs deep recursive DOM traversal with unbounded recursion (no depth counter), and the validator performs a TOCTOU check: file_size is checked at validation time, then the tool re-opens and reads the entire file into a std::string in execute() without re-checking size. If the file grows between validation and execution (or a mount/hardlink substitution occurs), arbitrary large HTML can be parsed. Lexbor's document parsing can consume substantial memory for deeply nested adversarial HTML. No output truncation limit exists either, so extracted content (especially with rich links) can be extremely large and flood the LLM context window (context/resource exhaustion).
items.proposed_fix: Re-check and enforce the file size limit inside execute() (not only in the validator) to close the TOCTOU window, add a maximum recursion depth bound to walk_node, and cap the total output/context size returned to the agent.
items.summary: TOCTOU on file-size limit + unbounded recursion/output size

items.description: In html_extract_text_validator.cpp (and similarly in html_extract_tables_validator.cpp, html_list_links_validator.cpp, html_list_images_validator.cpp), the user-supplied `path` is passed directly to validate_access and then file_size() is called on the canonical path. However there is no check that the target is actually a regular file rather than, e.g., a named pipe (FIFO), device node, or special file. std::filesystem::file_size on a FIFO or device returns a small/zero value, passing the 5MB check, but opening it in the tool's execute() (std::ifstream) can block indefinitely (read from a FIFO) or read unbounded streaming data (e.g. /proc, tty), causing resource exhaustion or hangs. Since validate_access canonicalizes and allowlist-checks the path, arbitrary users cannot specify these, but adversarial content within an allowed root (e.g. a fifo or symlink to a special file placed in the workspace) could still trigger this.
items.proposed_fix: Verify std::filesystem::is_regular_file(canonical_path) before accepting, to reject FIFOs/devices/sockets. Also open the file with O_NONBLOCK or stat it to guard against blocking reads on special files.
items.summary: Validators don't reject non-regular files (FIFO/device) -> blocking read risk

items.description: Both rotate and threshold use `image_manager::get_temp_image_path()`, which constructs a temp path from `get_project_tmp_dir()` plus a name based on the system clock timestamp (`"img_tmp_" + time_since_epoch().count() + ".tmp"`). This is a predictable name in a shared scratch directory and is written with a plain `img.write(temp_out)` (rotate/threshold) with no O_EXCL / no pre-created-then-opened-protected file. A local attacker with write access to the tmp dir could pre-create a symlink at the predicted path and redirect `img.write()` to an arbitrary writable file outside the cache (arbitrary file write) or to a file the agent is not meant to touch. Additionally, the cleanup `std::filesystem::remove(temp_path)` is commented out in both `image_manager::ingest_image` and `image_import_entry.cpp`, so temp files are leaked on disk. Mitigation: create temp files with random names opened with O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW, and remove the temp file after ingest.
items.proposed_fix: Generate temporary image output paths securely (random component via `mkstemp`/`O_EXCL`, reject symlinks with `O_NOFOLLOW`), and unlink the temp file after successful ingest (or RAII-scope its lifetime).
items.summary: Predictable temp output filename + symlink risk and leaked temp files (no cleanup)

items.description: The quantization lambda in `generate_image_thumbnail_json` does `static_cast<int>(val)` before `std::clamp(val, 0, 255)` inside `quantize`. If `val` (an averaged R/G/B value) is outside the `int` range or NaN/Inf (possible if `count` is fractional due to the way pixels are weighted, or after division), the `static_cast<int>` of NaN or a huge double is undefined behavior. In practice averaged pixel values stay small, but this is a latent memory-safety/UB concern given the input is attacker-controlled pixel data. Also the integer cast truncates before clamping, and `(int_val + 15) / 32 * 32` is fine. Recommend computing in double and clamping in the double domain before conversion, and guarding division by `count` (already guarded by `cnt <= 0.0` in `get_rgb`, but the accumulate path adds raw pixel values whose `red/green/blue` quantum may be large for non-8-bit depths).
items.proposed_fix: Guard NaN/Inf and range before narrowing: e.g. `double clamped = std::clamp(val, 0.0, 255.0); int int_val = static_cast<int>(clamped);` and handle NaN (`std::isfinite`) explicitly.
items.summary: Potential UB / truncation in quantize() from narrowing cast of untrusted double pixel value

items.description: The html_extract_tables_tool writes output to args_.safe_output_path (which was validated at runtime with validate_access(..., access_type::write)) - this part is reasonably safe. However, the extracted table cell content, captions, and headings from an untrusted HTML file are concatenated into the returned Markdown string and returned either as-is (when no output_path given) or written to a file. In either path the extracted text is untrusted and unescaped beyond pipe/whitespace sanitization. Since the tool is invoked by an LLM agent and output is fed back into context and/or saved as a Markdown artifact that may later be re-read/rendered, malicious cell content can inject Markdown (e.g. tables, links) or HTML that pollutes the agent context (context injection) or the generated artifact. Caption and heading text are inserted with headers (**Table: ...**) without escaping leading markdown characters.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize/escape Markdown control characters in all extracted text (caption, heading, cells) before emission, and consider treating the output as data (e.g. wrapped in a code fence or clearly labeled) to reduce prompt-injection surface when fed back to the LLM.
items.summary: Extracted table output is unescaped Markdown fed into LLM context/artifact

items.description: Duplicate helpers trim(), sanitize_cell()/sanitize_value() are re-implemented identically across html_extract_tables_tool.cpp, html_extract_text_tool.cpp, html_list_links_tool.cpp, and html_list_images_tool.cpp, with slightly diverging behavior over time (e.g. header {{name=...}} tokenization differs elsewhere). Security controls that need to be applied consistently (Markdown escaping, URL scheme filtering) are therefore duplicated and easy to miss in one file, leading to inconsistent sanitization across the plugin family. This is a maintainability concern that directly contributes to the injection issues noted in the other findings.
items.proposed_fix: Extract shared sanitization/escaping utilities into a single html plugin utility module (e.g. html_sanitize.h) used by all four tools, and centralize the hardening logic (Markdown escaping + URL scheme allowlist) there.
items.summary: Duplicated sanitization helpers across HTML plugins cause inconsistent hardening

items.description: In `generate_image_thumbnail_json`, `req_width = width * 2` and `req_height = height * 2` are computed in `int`. If `width`/`height` are large (near INT_MAX/2), the multiplication overflows to a negative value, and the subsequent `std::vector<std::vector<temp_pixel_data>> pixeldata(req_height, std::vector<temp_pixel_data>(req_width))` would attempt a huge/negative-length allocation → std::length_error/`bad_alloc` or, if it does not throw before use, out-of-bounds indexing in the `pixeldata[cY][cX]` access. There is no upper bound preventing this. Combined with the unbounded-dimension finding, require an explicit max dimension cap (well below INT_MAX/2) and compute sizes in `size_t` with an overflow check.
items.proposed_fix: Enforce a maximum width/height (e.g. reject `width > 4096 || height > 4096`), compute `req_width`/`req_height` in `size_t`, and add an explicit overflow/limit check before allocating the `pixeldata` vector.
items.summary: Integer overflow in req_width/req_height allocation arithmetic (no dimension cap)

items.description: In `image_threshold_validator`, `windowWidth` and `windowHeight` are validated only as `> 0`, with no upper bound. `adaptiveThreshold(windowWidth, windowHeight, offset)` uses these as the local neighborhood extent, and a very large window could cause excessive computation/memory in GraphicsMagick's adaptive threshold (and an odd/even/required-constraint unhandled). Recommended: impose a sensible upper bound (e.g. <= image dimension, or a fixed cap like 1024) and reject nonsensical values early. Note the tool itself re-scans every pixel row with `getConstPixels` which is O(N) after decode — combined with a huge window this compounds CPU cost.
items.proposed_fix: Add an upper-bound check on `windowWidth`/`windowHeight` (e.g. reject values > a configurable cap) before they reach `adaptiveThreshold`.
items.summary: Unbounded adaptiveThreshold window size (no upper bound validation)

items.description: In walk_node (html_extract_text_tool.cpp), the base_url used to absolutize relative hrefs is derived entirely from the untrusted HTML itself via extract_base_url(): it reads the `<base href="...">` element or `<link rel="canonical" href="...">`. An attacker who controls the HTML file fully controls base_url. If base_url is set to something like `javascript://` or `data:`, then a relative link `href="/foo"` becomes `[text](javascript://foo)` which is emitted into the LLM context as a JavaScript-protocol link. This amplifies the URL-scheme injection finding: even pages with only relative links can become javascript:/data: links via the attacker-chosen <base> tag. Additionally, extract_base_url's scheme parsing only handles "://" schemes; a base of "javascript:alert(1)" would fall through (no "://") and be returned verbatim.
items.proposed_fix: Treat <base>/<link canonical> as untrusted and do NOT use them to construct URLs that are emitted; or validate the resolved base_url scheme and only allow http/https before prepending. Never emit javascript:/data: URLs even when a malicious <base> tag requests it.
items.summary: Attacker-controlled <base>/canonical URL used to build emitted links -> URL scheme injection amplification

items.description: In html_list_images_tool.cpp the extracted image `src` (img.second) is emitted raw into a Markdown table row. Image src attributes frequently contain `data:` URIs (inline images) which can be arbitrarily large and contain base64-encoded content from the untrusted file. These are inserted verbatim into the tool result that is fed back into the LLM context, providing another vector for injecting large or malicious content into the agent's prompt and potential base64-encoded instruction payloads. Same applies to alt text (img.first) which only gets pipe/whitespace escaping (see the separate Markdown-injection finding).
items.proposed_fix: Filter out or truncate data: URIs and impose a per-value length cap on src/alt before inserting into the output table; treat image src as untrusted context-injectable data.
items.summary: data: image URIs and large alt/src injected verbatim into agent context

items.description: All three validators pass the agent-supplied `path` directly to `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(...)`. In `file_security_manager::validate_access` (src/agentlib/file_security_manager.cpp:125-141), any path containing `://` whose scheme is `file`, `tmp`, or `images` short-circuits and returns `true` WITHOUT checking the allowlist or the ignore patterns (`.ssh`, `.env`, `.aws`, `.gnupg`, etc.). The tool executors then resolve the path via `vfs->get_local_path()`, which the `file_vfs_provider::parse_uri` resolves to an arbitrary absolute path. Concretely, an agent can call hexdump/hexinspect/hexwrite with `path="file:///home/user/.ssh/id_rsa"` (or `file:///etc/passwd`), which resolves to that absolute filesystem path. Because hexwrite requests `access_type::write`, this yields BINARY WRITE capability to sensitive files outside the workspace, completely bypassing the intended allowlist/ignore security boundary. The root cause is in shared code (file_security_manager/virtual_file_system), but these hexedit plugin tools are the direct conduit and must validate/normalize the resolved local path (e.g., re-canonicalize the resolved path and re-run allowlist/ignore checks) before any open for read or write.
items.proposed_fix: Do not trust the raw URI returned by validate_access for file/tmp/images schemes. After building the local path (or before any open/read/write), canonicalize it and re-run the allowlist and ignore-pattern checks (e.g., expose and use the same checks applied to non-scheme paths, or forbid absolute paths from file:// URIs unless they fall within the allowed root). At minimum, reject file:// URIs that resolve outside the project allowlist and deny write for any path matching ignore patterns.
items.summary: file:// URI scheme bypasses allowlist and ignore patterns, enabling arbitrary read/write of sensitive absolute paths

items.description:
The `offset` parameter schema (hexwrite_validator.cpp:30) only enforces `minimum:0` with no upper bound. In execute(), when `start > current_size`, the code computes `pad_size = start - current_size` and allocates `std::vector pad(pad_size, 0)` before writing. A large offset (e.g., close to SIZE_MAX) triggers a huge allocation that can throw std::bad_alloc (uncaught, crashing the agent process) or cause the file to grow to an enormous size (filesystem exhaustion). This is an input-validation/resource-handling gap reachable directly from untrusted agent-provided arguments. Additionally, no cap is placed on the final file size produced by writes.

Risk is somewhat bounded because a human/LLM must supply the offset, but this is exactly the kind of guard that should be enforced in the validator (max offset) and/or by clamping the pad before allocation.
items.line_content:
size_t pad_size = start - current_size;
		std::vector<char> pad(pad_size, 0);
items.proposed_fix: Add an upper bound to `offset` (and optionally to the total written file size) in the validator schema, and/or cap `start` (e.g., reject offsets beyond a sane maximum such as 512MB) before allocating the pad buffer. Also wrap allocation/writes in try/catch for std::bad_alloc.
items.summary: hexwrite unbounded offset causes uncontrolled zero-padding allocation (OOM/DoS)

items.description: In `perform_http_get()` (called from `image_import_tool::execute`), libcurl is configured with `CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION` (line 58). The domain allowlist/blacklist (`allowed_domains.txt`) and the permission prompt are checked once against the *initial* URL's domain only (`extract_domain`, executed before the fetch). Any redirect encountered during the fetch is followed by libcurl WITHOUT re-validating the destination domain against the blocklist or prompting the user. A server on an allowed domain can therefore redirect to an internal address (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data, http://127.0.0.1:port, or other blacklisted domains) and the agent will download it. This is a classic SSRF vector that defeats the allowlist mechanism. Additionally `CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS` is not restricted (default allows most protocols incl. file/gopher), and `CURLOPT_MAXREDIRS` is not bounded. Recommended: set `CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS` to only http/https, set a `CURLOPT_MAXREDIRS` cap, and re-check the resolved (effective) URL's domain against the blocklist/permission prompt before following each redirect (e.g. disable FOLLOWLOCATION and loop manually re-validating each hop), and refuse connections to internal/link-local IPs.
items.proposed_fix: Set CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS to CURLPROTO_HTTP|CURLPROTO_HTTPS, set CURLOPT_MAXREDIRS (e.g. 5), and either disable FOLLOWLOCATION and re-validate each hop's resolved domain/IP against the blocklist before following, or register a CURLOPT_REDIRFUNCTION that enforces the allow/deny rules on every redirect target. Reject redirects to loopback/link-local/private addresses.
items.summary: SSRF via CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION bypasses domain allowlist/blocklist in image_import

items.description: In the `offset_by_name` resolution path of hexwrite execute() (lines 84-113), the file is opened and read fully into `std::vector<uint8_t> file_bytes(file_size)` with NO size cap, unlike hexdump_tool and hexinspect_tool which both enforce a 50MB limit. A large binary file (or a file that has already been grown by prior hexwrite zero-padding) will be loaded entirely into memory each time offset_by_name is used, potentially consuming excessive memory (DoS) on agent-controlled large files. Also, if the file fails to open here (`infile.is_open()` false), the code silently falls through and writes at offset 0, silently ignoring `offset_by_name` — a correctness/robustness issue.
items.proposed_fix: Apply the same 50MB file-size cap used by hexdump/hexinspect before allocating file_bytes, and surface an explicit error if the input file cannot be opened instead of silently proceeding to write at offset 0.
items.summary: hexwrite offset_by_name path reads full file with no size cap; silently ignores offset_by_name on open failure

items.description: hexdump_tool execute() line 141 computes `size_t limit = start + args_.size;`. Both operands are size_t. While `start` is validated to be `< file_data.size()` (<=50MB), `args_.size` has no upper bound in the schema (only `minimum:1`), so a very large size value can overflow the unsigned sum and wrap `limit` to a small value, causing the clamp at line 142-144 to be bypassed and producing garbled/truncated output (row loop iterates from an offset beyond the wrapped limit). There is no out-of-bounds memory access because the loop only reads offsets < limit within the buffer, but the arithmetic should be overflow-safe (e.g., compute `end = min(start + size, file_data.size())` using a checked/guarded addition) to avoid undefined/wrapped behavior.
items.line_content:
size_t limit = start + args_.size;
	if (limit > file_data.size()) {
items.proposed_fix: Guard the addition against overflow, e.g. `size_t limit = (args_.size > file_data.size() - start) ? file_data.size() : start + args_.size;` (or clamp using std::min with overflow checks). Optionally also add an upper bound for `size` in the validator schema.
items.summary: hexdump start+size unsigned integer overflow can bypass the limit clamp

items.description: In hexinspect execute(), structure summaries are written to tmp:// paths synthesized from the requested filename: `"tmp://inspected_structure_" + filename + ".md"` (line 134) and `"tmp://archive_contents_" + filename + ".md"` (line 140), where `filename = filesystem::path(requested_path).filename().string()`. The agent-controlled requested_path's filename component is interpolated into the tmp VFS URI without sanitization. Malicious or surprising filenames (containing '/', '..', or URI-reserved characters) could produce unexpected tmp paths or attempt to escape the intended tmp directory namespace via the memory VFS. Impact is limited to the in-memory tmp scheme, but the filename should be sanitized before embedding in a URI.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize/normalize the filename (e.g., strip path separators, '..', and control characters, or derive it from a validated safe name) before embedding it into the tmp:// URI.
items.summary: hexinspect interpolates unsanitized filename into tmp:// URI for structure summary

items.description: The `data` parameter in hexwrite has no length cap in the validator schema (only `required` and non-empty). `parse_hex_string` decodes the entire string into a byte vector with no limit, and execute() writes the full buffer to the file (line 152) potentially after growing the file with zero padding. An agent can therefore drive unbounded file growth / memory usage on the filesystem with a single call (no size upper bound is enforced anywhere in the write path). Whereas the read tools cap at 50MB, the write tool has no analogous cap on the amount of data it can write or the resulting file size.
items.proposed_fix: Add an upper bound on the allowed data length (and/or maximum resulting file size) in the validator, and reject writes that would exceed it before decoding/allocating the byte buffer.
items.summary: hexwrite data length uncapped -> unbounded memory use and file growth

items.description: In `perform_http_get()` (image_import_entry.cpp lines 39-70), the `write_callback` appends bytes to an unbounded `std::string` with no maximum size cap, and `curl_easy_perform` downloads the entire remote resource into memory. The validator only checks that the URL has an http/https scheme; it does NOT impose any `CURLOPT_MAXFILESIZE` (or `CURLOPT_MAX_RECV_SPEED_LARGE`) limit. Combined with `CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION`, a malicious or redirecting URL can return an arbitrarily large payload (e.g. many GB), leading to unbounded memory growth and an OOM/DoS of the agent process. Additionally, the full downloaded data is later passed to GraphicsMagick `ingest_image`, so an attacker who supplies an enormous remote file can also trigger heavy decode work. Note that the initial resolution happens before any permission check, so this resource exhaustion is reachable once network permission is granted. Recommended: cap the download size (CURLOPT_MAXFILESIZE, e.g. a few hundred MB), enforce a decode-time resource budget, and check the declared Content-Length against the cap before buffering.
items.proposed_fix: Set CURLOPT_MAXFILESIZE_LARGE (e.g. 100MB) and/or CURLOPT_MAX_RECV_SPEED_LARGE + CURLOPT_LOW_SPEED_TIME to bound download size; enforce a write_callback maximum so an oversized body aborts the transfer (return 0 from the callback to abort). Validate the Content-Length header before buffering where available.
items.summary: Unbounded HTTP download into memory (no size cap) → resource-exhaustion/OOM DoS in image_import

items.description:
The `extract_domain()` function (image_import_entry.cpp lines 15-23) uses the regex `^(https?://([^/:]+))` to extract a domain for allowlist/blacklist comparison and for `is_local_ip()` classification (lines 25-37). This parsing is unreliable and can be bypassed:
