1. The regex stops at the first `:` or `/` that is not part of the `https?://` scheme prefix. A URL such as `http://evil.com@127.0.0.1/` would match `evil.com` (the userinfo/authority trick) while libcurl connects to `127.0.0.1`, letting an attacker smuggle an SSRF to localhost under an allowed domain.
2. `is_local_ip()` only checks literal string prefixes (`192.168.`, `10.`, `172.`, `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`). It misses many private/internal targets: `127.0.0.2`-style loopback variants, hex/octal IP encodings (e.g. `0x7f000001`, `0177.0.0.1`), IPv6 loopback variants like `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1`, `[::1]` bracketed forms, link-local `169.254.x.x`, and DNS names that resolve to internal IPs. The blocklist/allowlist and `is_local_ip` decision are all based on this superficial string parsing rather than actual-resolved addresses.
3. The `172.` prefix check is overly broad/reversed logic: it treats *every* 172.x.x.x host as local, which is only partially true (172.16.0.0/12), but more importantly the classification and the allowlist are bypassed by the parsing gaps above.
The result is that even the user-prompt, allowlist, and blocklist protections can be evaded to reach internal hosts. Recommended: resolve the hostname to its actual IP(s) (getaddrinfo) and classify by resolved address ranges, reject non-http(s) userinfo/authority forms, reject URLs whose authority contains '@', and perform the SSRF classification on the *effective* (post-redirect) URL.
items.proposed_fix: Use a strict URL parser, reject URLs containing userinfo with '@', resolve hostnames to IPs and classify by CIDR (loopback, link-local, private RFC1918, IPv6 ULA), and classify the effective post-redirect URL. Optionally leverage an existing SSRF-safe fetch helper if one exists elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. the web_fetch tool) instead of this bespoke parser.
items.summary: Fragile domain regex + incomplete is_local_ip classification enable SSRF to internal hosts

items.description: In `image_getdata_tool::execute`, when `thumbnail` is true, the code decodes the source image with GraphicsMagick (line 65 `Magick::Image img(src_path)`) and renders the *full* source image into memory BEFORE applying any size limit. The size-cap check (`file_size > limit`, lines 99-106) only runs on the on-disk file size and only when `buffer` is still empty (i.e. after the thumbnail path already ran AND filled buffer). Because GraphicsMagick fully decodes the source, a large image (e.g. a 20,000x20,000 PNG, or a decompression-bomb that expands from a tiny file to huge dimensions/pixels) is fully expanded into memory during decode — the ~50KB `limit`/`max_bytes` guard does nothing to bound the decode-work or peak memory during the expensive thumbnail generation. This is a decompression-bomb / resource-exhaustion vector: a small file that decodes to a huge image can consume large amounts of memory/CPU even though the final base64 payload is small. The limit check should be applied to the *source* (reject huge-dimension sources up front based on columns()*rows() or file size) before decoding, and GraphicsMagick resource limits should be enforced. Note also that when the thumbnail decode throws, `buffer` stays empty, the raw file bytes are then read and the size limit IS applied to them — so the raw-file path is bounded, but the thumbnail-decode path is not.
items.proposed_fix: Apply the max_bytes/limit guard to the source file and/or decoded pixel count (img.columns()*img.rows()) BEFORE performing the thumbnail decode, and set GraphicsMagick resource limits (e.g. Magick::ResourceLimits::memory / area) to bound decode memory. Reject sources whose pixel area would exceed a sane cap before zooming.
items.summary: thumbnail decode of source happens before size limit — decompression-bomb / memory DoS in image_getdata

items.description: Every image-modifying tool in this set (image_compose_tool.cpp line 25-26, image_crop_tool.cpp line 25, image_grayscale_tool.cpp line 27, image_mirror_tool.cpp line 25, image_resize_tool.cpp line 25, and by extension rotate/threshold) does `Magick::Image img(args_.safe_path)` and fully decodes the VFS-sourced image into memory with NO GraphicsMagick resource limits configured (no Magick::ResourceLimits::memory, area, width, height, or pixels set). The VFS `ingest_image` path only parses the *header* for PNG/JPEG dimensions — it does not fully decode — so a "decompression bomb" (a small byte file declaring huge dimensions/planes, or a highly-compressed format that expands enormously) can be ingested and registered in the VFS without being caught, and is then fully expanded in memory by any of these modify tools. Because the validated source may be attacker-supplied remote content via image_import, this is a memory-exhaustion/DoS vector. The crash/catch here only handles exceptions after the fact. Recommended: configure GraphicsMagick resource limits (memory, map, area/pixels, and width/height) globally or per tool, and reject images whose declared pixel dimensions exceed a sane cap before decoding.
items.proposed_fix: Set Magick::ResourceLimits (memory, map, area/pixels, width, height) at GraphicsMagick initialization, and/or validate decoded dimensions against a hard cap before processing in each tool. Apply to all image modify tools sharing this pattern.
items.summary: Unbounded GraphicsMagick decode without resource limits → memory-exhaustion on decompression-bomb images

items.description:
Several code paths leak temporary image files that are no longer needed after successful ingestion:
- image_manager::ingest_image (src/images/image_manager.cpp line 359) has `// std::filesystem::remove(temp_path);` commented out.
- image_import_entry.cpp line 233 has `// std::filesystem::remove(temp_out); // Cleanup temp file` commented out.
- Every modify tool (resize/crop/compose/grayscale/mirror/rotate/threshold) calls `get_temp_image_path()` to create a temp file and `ingest_image(temp_out, ...)`, which never removes the source temp file.
`get_temp_image_path()` returns monotonically-increasing timestamp-named files under the project tmp dir (fs_utils.cpp get_project_tmp_dir). Over many tool invocations these files accumulate on disk indefinitely — a disk-space leak. While disk-space exhaustion in a user-writable project dir is a lower-severity concern than in a shared service, it is still unbounded growth driven by agent tool usage. Recommended: use a RAII temp-file guard that removes the file on scope exit (and restore the remove in ingest_image), matching the comment intent.
items.proposed_fix: Implement a RAII scoped temp-path guard (delete-on-destruct) and use it for all temp image files, and un-comment/re-enable the temp removal in image_manager::ingest_image after the copy completes.
items.summary: Temp image files never cleaned up → unbounded disk-space accumulation

items.description: In `image_resize_tool::execute`, the target dimensions are derived directly from agent-controlled inputs without any upper bound: `newX`/`newY` are validated only as `> 0` (image_resize_validator.cpp lines 49-56), and `ratio` is validated only as `> 0.0` (line 57). There is no maximum dimension or pixel-area cap. Execute then computes `target_w = (int)(orig_w * ratio)` (or uses newX/newY directly, which can be up to INT_MAX since they are `int`) and calls `img.zoom(Magick::Geometry(target_w, target_h))` (line 51). Because no GraphicsMagick resource limits are configured, requesting an enormous zoom (e.g. newX=2000000000, or a huge ratio on a large source) forces GraphicsMagick to allocate memory proportional to the target pixel area, which can be on the order of gigabytes to exabytes and cause an OOM crash of the agent process. Recommended: enforce a hard upper bound on target_w/target_h and total pixel count (e.g. reject targets exceeding a few thousand pixels per side or a total-pixel cap), and set GM resource limits.
items.proposed_fix: Validate an upper bound on newX/newY/ratio in the validator (e.g. reject newX/newY > some max like 10000, and ratio beyond a sane max), and cap computed target_w/target_h/total pixels in execute before calling zoom. Also set GraphicsMagick memory/area resource limits.
items.summary: Unbounded zoom target dimensions (newX/newY/ratio) → OOM via huge image allocation in image_resize

items.description: In `image_crop_tool::execute`, the validator (image_crop_validator.cpp) only enforces `width > 0`, `height > 0`, `x >= 0`, `y >= 0`. There is NO check that x+width <= orig_w or y+height <= orig_h. `img.crop(Magick::Geometry(width, height, x, y))` is called at line 34. GraphicsMagick's behavior when the crop rectangle extends beyond image bounds is to clamp to the image — this is handled, and the final `img.page(Geometry(width, height, 0,0))` resets the virtual canvas, so out-of-bounds crop does not cause a memory-safety issue per se. However, the report code at lines 54-56 computes `args_.x + args_.width - 1` as `int` (width/x are `int`). With attacker-controlled large int values (up to INT_MAX), `args_.x + args_.width - 1` can overflow signed int (UB) and produce a bogus/negative reported extent. Similarly `compose_tool` lines 33-44 perform `main_w - args_.x`, `args_.x + placed_w - 1` etc as int math with agent-controlled x/y — an overflow here could mis-branch the boundary check (`args_.x >= main_w` with x near INT_MAX would correctly reject, but other combinations can overflow). Recommend validating x+width/y+height against orig bounds in execute and computing report extents in 64-bit to avoid signed integer overflow (UB).
items.proposed_fix: Validate that x+width <= orig_w and y+height <= orig_h (as int64) in execute before cropping, reject oversized rectangles, and compute all report extents using int64_t arithmetic to prevent signed integer overflow.
items.summary: int overflow in crop report extent and missing x+width bounds check

items.description: In `image_grayscale_tool::execute`, `row[x].red / MaxRGB` (line 43) divides a `Quantum` (unsigned char or 16-bit) by `MaxRGB` (an int constant) and multiplies by 255.0 as a double — that itself is fine, but in `image_threshold_tool.cpp` line 46 the same expression `(static_cast<double>(row[x].red) / MaxRGB) * 255.0 > 127.0` is used for thresholding which is logically acceptable. The more notable issue here is that the average-luminance loop (grayscale lines 38-45) iterates over every pixel (`img_w * img_h`) with `getConstPixels` but the tool does NOT verify the decoded image is within a pixel budget first (same decompression-bomb concern as resize/compose). If the source is a huge image (ingested from an untrusted remote file), the double loop over all pixels is additional CPU cost on top of the unbounded decode. Recommend bounding total pixel count before iterating and before decode (shared with the earlier 'unbounded decode' finding). The grayscale/threshold tools also call `img.getConstPixels(0, y, img_w, 1)` per row which is repeated allocation work; consider `getConstPixels` for the full area. This is a secondary note; the primary risk is the pre-decode bound (see the resize/compose decode finding, which applies across all modify tools).
items.line_content:
for (int y = 0; y < img_h; ++y) {
			const Magick::PixelPacket *row = img.getConstPixels(0, y, img_w, 1);
items.proposed_fix: Enforce a decoded-pixel-count budget before iterating/decoding (shared GM resource limits), and where practical fetch the whole pixel region in a single getConstPixels call rather than per row.
items.summary: Grayscale/threshold full-pixel scan unbounded by pixel budget (performance/DoS on huge images)

items.description: In `image_export_tool::execute`, the VFS-output branch reads the entire source image into memory via `file_content = std::string((istreambuf_iterator<char>(ifs)), istreambuf_iterator<char>())` (lines 73-77, 79-82, 85-89) with NO size bound. The source is a VFS-cache image that was previously imported — and import allows arbitrarily large remote or local images (no max size enforced at ingest). Reading a multi-GB source fully into memory here (and in the getdata raw path) can exhaust process memory. The `max_bytes` limit is only enforced by the standalone image_getdata tool; image_export performs no equivalent cap. Recommend capping the read (e.g. stream/copy in chunks, or reject source files above a threshold), especially since the output must be buffered before `vfs->write_file`.
items.proposed_fix: Enforce a maximum source size before buffering into memory (reject or refuse above a threshold), or stream-copy the file to the destination in bounded chunks instead of loading the whole image into a std::string. Apply the same bound to all unbounded ifstream reads in this file.
items.summary: image_export reads entire (potentially huge) source image into memory with no size cap

items.description: `images::image_manager::get_temp_image_path()` (src/images/image_manager.cpp lines 327-332) returns `img_tmp_<timestamp_nanoseconds>.<ext>.tmp` under the project tmp dir, with no uniqueness guarantee and no cleanup (`// std::filesystem::remove(temp_path);` is commented out at line 359 of ingest_image). Multiple concurrent/quick tool invocations could produce colliding names or leak files. More importantly for security/resource handling, since temp files are never deleted, an agent that repeatedly runs image tools (resize/crop/compose/grayscale/etc.) accumulates one temp file per operation indefinitely. This is a disk-exhaustion vector in addition to being poor hygiene. Recommend using a RAII guard that removes the temp file when the ingestion completes or on scope exit, and guaranteeing uniqueness (e.g. append a random component).
items.proposed_fix: Use a RAII scoped temp-file guard that deletes on destruction, and make the temp name unique (append a monotonic counter or random suffix). Re-enable removal in ingest_image.
items.summary: get_temp_image_path leaks temp files (no cleanup) — disk accumulation across tool calls

items.description: In `image_getdata_validator::validate_args_impl` (line 26), `args_.max_bytes = (parsed.max_bytes > 0) ? parsed.max_bytes : 51200;` accepts ANY positive user-supplied value with no upper bound. An agent (or a prompt-injection from the model) can request an arbitrarily large `max_bytes` (e.g. 2GB), which in the raw-read path at image_getdata_tool.cpp would permit reading and base64-encoding a very large image file into memory/context. The tool is nominally meant to cap returned data at ~50KB, but the cap itself is attacker-controlled. Recommend clamping max_bytes to a fixed upper bound (e.g. min(max_bytes, some maximum like 1MB)) in the validator.
items.proposed_fix: Clamp max_bytes to a safe upper bound (e.g. std::min(parsed.max_bytes, MAX_READ_BYTES)) in the validator so the returned-data limit cannot be arbitrarily inflated.
items.summary: image_getdata max_bytes is unbounded → can be inflated to read/encode very large images

items.description: In `image_import_entry.cpp`'s `perform_http_get` (lines 50-60), libcurl is set up with `CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION`, `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT`, and a user-agent, but **no TLS verification options are intentionally set**, so curl uses its defaults. More importantly there is no `CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS`/`CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS` restriction and no `CURLOPT_MAXREDIRS`. Since `CURLOPT_URL` accepts only http/https per the validator, protocols are nominally limited, but a redirect to a `file://`-style or other scheme could be followed under default redir-protocol settings. Also there is no server certificate pinning/validation override, which is fine (defaults are secure), but the lack of explicit `CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS` to http/https plus unrestricted redirect count weakens the SSRF posture described in the follow-location finding. Recommend explicitly limiting redirect protocols to http/https and capping redirects.
items.proposed_fix: Set CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS to CURLPROTO_HTTP|CURLPROTO_HTTPS and CURLOPT_MAXREDIRS to a small value; consider CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION disabled with manual per-hop domain re-validation.
items.summary: libcurl redirect-protocol not restricted to http/https and redirect count unbounded

items.description: libcurl is configured with CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION=1 and no redirect limit or per-redirect verification. The domain-approval / allowlist mechanism (lines 88-154) only checks the *initial* URL's hostname. After the user approves the top-level domain, a 3xx response can redirect to ANY host — e.g. a public site 302'ing to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (cloud metadata) or http://127.0.0.1:PORT/ (internal service). This is a textbook SSRF-by-open-redirect and completely bypasses the intended "Allow connection to <domain>" authorization boundary. The fetch in perform_http_get() is invoked with the raw URL and follows redirects with no re-check against the allowlist, is_local_ip(), or any resolved-IP validation. Recommendation: disable auto-follow (CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION=0) and implement a manual redirect loop (CURLOPT_HEADERFUNCTION / status code inspection) that validates each hop target against the same domain-approval + IP-blocklist policies before following, or use CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS plus per-redirect SSRF checks.
items.proposed_fix: Set CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION to 0 and implement a bounded manual redirect-following loop that re-runs SSRF/domain checks on every Location header target (validate scheme, resolved IP, allowlist) before issuing the next request. Also set CURLOPT_MAXREDIRS as a defensive cap.
items.summary: SSRF via open redirect: CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION follows redirects to arbitrary internal hosts without re-validation

items.description: write_callback() appends every received chunk to the std::string indefinitely (lines 38-44). There is no CURLOPT_MAXFILESIZE and no callback-side byte counter with an upper bound. A malicious or large server can stream data for the full 30s timeout, exhausting memory (the whole body is buffered even when only the first 20000 chars are returned — truncation at lines 201-204 happens only AFTER the full body is already in memory). When output_path is set, the unbounded buffer is written to disk as well. This is a resource-exhaustion / DoS vector reachable from any URL whose domain was approved. Recommendation: enforce an explicit max download size (e.g. refuse to append beyond a cap, abort the transfer with a clear error) and/or rely on a documented CURLOPT_MAXFILESIZE, and enforce a separate connect timeout.
items.line_content: static size_t write_callback(void *contents, size_t size, size_t nmemb, void *userp)
items.proposed_fix: Add a size limit in write_callback (return 0 / abort when a configured cap like ~20-50 MB is exceeded) and set CURLOPT_MAXFILESIZE. Cap should also be documented in validate_args or the schema. Optionally add CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT distinct from the total CURLOPT_TIMEOUT.
items.summary: No download size cap: unbounded response buffering causes memory/disk exhaustion (DoS)

items.description: The SSRF defense is entirely string-based. is_local_ip() only inspects the domain text (line 24-36) and is used solely to decide which buttons the permission prompt shows — it never influences whether the fetch proceeds. perform_http_get() connects directly to what libcurl resolves, with no check of the resolved address family/range before connecting. This leaves multiple bypasses: (1) DNS names that resolve to internal addresses (e.g. 127.0.0.1.nip.io, localtest.me, intranet hostnames) are treated as "remote"; (2) alternate numeric encodings (2130706433, 0x7f000001, 0177.0.0.1) evade the string checks; (3) DNS rebinding — an attacker can resolve an approved hostname to a public IP during the permission prompt / validation and an internal IP at fetch time, with no re-validation at connect. Because there is no resolve-then-connect pinning, any domain approval is effectively meaningless as an SSRF control. Recommendation: resolve the hostname, reject private/link-local/loopback/metadata ranges from the *resolved* addresses, and re-resolve+re-check immediately before connecting (and per redirect hop) to mitigate rebinding.
items.proposed_fix: Before connecting, resolve the target host and block any resolved address in a private/unroutable/loopback/link-local/metadata range (127.0.0.0/8, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 169.254/16, fc00::/7, fe80::/10, ::1). Re-validate per redirect hop and re-resolve at connect time to mitigate DNS rebinding.
items.summary: SSRF: no resolved-IP validation/DNS-rebinding protection; allowlist and is_local_ip operate only on the raw hostname string

items.description: extract_domain() uses the regex ^https?://([^/:]+) which captures everything up to the first ':' or '/'. It does not strip userinfo or the port. For a URL like http://user:pass@host/ the captured 'domain_' includes "user:pass@host" (and even 'attacker@127.0.0.1' for http://attacker@127.0.0.1/). Because the allowlist match (line 97) and the permission prompt (line 123) are keyed off this malformed domain_, the operator is approving a string that does not correspond to the host actually being connected to. In the attacker@internal-IP case the display leaks the internal address and, if ever saved as an 'A:' allowlist line, grants authorization to an internal target while appearing to be the 'attacker' host. Recommendation: parse the URL properly (e.g. URL-parse library or curl_url API) and use the hostname component alone for authorization, rejecting URLs that contain userinfo credentials.
items.proposed_fix: Use a real URL parser to extract the canonical hostname (excluding userinfo and port) for allowlist/authorization decisions, and reject URLs containing userinfo (user:pass@) outright.
items.summary: extract_domain regex captures userinfo/credentials, allowing authz decision to target the wrong host

items.description: is_local_ip() has multiple correctness issues that undermine its role (however weak) in the SSRF decision: (1) It checks only exact '127.0.0.1' rather than the whole 127.0.0.0/8 loopback block (e.g. 127.0.0.2 is not flagged). (2) It does not flag 169.254.0.0/16 link-local — importantly the AWS/GCP/Azure metadata address 169.254.169.254 — or the IPv6 loopback/link-local/ULA ranges (::1, fe80::/10, fc00::/7). (3) The '172.' prefix check is far too broad: private RFC1918 space is only 172.16.0.0/12, so public addresses such as 172.0.x.x and 172.32.x.x are incorrectly treated as local. (4) Alternate numeric encodings (decimal/hex/octal IP literals) are not recognized. Since this function only alters the permission prompt's available buttons, the practical impact is limited UX/authorization confusion, but it should be corrected to a proper address-range test (ideally on resolved addresses, not the string) if it is to contribute any SSRF signal.
items.proposed_fix: Replace string-prefix heuristics with proper CIDR-based checks on normalized/resolved IPs: loopback 127/8, private 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, link-local 169.254/16, ::1, fe80::/10, fc00::/7. Handle decimal/hex/octal IP literals.
items.summary: is_local_ip() is incomplete and over-broad: misses link-local/metadata and IPv6 private ranges; flags some public 172.x as local

items.description: While validate_args_impl() restricts the *initial* scheme to http/https (web_fetch_security.cpp line 38), the follow-location behavior is not constrained with CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS, so redirect targets are only limited by libcurl's built-in defaults, which historically permit broad protocol sets. There is no explicit restriction preventing a redirect from downgrading https to http (silently losing TLS confidentiality/integrity) or from switching to a non-web scheme. If the fetch target or an intermediary issues a 3xx to such a scheme, it may be followed depending on the linked libcurl configuration. Recommendation: explicitly set CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS to only allow HTTP and HTTPS, and enforce that an https request never silently redirects to http (or at minimum surface a clear warning/error on downgrade).
items.proposed_fix: Set CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS = CURLPROTO_HTTP | CURLPROTO_HTTPS and CURLOPT_PROTOCOLS likewise; detect and reject https->http downgrade in the manual redirect handling.
items.summary: No CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS / protocol restriction; HTTPS->HTTP and scheme-changing redirects are not constrained

items.description: perform_http_get() never explicitly sets CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER or CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST, so certificate verification depends entirely on the linked libcurl build's defaults and the availability of a CA bundle at runtime. In headless/sandboxed environments a CA bundle may be absent, and behavior could silently differ (and some builds disable verification by default). The options should be set explicitly (verify on, verify hostname on) to make TLS posture deterministic, and a failure should be surfaced rather than silently accepted. Note this interacts with the https->http redirect concern above.
items.proposed_fix: Explicitly set CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=1L and CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST=2L, configure/verify a CA bundle path (CURLOPT_CAINFO) for the sandbox environment, and treat TLS verification failure as a hard error.
items.summary: TLS verification relies entirely on libcurl defaults with no explicit configuration or downgrade guard

items.description: The raw fetched body (up to 20000 chars) is wrapped in a fenced block and returned verbatim into the agent's tool-output stream (lines 201-206), and, when a filter is applied, the filtered text is returned as well. Because this content originates from an arbitrary (possibly attacker-controlled) website, it becomes a prompt-injection channel: a hostile page can embed instructions that the LLM may treat as authoritative. This is inherent to the tool's stated purpose (reading docs), but the risk should be acknowledged/documented, and the caller/UI should treat web_fetch output strictly as untrusted data. Consider an explicit prefix indicating the content is untrusted fetched data, and avoid auto-executing extracted directives.
items.proposed_fix: Document that web_fetch output is untrusted attacker-controllable data; consider labeling the returned block as untrusted content and ensure downstream handling (filters, agents) does not treat it as trusted instructions.
items.summary: Fetched web content is returned directly into the LLM context (prompt-injection surface)

items.description: When is_async is enabled the tool launches a detached std::thread (line 208) that, after the command completes, calls `agent->replace_tool_result(...)` and `agent->inject_context(...)` on the shared ai_agent (obtained via weak_agent.lock()). These agent methods are almost certainly part of the main/ui or LLM event loop state and are invoked from a detached worker thread with no synchronization. If replace_tool_result/inject_context mutate shared state (LLM context, tool result storage, queues) without their own locking, this is a genuine data race that can corrupt LLM context or crash the editor. Also, `runner` (terminal_command_runner) is captured by value in the thread and `interaction_` member is shared; get_final_output()/utf8::sanitize runs concurrently with any UI reads of the same terminal_parser state. Recommend: restrict async injection to the main thread event loop (post the completion via the event queue / trigger_ui_update mechanism rather than calling agent methods directly from the worker), and ensure the worker only produces data while agent methods are invoked on the owning thread. At minimum, add a documented threading contract and synchronization for the agent methods invoked here.
items.proposed_fix: Route async command completion back through the main thread. For example, push a completion event carrying (tool_call_id, output, cmd) onto ctx.queue and have the main/editor thread call replace_tool_result()/inject_context() on the owning thread. Keep the worker thread limited to execute() + collecting output.
items.summary: Async worker thread calls agent methods that may not be thread-safe (data race / use-after-release)

items.description: run_shell_command_tool::validate_runtime() ignores its ctx/out_error and always returns true (lines 108-111). The runtime context carries fs_security and the active agent, and is the canonical place to refuse execution (e.g., in paranoid mode when the systemd user bus is unavailable, or when the current agent is not approved for arbitrary shell). Crucially, when ctx.queue is null the execute() path refuses to prompt the user (line 137-139), but validate_runtime() never checks this, so there is no early guarantee that a permission prompt can even happen. Since the tool validator's create_tool_impl and validation gate run in validate_args_impl, the actual runtime approval dialog is only enforced inside execute(). Recommend: implement validate_runtime to verify a permission-prompt pathway is available (non-null ctx.queue) and that the environment genuinely supports sandboxed execution, returning out_error to block execution safely before any side effects occur.
items.proposed_fix: Implement validate_runtime to (1) require a non-null ctx.queue (so user approval can always be requested), (2) enforce paranoid-mode/unsandboxable conditions, and (3) set out_error with a descriptive message instead of unconditionally returning true.
items.summary: validate_runtime always returns true; sandbox/bypass cannot be vetoed and permission gating can be skipped

items.description: Disputed. The crash-catcher LD_PRELOAD mechanism is implemented soundly: build_command (command_runner.cpp:377-378) injects both `-p Environment=LD_PRELOAD=<lib_path>` and `-p Environment=TURBOSTAR_DUMP_DIR=<dir>`, and when the lib dir is outside the project it is made accessible in the sandbox mount namespace via `-p BindReadOnlyPaths`/`-p ReadOnlyPaths` (lines 392-411). The claim that the preload is "silently dropped" is speculative and not substantiated by any demonstrated defect. The described fix (post-hoc verification/telemetry) is a hardening enhancement, not a correction of a confirmed bug.
items.proposed_fix: Add a verification step that confirms libturbocatch.so was actually preloaded inside the sandboxed unit (e.g., check for a cookie/marker or probe within the unit) and emit a warning when it was not, rather than silently assuming crash catching works.
items.summary: Crash-catcher LD_PRELOAD may not be honored inside systemd-run sandbox, weakening crash-catcher guarantee

items.description: The command output returned to the LLM (both sync at lines 238-256 and async at lines 212-230) is taken from runner->get_final_output(), which only applies utf8::sanitize() (terminal_command_runner.h line 92). utf8::sanitize() (utf8.cpp 112-153) only fixes invalid UTF-8 byte sequences; it does NOT strip ANSI escape sequences or control characters. Although the input command is blocked if it contains a literal 0x1b (run_shell_command_security.cpp line 35), a malicious payload does not need the command to contain raw ESC: it can print ANSI/CSI sequences by other means (printf '\\033...', echo -e, a program that emits colors). The captured output is embedded into fenced code blocks injected into the LLM context (line 222/256). A hostile command can therefore inject terminal-control text (or visually misleading 'tool finished' text / fake tool calls) into the agent's context, which is a prompt/analysis injection vector. There exists utf8::sanitize_terminal_output() (utf8.cpp 287-331) that strips ESC-based control sequences, but it is not applied here. Recommend applying sanitize_terminal_output (or equivalent control-character stripping) to the output before returning it to the LLM and before UI display.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize command output with utf8::sanitize_terminal_output() (plus stripping of control chars) before returning it to the LLM in both the sync and async paths.
items.summary: Output returned to the LLM is not ANSI/terminal-sanitized, enabling terminal injection into the agent context

items.description:
fs_replace_content resolves its write target differently than fs_write_file and this creates a sandbox/authorization bypass.

In fs_replace_content_validator::validate_args_impl, the path is passed through ctx.fs_security.validate_access(path, write, ...). In file_security_manager::validate_access, any path containing "://" with scheme "file"/"tmp"/"images" short-circuits at lines 125-131 and is approved UNCONDITIONALLY (out_resolved_path = the requested URI) — the workspace allowlist is never consulted. This is by design for the VFS layer, which is expected to guard writes internally.

In execute_disk_fallback (line 441-445), the tool does NOT go through create_file (which for file_vfs_provider has a project-root containment guard). Instead it calls vfs->is_local_path_available(safe_path) then vfs->get_local_path(safe_path) and opens that local path directly with std::ofstream(..., trunc). file_vfs_provider::get_local_path returns parse_uri(raw_uri) = weakly_canonical(path) with NO containment check.

Consequence: passing path="file:///etc/passwd" (or file:///.. / any absolute local path) is approved by validate_access, get_local_path resolves it to the real absolute filesystem path, and the tool reads+rewrites that file — a write to ANY location the process can write, outside the allowed project root. fs_write_file is protected from this exact vector only because its execute() routes file:// writes through vfs->write_file() -> file_vfs_provider::create_file(), which enforces the project-root traversal guard. fs_replace_content skips that guard.

Recommended fix: for VFS-backed safe_paths, route the write through the provider (vfs->write_file / a guarded writer) exactly as fs_write_file does, or re-run a canonical allowlist check (e.g. verify the resolved local path is within the allowed workspace root) before opening the output stream directly.
items.proposed_fix: Before opening the output ofstream in execute_disk_fallback, re-validate the fully resolved local path against the security allowlist (call ctx.fs_security.validate_access on the resolved path, or reject non-project-root schemes), or write through the VFS provider's guarded create_file like fs_write_file does. Do not open std::ofstream directly on get_local_path() output for file:// scheme.
items.summary: Arbitrary file write via file:// scheme bypasses workspace allowlist in fs_replace_content

items.description:
fs_write_file_raw_args deserializes path/content/append with NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_NON_INTRUSIVE_WITH_DEFAULT, so an absent or non-string/non-present 'content' silently defaults to an empty string. The validator only checks parsed.path.empty() and never validates that 'content' is present, is a string, or is non-empty.

Because fs_write_file_tool::execute() opens the file with mode = std::ios::binary (i.e. std::ios::trunc is implied by default ofstream open) when append==false, calling the tool without 'content' (or with empty content) OVERWRITES an existing file to zero bytes. The JSON schema also does not list 'content' as required (only 'path' is required). This is an unintended destructive write that is easy to trigger from the agent/caller and should be rejected at validation time.

Severity is medium: the write is still constrained to the allowed workspace by validate_access, but the truncation-to-zero on a missing/empty content field is a correctness and safety problem and should be prevented up front.
items.proposed_fix: Validate 'content' in validate_args_impl: require the key is present and is a string; decide whether empty content is permitted (e.g. error on missing key). Also list 'content' in the schema 'required' array. If empty content with append=false is a legitimate "truncate to empty" operation, gate it behind an explicit signal rather than an empty default.
items.summary: fs_write_file validates path but not 'content'; missing content truncates files to zero

items.description:
In fs_replace_content_tool::execute_disk_fallback, multiple size_t->int narrowing conversions on untrusted file sizes can overflow and defeat the scope/limit checks:

1) fallback_find_symbol_range (line 161): `out_end = std::min(static_cast<int>(file_lines.size()), out_start + 120);` — file_lines.size() is size_t cast to int; a file with more than INT_MAX lines would wrap negative. Also line 158 `out_start = static_cast<int>(i + 1)`.

2) In the relaxed-match indent-shift block (lines 601-621), `file_lines[start_line - 1]` is indexed with start_line derived from file_lines.size() (line 595: relaxed_matches are 1-based line numbers from i+1 where i < file_lines.size()). The guard at line 601 checks `start_line >= 1 && start_line <= static_cast<int>(file_lines.size())`, but if file_lines.size() exceeds INT_MAX the cast is negative and the guard is bypassed, leading to an out-of-bounds read on file_lines[start_line-1].

While these are extreme edge cases (files > 2G lines), the intent here is that an LLM-supplied target/line operates on attacker-influenced indices; the size_t->int narrowing is unchecked. Prefer size_t throughout, or validate against SIZE_MAX bounds before casting.

3) start_line negative from line_hint is guarded (validator requires >=1), so the primary risk is the size-related narrowing.
items.proposed_fix: Use size_t for line indices derived from file_lines.size() and validate (e.g. file_lines.size() < INT_MAX) before casting to int, or add an early reject for oversized files.
items.summary: Unchecked size_t->int narrowing on line counts can overflow bounds checks for huge files

items.description:
fs_replace_content_defaults: the tool reads then rewrites the ENTIRE file via an ofstream opened with std::ios::binary | std::ios::trunc in execute_disk_fallback (lines 660-666). This is a non-atomic read-modify-write.

Two concerns:
1) TOCTOU / lost-update: the file content is read at line 447-454, and later the whole file is rewritten. If the user or another process modifies the file between the read and the truncating write, those changes are silently clobbered because the write path is trunc+rewrite of the in-memory snapshot. A diff patch application (fs_replace_content's purpose) cannot detect this without comparing against the original read. fs_write_file has a file_drift_tracker (erased at line 41 in fs_write_file_entry) to detect such drift, but fs_replace_content has no equivalent drift/conflict check.

2) There is no fsync / durability guarantee; a crash mid-write can leave a truncated file. Given the tool's purpose (mutating source files), an atomic write (write to temp file in same dir, then rename) would reduce both the partial-write truncation risk and, when combined with a pre-write content comparison, the lost-update risk.

Severity is medium because this is the primary mechanism for the 'file://' bypass identified separately (direct trunc-write of get_local_path()), and the write is not guarded by any atomicity or pre-write revalidation.
items.proposed_fix: Write via an atomic temp-file+rename in the same directory to avoid partial truncation, and adopt the file_drift_tracker / pre-write content comparison that fs_write_file uses so the tool detects concurrent modifications instead of silently clobbering them.
items.summary: Non-atomic trunc+rewrite write path: lost-update clobber and partial-write truncation risk

items.description: The `path` parameter is taken from untrusted LLM input and passed through `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(raw_path, access_type::write, ...)`. For any `file://` URI, the shared `file_security_manager::validate_access` (file_security_manager.cpp:125-144) short-circuits: `if (scheme == "file" || scheme == "tmp" || scheme == "images") { out_resolved_path = requested_path; return true; }`. This returns true WITHOUT checking the project allowlist, WITHOUT applying the ignore patterns (.ssh, .env, .aws), and without the on-disk permission test. `args_.safe_path` is then set to the raw URI. Later, in `execute_disk_fallback` (fs_replace_lines_entry.cpp:550-554), `vfs->get_local_path("file:///etc/foo")` resolves to `/etc/foo` and the tool writes to that arbitrary absolute path directly via `std::ofstream`. As a result the agent can overwrite files outside the allowed workspace and even files matching ignore patterns (e.g. `file:///home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys` or `file:///etc/passwd`), bypassing the sandbox's write authorization. This is a sandbox/write-authorization bypass. Root cause originates in the shared file_security_manager, but this tool materializes it and performs no defense-in-depth re-validation of the resolved disk path.
items.proposed_fix: Do not accept `file://` (or any URI scheme) for write in this tool without re-running the local allowlist/ignore checks on the resolved disk path. After obtaining the resolved local path via get_local_path(), canonicalize it and verify it is (a) not ignored and (b) within an allowed write root before opening for writing. Better: reject non-relative, non-workspace paths outright and refuse to let the shared manager's unconditional file:// acceptance reach the disk write. Consider adding O_NOFOLLOW/no-symlink-escape enforcement as defense in depth.
items.summary: file:// URI scheme bypasses allowlist & ignore patterns on write

items.description: At fs_replace_lines_entry.cpp:625 `std::ofstream out(path_to_use, std::ios::binary)` opens the target for writing with default flags: it follows symlinks and has no O_NOFOLLOW/O_CLOEXEC. The security validation (`validate_access`) canonically resolved the path earlier (weakly_canonical), but the path is re-opened at write time with `path_to_use` derived independently. There is no check that the file at write time is a regular file, and no confirmation that the resolved disk path still matches the allowlisted canonical path (no re-validation / TOCTOU protection). If a symlink is placed (or swapped) at/under the path between validation and write, the write follows it and can clobber an arbitrary file. Additionally, when the VFS path translation is used, the tool writes to `get_local_path()` without verifying that this resolved path is still subject to the allowlist/ignore rules (see the file:// finding). Recommend opening with O_NOFOLLOW via posix open, verifying the final resolved path is a regular file inside an allowed root, and re-running validation immediately before the write.
items.proposed_fix: Open the file with O_NOFOLLOW (and O_CLOEXEC) and verify it is a regular file (lstat) immediately before writing. Re-resolve the canonical path and re-check allowlist/ignore rules at the moment of writing to close the validation→write TOCTOU window.
items.summary: Write follows symlinks / no re-validation of resolved path before ofstream open (TOCTOU/symlink escape)

items.description: In run_shell_command_entry.cpp lines 119-126 the "Always allow" rule is checked and served WITHOUT re-prompting the user. Once the user selects "Always" for a bare command string, run_shell_command_tool::execute() will run that exact command string on every subsequent invocation with no permission prompt at all. This is a standing approval decision for a powerful arbitrary-command tool. An agent that later obtains the same command string (e.g., replayed via tool-call history, agentcli_record/replay, or A2A remote agents) can execute it without any user confirmation. The g_command_perms is in-memory only so it resets on restart, but it is still an unbounded, unconditional standing grant for the single highest-risk tool. It is not scoped to an agent identity, a TTY session, or a maximum run count. Recommend documenting the risk, tying 'always' grants to a session and to the invoking agent identity, and ensuring remote/A2A agents cannot inherit a prior user's 'Always' grant.
items.proposed_fix: Scope 'Always' grants to the invoking agent/session and consider a bounded number of re-prompts; do not let the grant silently persist across agent identities or be replayed from tool-call history without user awareness.
items.summary: 'Always' approval persists globally and is keyed only by raw command string, serving later calls without re-prompting

items.description: The 'force=true' flag is described in the tool schema as 'requires explicit user approval'. However, force=true does two things that weaken safety: (1) In validate_args_impl (run_shell_command_security.cpp lines 41-49) it bypasses the entire re-steering guard, so a command that reliably maps to a native tool (git status, meson test --list, grep, sed/head reads, find) is pushed straight through to execution (still gated on the user prompt, but the semantic guard is skipped). (2) In execute(), force has no effect on the permission flow; it does NOT actually force/strengthen the approval - it only disables the re-steering recommendation. There is no separate, stronger confirmation for force=true even though the documentation implies heightened approval. Recommend: make force=true require a distinct, explicit 'Are you sure' approval step (or equivalent elevated confirmation), and ensure re-steering is the only thing it bypasses.
items.proposed_fix: Add an explicit, elevated approval prompt for force=true commands rather than treating them identically to normal commands, and document that force only bypasses re-steering.
items.summary: force=true bypasses re-steering guard and is documented as 'explicit approval' but adds no stronger approval gating

items.description: When is_shell_display_access() is true, set_allow_display(true) propagates to build_command (line 297 in command_runner.cpp): network isolation is lost. Because the condition `if (!network_access_ && !allow_display_)` adds PrivateNetwork=true, enabling display also disables PrivateNetwork for the otherwise network-isolated strict agent profile. This means a single config flag (shell_display_access_) silently removes network sandboxing from the highest-risk tool, even though display access and network access are orthogonal concerns. The strict_agent_profile sets network_access_=false, so the intent is clearly no network. Enabling display must not reopen the network. Recommend decoupling: always enforce PrivateNetwork=true under the strict agent profile unless network access is explicitly granted, independent of the display flag.
items.proposed_fix: Enforce PrivateNetwork=true for the strict agent profile regardless of display access. A separate explicit 'network access' grant should be the only way to remove network isolation.
items.summary: Enabling shell display access also disables PrivateNetwork isolation (X11 + direct network disclosure)

items.description: Two dismissal vectors for the timeout/resource-limit control: (1) After building final_command, execute() checks for '2>' or '>&' substrings and skips appending '2>&1' (command_runner.cpp lines 488-490). A command containing either substring (e.g. an innocuous 'echo 2>/dev/null') suppresses stderr capture. (2) run_shell_command_security.cpp lines 30-38 only validates `command` is non-empty and contains no 0x1b byte, but `timeout` and `async` are accepted with no upper bound. A permissive (or malicious/tool-injected) timeout of a very large value defeats the 300s default, and there is no cap on it at the CLI/validator level. Since the process group kill (command_runner.cpp line 577) is only triggered by should_continue()/timeout, an unbounded timeout removes the primary supervisor kill for runaway/fork-bomb commands. Recommend: (a) always redirect stderr to stdout regardless of the command contents so the supervisor can observe the child's progress, and (b) clamp timeout to a sane maximum (e.g. <= 3600s) and reject/cap oversized or negative values in validate_args_impl.
items.proposed_fix: Clamp timeout to a maximum and reject negative/oversized values; make stderr capture unconditional in command_runner::execute so the supervisor can always observe/kill runaway children.
items.summary: timeout is unbounded/negative-capable and stderr capture can be suppressed, undermining the runaway-command kill path

items.description: Disputed on impact. Calling args["command"].get<std::string>() on a missing key does throw an njson type_error, but tool_registry::prepare_tool wraps the entire validate_args call in a try/catch (tool_registry.cpp:329-344) and converts any thrown exception into an error message ("Error parsing tool arguments: ..."). It therefore does NOT propagate as an unhandled exception and cannot crash/abort the agent tool invocation as claimed. The underlying defensive-coding recommendation (guard with contains(is_string) and set out_error) is a reasonable robustness improvement, but the described impact and severity (medium, crash) are overstated.
items.proposed_fix: Guard with args.contains("command") && args["command"].is_string() before extraction and return a validation error (out_error) instead of throwing.
items.summary: Missing/wrong-typed 'command' JSON key throws an unhandled njson exception from the validator

items.description: Disputed. tool_registry::prepare_tool creates a transient validator instance per tool invocation via `auto validator = factory();` (tool_registry.cpp:287), with the explicit comment "Create a transient validator instance for this execution to ensure thread-safe state!". Each execution therefore holds its own validator (and its own parsed_args_) — it is never shared across concurrent validate_args_impl/create_tool_impl calls. The mutable qualifier is stylistically unusual but does not introduce a practical data race given the per-invocation instantiation pattern. No concurrency hazard is demonstrable from this code path.
items.proposed_fix: Avoid shared mutable validation state; pass validated args out of validate and into tool construction directly rather than stashing them in a mutable member.
items.summary: Mutable shared parsed_args_ in validator is unsafe under concurrent validation

items.description: evaluate_shell_command_resteer interpolates regex capture groups into suggested_tool/explanation and embeds them directly into the user-facing denial error (run_shell_command_security.cpp line 44-45) without quoting or escaping the MV from the command/filename/path. In particular, this code builds `fs_read_lines(path="{}")`/`fs_grep_files(pattern="{}", path="{}")` strings where the captured file path, keyword, pattern, and file name come straight from the (untrusted) command line. A crafted command (e.g. a filename containing a quote or backslash, or a pattern with injection metacharacters) can produce a misleading/invalid suggested tool call that the user might copy-paste thinking it is a safe native call, or that is fed back to an agent. The converted values are never shell-escaped (escape_shell_arg is not used) and never validated for being a plausible identifier/path. Recommend validating/sanitizing capture groups (reject or escape non-path-safe characters) before interpolating them into suggestions, and quoting the embedded values.
items.line_content:
rec.suggested_tool = std::format("fs_read_lines(path=\"{}\", start_line={}, end_line={})", file_path, s_line, e_line);
		rec.explanation = std::format("To read lines from '{}', use the native 'fs_read_lines' tool instead of shell sed.", file_path);
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize/validate captured path and pattern values before interpolating them into the suggested tool call strings (escape quotes/backslashes, reject implausible characters), so a crafted filename cannot forge a misleading recommendation.
items.summary: Re-steering suggestions interpolate untrusted captures without escaping, enabling misleading forged tool-call strings

items.description:
fs_replace_content_validator::validate_args_impl performs its own raw string check `raw_path.find("..") != std::string::npos` to block traversal (lines 14-17), while fs_write_file_validator does NOT perform any such check and instead relies entirely on file_security_manager::validate_access weak_canonicalization.

The two tools are inconsistent in where and how path traversal is defended:
- fs_write_file relies on canonicalization + allowlist (correct but TOCTOU on symlink swap between validation and open).
- fs_replace_content's raw ".." substring check is brittle: it rejects legitimate paths/filenames containing ".." (e.g. a directory literally named "..foo" or a path component containing two dots), and it provides a false sense of security since the real protection (canonicalization) is what actually blocks traversal. Worse, the substring check does nothing to stop the file:// scheme abs-style bypass (a `file:///etc/...` path contains no '..').

Recommendation: drop the brittle substring check and rely on a single shared, canonicalization-based guard in file_security_manager for both tools, so the protection is uniform and correct.
items.proposed_fix: Remove the ad-hoc '..' substring check and centralize traversal protection in file_security_manager::validate_access (canonicalize + allowlist) for both tools, avoiding false negatives/positives and scheme bypasses.
items.summary: Inconsistent & brittle '..' traversal check in fs_replace_content vs fs_write_file

items.description: In `validate_runtime`, remove/replace edits are validated with overly-permissive matching: lines are compared after `utf8::trim()`, and a match is accepted when `actual_trimmed.find(expected_trimmed) == 0` (prefix match of the trimmed line). This means an edit whose `original_text` only loosely matches the first line (e.g. differing indentation or differing subsequent lines) is treated as a verified match. A `remove`/`replace` then blindly erases `lines_to_remove = newlines(original_text)+1` lines from `lines.begin()+idx` regardless of whether the erased lines actually correspond to the user's intent. Because this applies to untrusted LLM-supplied content, the tool can remove more or different lines than the original_text specifies, corrupting the file (data-integrity loss). Combined with no per-line equality confirmation for the removed range, this is a weak verification that can produce unintended destructive edits. Severity is medium rather than critical because it still operates within the allowlisted file.
items.proposed_fix: Require exact (or near-exact) equality of the affected block rather than a trimmed prefix match when accepting a verify, so a remove/replace can only erase lines that actually correspond to the provided original_text. At minimum, verify the full multi-line block matches (not just the first line) before granting a match, and bound-check `idx + lines_to_remove <= lines.size()` right before the erase in execute_disk_fallback.
items.summary: Permissive trimmed-prefix original_text matching can erase non-matching lines

items.description: The vector erase/replace operations at lines 580, 599 in `execute_disk_fallback` compute `idx = edit.line_number - 1` and erase `[idx, idx + edit.lines_to_remove)`. The bounds are validated in `validate_runtime` (called before execute), but `execute_disk_fallback` re-reads the file independently from disk and re-applies all edits with NO bounds re-check (no `idx >= 0`, no `idx + lines_to_remove <= lines.size()` guards), and validation and execution are separate passes (TOCTOU). If the file changed between validation and execution (e.g. concurrent edit, drift, or the earlier live-edit path altering disk state), an out-of-range erase/insert against `std::vector` is undefined behavior (crash or memory corruption). Also, the deduplication/sorting logic assumes strictly descending order, but the `execute()` path always runs the live-document JSON path first without independent bounds checks. Recommend adding explicit bounds assertions before each erase/insert in execute_disk_fallback and treating any violation as a hard error rather than UB.
items.proposed_fix: Before each `lines.erase(...)` / `lines.insert(...)`, validate `idx >= 0`, `idx <= lines.size()`, and `idx + lines_to_remove <= lines.size()`, returning an explicit error (and aborting the whole operation) otherwise. Consider doing all validation and mutation in a single read-lock-free consistent snapshot to eliminate the TOCTOU between validate_runtime and execute_disk_fallback.
items.summary: Missing bounds checks on erase/insert in execute_disk_fallback (TOCTOU UB)

items.description: The `execute_disk_fallback` builds `result_msg` by embedding file/line content verbatim: `result_msg += std::format("{}: {}\n", l, lines[l - 1])` at lines 744, 749, 756, and the brace-warning text is also derived from that content. This string is returned to the framework and rendered to the user and fed back into the LLM. Since the file content is LLM-supplied (untrusted), embedded ANSI/terminal escape sequences, control characters, or format directives within the edited lines will be emitted unescaped. This creates a terminal-control/format-injection primitive (e.g. an agent writing `\x1b[2J`, fake prompts, or payloads into a file and having them rendered). The comment-heavy, possibly AI-authored content in a codebase is especially likely to contain such sequences. Recommend sanitizing/escaping control characters (strip ANSI, control bytes) before echoing content into result text, and ensure the render path (`format_lines`, `wrap_text`) cannot interpret embedded escapes.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize each line before embedding into result_msg (e.g. strip C0/C1 control bytes and ANSI escape sequences, or escape them), and sanitize at the rendering boundary in `format_lines`/`wrap_text`. Consider using an existing strip_ansi/strip_utf8-like filter before echoing to the user.
items.summary: File content echoed into tool result without sanitizing control/ANSI escape sequences

items.description: In `fs_replace_lines_tool::execute` (lines 490-508), when the file is open in a live document, the code builds `edits_json` (a JSON payload of all edits) with the stated intent of calling `ctx.doc_provider->apply_live_edits(args_.safe_path, ...)`, but the call is never made — the code only computes the payload and immediately falls through to `execute_disk_fallback`. This is effectively dead code with a stale/inaccurate comment. More importantly, it is a safety smell: there is no synchronization guaranteeing that the disk file and any open editor buffer agree on pre-edit state before `save_all_documents()`/`execute_disk_fallback` overwrite the file. If an open in-memory buffer has unsaved changes, disk-based edits could silently clobber the buffer's state, or vice-versa. Recommend either (a) implementing and synchronizing the live-edit path with the disk fallback so only one authoritative write occurs, or (b) removing the dead JSON-payload block and explicitly documenting/handling the disk-vs-open-buffer conflict, ideally refusing to edit a file whose buffer differs from disk.
items.proposed_fix: Either wire up a single authoritative apply path that is consistent between the open editor buffer and disk (apply the edits to the live buffer and persist once), or delete the unused JSON block and guard against editing a file whose open buffer state differs from disk (reject with a clear error if unsaved drift exists).
items.summary: Dead live-edit path: JSON payload built but apply_live_edits never called; risk of buffer/disk divergence

items.description: escape_markdown only escapes '|' and strips '\r'/'\n'. Every other byte — including ESC (0x1b), TAB (0x09), DEL (0x7f), and other control characters — is copied verbatim into the returned Markdown table. Critically, both the VFS binary check (line 118) and fs_utils::is_binary_file explicitly whitelist ESC and TAB, so a file containing ANSI escape sequences is NOT rejected as binary and its escapes are passed straight through to the agent's tool output. An attacker (or a malicious/compromised text file in the workspace, e.g. a README or log) can embed terminal control sequences such as \x1b[2J, \x1b[0;31m, or OSC \x1b]0;...\x07 that will be rendered when the result is displayed in a terminal, enabling terminal injection / cursor-manipulation / status-bar spoofing. This is the classic control-char-injection vector this review targets, and it is even more direct on the open-document path (lines 75-93) where there is no binary filter at all. Recommend stripping or escaping all control characters (e.g. reject c < 0x20 and c == 0x7f, or replace with a visible notation) in escape_markdown.
items.proposed_fix: In escape_markdown, additionally handle control characters: strip ESC, TAB, DEL and any c in [0x00,0x1f] / 0x7f (or replace with a printable placeholder) so ANSI escape sequences and terminal control bytes can never reach the output. For example: `else if (static_cast<unsigned char>(c) < 0x20 || static_cast<unsigned char>(c) == 0x7f) { /* drop or escape */ }`.
items.summary: Control-character (ANSI/ESC) injection into tool output; escape_markdown fails to sanitize ESC/TAB

items.description: The workspace path is validated/canonicalized against the allowlist at validation time (fs_regexp_lines_security.cpp via ctx.fs_security.validate_access), and symlinks are resolved there. But the resolved canonical path is then re-tested here with stat() and reopened separately with `std::ifstream` (which follows symlinks). If the on-disk object is swapped between validation/stat and the actual open (a classic TOCTOU), the code can read a different file than the one that was allowed — e.g. a regular workspace file replaced by a symlink or hardlink to an out-of-workspace path such as /etc/passwd. Within a user-writable workspace this is an exploitable sandbox-bypass primitive. Since there is no file-descriptor pinning (no O_NOFOLLOW/O_CLOEXEC, no fstat comparison against the validated inode), the allowlist guarantee is not upheld at read time.
items.proposed_fix: Open the file once with a hardened open (open(..., O_RDONLY | O_CLOEXEC | O_NOFOLLOW)), then fstat() the fd and verify it corresponds to the validated/canonicalized path (compare st_dev/st_ino against the stat taken at validation, and confirm S_ISREG), then read from the fd. This eliminates the check-then-use window and prevents following swapped symlinks.
items.summary: TOCTOU race between stat() and ifstream open in disk fallback can bypass allowlist via symlink swap

items.description:
In fs_regexp_lines_tool::execute, the open-editor-document path (lines 75-93) performs NO size limit (unlike the 50MB cap applied to the VFS and disk paths) and NO binary-content check. It iterates over every line of the open document and appends matches to the Markdown string. A very large open document generates a huge output string with no truncation cap other than the MAX_MATCHES count (which still caps at 1000 lines of potentially very long content, each line possibly megabytes long). This is inconsistent with the other two read paths and can produce unbounded/oversized tool responses that blow up the agent context.

Also note the doc path bypasses the escape_markdown control-char protection issue noted separately.
items.proposed_fix: Apply the same 50MB size guard and per-line length cap to the open-document branch, or stream it with a byte budget. Since open documents are already in memory, at minimum cap accumulated output bytes so a pathological document cannot produce an unbounded tool result.
items.summary: Open-document read path has no size limit and no binary check (unbounded output, inconsistent with VFS/disk paths)

items.description: fs_regexp_lines_tool caches the compiled RE2 in a `mutable std::unique_ptr<re2::RE2>` (fs_regexp_lines.h line 25) and compiles it in validate_runtime. validate_runtime is a non-const method with the context parameter commented out. If validate_runtime is invoked multiple times (e.g. re-validated before each execution in a shared-mutable lifecycle), the regex would be silently recompiled, but more importantly if the tool instance is shared across threads the lazy/mutable compilation introduces a data race (both read and write of compiled_regex_ without synchronization). Additionally the RE2 options do not bound resource usage: there is no max_mem set, so a pathological user-supplied pattern could potentially consume large memory during compilation/matching. RE2's linear-time guarantee bounds runtime, but memory use under expensive patterns is not bounded here. Prefer constructing the RE2 once (immutable) in the constructor/create-tool path, and set an explicit RE2 max_mem limit.
items.proposed_fix: Compile the RE2 eagerly (in the validator/create-tool path or tool constructor) and store it immutably rather than lazily recompiling in validate_runtime via a mutable member. Set RE2::Options set_max_mem to bound memory. If the tool may be shared across threads, guard the compiled regex with a mutex or make it const-initialized.
items.summary: Lazy mutable RE2 compilation with unbounded max_mem and no thread-safety guard

items.description: read_from_disk() gates text output on fs_utils::is_binary_file(), but that heuristic only inspects the first 4096 bytes of the file (a single buffer read) and explicitly treats ESC (0x1b), tab, newline etc. as non-binary. Consequently: (1) any ANSI escape sequence or control character located at or after byte offset 4096 is never detected as binary and is emitted verbatim into the returned result_text inside the code fence; (2) even inside the first 4KB, ESC-based escape sequences pass the guard. Malicious/edited file content can inject terminal control sequences or markdown-breaking characters into the LLM prompt/output and downstream UI rendering. Recommend sanitizing/escaping control characters (especially ESC) on every line emitted, and/or strengthening the binary-detection to cover the full range actually emitted.
items.summary: fs_read_lines: control-char/ANSI escape injection into output (binary check only scans first 4KB and whitelists ESC 0x1b)

items.description: read_from_disk() uses stat() and only enforces a 50MB size bound; it never verifies the target is a regular file (S_ISREG). For a FIFO or device node that resolves inside the allowlisted workspace, st_size is 0 (bypassing the 50MB guard), is_binary_file() returns false for non-regular files, and the subsequent std::getline loop will block indefinitely or read unboundedly (e.g. a FIFO opened for reading with no writer, or a pseudo-device). Recommend checking sb.st_mode & S_IFMT == S_IFREG (after canonicalization, which resolves symlinks) and refusing non-regular files, consistent across fs_read_lines, fs_read_binary, fs_read_symbol and fs_regexp_lines. Consider an S_ISREG/special-file guard via a shared helper.
items.summary: fs_read_lines: special-file (FIFO/device/symlink) not rejected -> potential unbounded blocking read / DoS

items.description: Inside the 50MB ceiling a single very long line (e.g. a minified file or a single-line 50MB blob) is materialized fully into one std::string via std::getline, and total_file_lines computation plus read_from_disk's forward scan always iterate the entire file even when only a narrow range is requested. This is bounded by the 50MB check so not a severe vuln, but combined with no per-line cap it allows large single allocations and wasted I/O. Recommend a per-line byte cap and, where feasible, computing the line count only once / not scanning the full file for a small slice.
items.summary: fs_read_lines: no per-line length cap; whole file always scanned for line count even for narrow ranges

items.description: In the VFS branch (lines 27-54), the 50MB bound is applied AFTER computing len and reading view, but the actual returned data is capped at 50MB and start is validated against view.length(). However, the disk branch checks st_size > 50MB only via sb.st_size from stat(); the offset/size handling uses int → streamsize arithmetic (sb.st_size - args_.offset) with no S_ISREG check, so a FIFO/device inside the allowlist has st_size==0 and this passes validation; also a negative offset is pre-clamped in the validator (parsed.offset < 0 -> 0). The 50MB cap is applied AFTER reading the whole view in the VFS case: fs_utils::format_binary_output receives a span of up to 50MB and hex-encodes it into a ~150MB output string, which could overshoot the intended size limit / memory. Recommend: apply the size cap before reading, verify S_ISREG for disk special files, and place a hard ceiling on the formatted output size, not just the raw read size.
items.summary: fs_read_binary: no S_ISREG special-file guard; hex output can balloon 3x beyond 50MB raw cap

items.description: In execute(), when reading from a VFS URI or from disk, fs_read_symbol does not apply fs_utils::is_binary_file() nor any 50MB size guard in read_lines() or count_total_lines(). The read_lines() disk path (lines 271-285) uses std::getline with no size/binary validation, so a binary or oversized file inside the allowlist can be slurped into memory and its control bytes embedded verbatim into the LSP content and the returned output. In particular the content read at lines 134-137 (content.assign(istreambuf_iterator...)) has no size limit before lsp_open_document, and symbol line output at lines 222-223 emits raw line text with no control-char sanitization. All other read tools gate on is_binary_file()/50MB and sanitize output; fs_read_symbol is the outlier. Recommend adding the same is_binary_file + 50MB guard and control-char escaping for emitted lines.
items.summary: fs_read_symbol: no binary/size guard and no control-char sanitization on content read/emitted

items.description:
Unlike fs_glob (which calls validate_access per matched file) and fs_list_dir (which validates every entry before listing), fs_grep_files relies ONLY on the initial safe_search_path validation and then reads every file encountered by recursive_directory_iterator directly via stat() + std::ifstream without re-validating through file_security_manager::validate_access.

The traversal does `if (!fs::is_regular_file(path)) continue;` (line 514) and `stat()`/`is_binary_file` in process_file, all of which FOLLOW symlinks. A symlink placed anywhere under the search path that points to a sensitive file outside the project root (e.g. /etc/passwd, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, /var/lib/...) will be resolved by stat()/is_regular_file and its CONTENTS read, grep'd, and returned to the LLM (including content lines in the output). This is a sandbox-bypass / sensitive-information-disclosure hole that the other two search tools close by re-validating each path through the canonicalizing allowlist check.

Fix: before reading each file in process_file (and in the VFS branch), resolve/canonicalize via ctx.fs_security.validate_access(path, read, ...) and refuse to read if it fails, mirroring fs_glob_entry.cpp line 110 and fs_list_dir_entry.cpp line 180.
items.summary: fs_grep_files reads files during traversal without per-file validate_access — symlink files pointing outside the sandbox are searched and disclosed

items.description:
The `limit` argument (number of detailed match lines to return) is read directly from the LLM-supplied JSON with no upper bound, unlike context_lines which is clamped to [0,10]. A prompt-injected or erroneous agent can pass limit=100000+ and each detailed match expands into a context block of up to 2000 characters (line 605 in fs_grep_files_entry.cpp). This can produce megabytes of source-file content copied into the LLM context, leaking file contents and flooding/blowing out the context window.

Compare: fs_glob hard-caps at 100 results and fs_list_dir relies on directory size, but fs_grep_files allows an arbitrarily large limit. Recommend clamping limit to a sane maximum (e.g. min(limit, 1000 or 500)) in the validator, and also guard against negative limit values (currently a negative limit would silently suppress all matches).
items.proposed_fix:
Clamp in validate_args_impl:
```
args_.limit = raw_args.value("limit", 50);
if (args_.limit < 0) args_.limit = 0;
if (args_.limit > 1000) args_.limit = 1000; // or another sane cap
```
and document the cap in the schema description.
items.summary: fs_grep_files 'limit' parameter is unbounded (no upper clamp), enabling context-window / output exfiltration

items.description:
find_matching_impl_file() (codemap_utils.cpp:534) constructs sibling candidate paths (header_path.parent_path / stem + .cpp/.c/.cc/.cxx) and returns the first that std::filesystem::exists(). The returned path is then passed to get_document_codemap_symbols(matching_impl, ...) (line 72), which reads it via a raw std::ifstream (codemap_utils.cpp:296) and also lsp_open_document() without any file_security_manager::validate_access check.

The impl file sits in the same directory as the already-validated canonical header, so in the common case it is inside the allowed root. However, the path is reconstructed and read without canonicalization or allowlist re-check, so a symlink named foo.cpp (in the same dir as a validated foo.h) that points OUTSIDE the sandbox (e.g. /etc/shadow) will be followed and its content read and fed to the LSP/codemap machinery. This is a TOCTOU / symlink-following gap that bypasses the protection that the primary path got in the security stage. Recommend resolving and validating matching_impl through validate_access (and using the canonical result) before reading, and skipping if validation fails.
items.proposed_fix: In execute(), after obtaining matching_impl, run it through ctx.fs_security.validate_access(matching_impl, read, safe_impl, err) and only proceed if it succeeds, using safe_impl for get_document_codemap_symbols.
items.summary: fs_file_codemap reads matching impl file obtained by find_matching_impl_file without re-validating access — symlink-to-sensitive-file read

items.description: For every file matched by the glob (up to the hard cap of 100), the tool calls fs_utils::count_lines_in_file() which opens and reads the ENTIRE file bytes to count newlines, purely to display a line-count metadata column. A broad glob (e.g. `**/*`) can therefore cause up to 100 large files to be read in full into memory just for metadata. For huge generated/binary-ish or multi-GB files this is an avoidable resource-exhaustion / latency vector. Suggest a size gate (only count lines for files under a size threshold) or using the pre-existing size to skip, and/or capping. Bounded but wasteful; low severity.
items.proposed_fix: Skip count_lines_in_file for large files (e.g. if file_size exceeds a few MB), or compute lines lazily/only when requested. Optionally reuse a capped streaming line counter that stops early.
items.summary: fs_glob reads entire file contents via count_lines_in_file to compute metadata for every matched file (up to 100) — resource exhaustion / DoS

items.description: In format_entries_table, the filename (from the filesystem) is inserted directly into a Markdown table cell without escaping. A filename containing '|' (or ANSI/control characters, newlines) can break the table structure, inject fake columns/rows, or inject markup into the tool result that is later rendered to the user/LLM. The rich_metadata path replaces '|' with ',' for the details column but the filename column is never sanitized. Since filenames are attacker-influenceable in a repo (e.g. a malicious repo can contain a file literally named `evil |x|`), this should be escaped. Low severity (no direct code exec), but it is an output-injection/formatting-integrity issue. Note fs_grep_files correctly marks up its filenames via escape_markdown(), so be consistent.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize the filename before inserting into the table (replace '|' with e.g. '\\|' or ',' and strip control chars), mirroring the replacement already applied to the details column.
items.summary: fs_list_dir embeds filenames into Markdown table without escaping '|'/control characters — table/injection risk

items.description: The validator leaves max_symbols defaulting to 0 = "unlimited"/no cap and full=true by default. For a very large file (e.g. a generated or bundled translation unit with tens of thousands of symbols) the returned codemap table enumerates every symbol with start/end line, producing an arbitrarily large output that floods the LLM context. While max_symbols can be supplied, there is no enforced upper ceiling on the emitted table. Recommend defaulting max_symbols to a sane cap (e.g. a few hundred) or enforcing an upper bound, while still noting the total/omitted count so the agent can opt into more with full=true if needed. Low-to-medium context-exhaustion concern.
items.proposed_fix: Default max_symbols to a reasonable bounded value and/or clamp any supplied value to an upper ceiling, keeping the 'Top N of M symbols' + omitted hint surfaced by format_codemap_table.
items.summary: fs_file_codemap default max_symbols=0 (unlimited) + full=true can emit an unbounded codemap table for very large files

items.description: Duplicate-search detection is implemented with a file-scope mutable static struct, g_last_search, that is read and written in execute() (lines 191-205) with no locking. If the agent invokes tools concurrently (the application uses multiple threads/terminal windows and models), two fs_grep_files executions can race on this global, producing torn reads, false duplicate warnings, or incorrect duplicate-suppression. This is a correctness bug and a potential source of non-deterministic tool results (untrusted/confusing feedback to the LLM) rather than a privilege issue. Recommend making duplicate-tracking per-context (store it in tool_context) instead of a process-global, or protect with a mutex.
items.proposed_fix: Move last-search duplicate state into the per-conversation tool_context (or protect g_last_search with a mutex), so concurrent executions do not race.
items.summary: fs_grep_files uses a mutable global (g_last_search) for duplicate-detection without synchronization — data race under concurrent tool execution

items.description: `find_redirect_file(base_dir, rel_path)` (line 96) constructs `base_dir / rel_path` and, if the file exists, returns it for reading. `rel_path` comes verbatim from the `.so ` directive parsed out of the man page's raw content (lines 362-373). Two escape vectors exist: (1) `std::filesystem::path /` gives precedence to an absolute right-hand operand, so a crafted `.so /etc/...` directive would read an arbitrary absolute path such as `/etc/passwd` or `/etc/shadow`; (2) a relative `../../...` path traverses upward out of `/usr/share/man`. The resulting file is then gzip-decompressed/read by `decompress_man_page()` (line 73) and rendered back into the LLM context via `troff2md()` (line 402). This is effectively an arbitrary file read that bypasses the nominal man-page search boundary. Although system man pages are normally trusted, a malicious/planted man page (e.g. from a downloaded package) can exfiltrate arbitrary file contents into the agent context.
items.line_content: static std::filesystem::path find_redirect_file(const std::filesystem::path& base_dir, const std::string& rel_path) {
items.proposed_fix: Constrain the redirect target to stay within base_dir. After computing `target`, normalize it (lexically_normal) and verify it is still inside `base_dir` (e.g. using `std::filesystem::weakly_canonical` and checking the path prefix / `lexically_relative` does not start with `..`). Reject absolute `rel_path` outright and reject any path whose normalized form escapes base_dir. Also reject `.so` targets whose extension is not a recognized man suffix.
items.summary: fs_man .so redirect allows reading files outside the man base_dir (path traversal / arbitrary file read)

items.description: The synchronous execution path (lines 122-146) returns `runner.get_final_output()` wrapped in a bash code block with no length cap.
