In contrast, the async path (lines 101-105) explicitly caps output at 10,000 characters 'to protect context window' before injecting it. A file or build step that emits a very large amount of output (e.g. a template-expansion-heavy file, many warnings, or a runaway preprocessor) will dump the entire unbounded buffer into the LLM context in sync mode, inflating the context window and potentially enabling a context-DoS. This is the same risk the code already guards against in the async branch.
items.proposed_fix: Apply the same 10,000 character cap used in the async branch to the synchronous return value before formatting `output` into the returned string (and before appending the crash-notification text, so the advisory isn't truncated away).
items.summary: fs_compile_file sync execution path returns unbounded output into LLM context (no 10k cap)

items.description: `validate_args_impl` (line 12) whitelists only `"path"` and `"async"` as accepted keys and returns an error for any other key. The tool's parameter schema (fs_compile_file.h lines 48-51) advertises a `timeout` parameter, the args struct (`fs_compile_file_args`) declares a `timeout` field defaulting to 600, and the async path uses `args_.timeout` to set the runner timeout (fs_compile_file_entry.cpp line 85). Because the validator rejects any `timeout` key, a caller can never actually set a custom timeout even though the documented interface permits it - the documented parameter is effectively dead. This is a functional inconsistency between the schema and the validator rather than a sandbox/security bypass, but it is a correctness defect worth fixing.
items.proposed_fix: Add `it.key() != "timeout"` to the whitelist in `validate_args_impl` so `timeout` is accepted, matching the schema and the args struct.
items.summary: fs_compile_file validator rejects the `timeout` argument its own schema advertises

items.description: The `execute()` method enumerates every matching compiler error from `build_error_manager` (loop at line 70) and every live LSP diagnostic (loop at line 98) and emits them all into a Markdown table with no length cap. For a file with a very large number of diagnostics (e.g. a header with hundreds of cascading errors, or a file submitted to mass analysis), the entire set is returned to the agent. Unlike fs_compile_project and the async fs_compile_file path, there is no output guard here, so this can blow out the LLM context window with repetitive diagnostic data.
items.proposed_fix: Cap the number of diagnostics rendered (e.g. first N entries) and/or cap total output length (e.g. 10k chars) with an explicit truncation notice, mirroring the guards used by the other compile tools.
items.summary: fs_compile_info emits unbounded compiler/LSP diagnostics into the LLM context

items.description: `decompress_man_page()` (lines 73-93) streams an entire gzip file (or reads an entire plain file via `stringstream << rdbuf()`) into memory with no size limit, and `execute()` returns the full rendered Markdown (or writes it all) without a length cap when no `filter`/`output_path` is supplied. A very large man page (or a maliciously large/decompression-bomb `.gz` file encountered via the redirect path) causes unbounded memory consumption and returns an arbitrarily large document into the LLM context.
items.proposed_fix: Enforce a maximum decompressed/read size (e.g. stop gzread at a byte budget and fail gracefully), and cap the returned Markdown length with an explicit truncation notice when no filter is applied.
items.summary: fs_man reads/gzip-decompresses unbounded file sizes with no size limit

items.description: `args_.timeout` (and in fs_compile_project) is passed straight through to `runner->set_timeout()` with no upper-bound validation by either validator. `timeout` is a JSON integer under the agent's control, so the LLM (or a hijacked/tricked agent) can request an effectively unbounded timeout (up to INT_MAX seconds), keeping a compile subprocess alive for an unbounded duration. Since these tools run detached threads with no cancellation on agent teardown, this is a resource-exhaustion / hang vector rather than a data-integrity issue.
items.proposed_fix: Validate `timeout` during argument validation and clamp it to a sane maximum (e.g. reject or clamp values above a configured cap like 3600s), in both fs_compile_file and fs_compile_project validators.
items.summary: Compile tools accept an unbounded `timeout` value (no upper bound), enabling resource-exhaustion

items.description: lines is sliced with iterators into raw_lines: raw_lines.begin() + (offset - keep_prev) and raw_lines.begin() + (symbol_end_idx + keep_next + 1). When a symbol match is at the top of the file, offset (= match_start - expanded_start) is small; but when match_start == expanded_start, offset == 0 and keep_prev == 0, so slicing begins at begin()+0 which is fine. However, there is a genuine out-of-range risk: if the LSP-reported range or total_lines are inconsistent (e.g. match_end beyond the file end after count_total_lines diverges from read_lines' returned line count, which can happen when the file is read from disk vs. an editor snapshot that has fewer lines), then symbol_end_idx + keep_next + 1 can exceed raw_lines.size(), making the second iterator `raw_lines.begin() + N` with N > size() → undefined behavior in the vector range constructor. The subsequent `is_whitespace_only(raw_lines[symbol_end_idx + 1])` checks are guarded by size comparisons, but the final range-constructor slice (line 206) is NOT bounds-checked and adds keep_next on the raw index. Recommend computing the slice bounds defensively (clamp to [0, raw_lines.size()]) before constructing the sub-vector.
items.summary: fs_read_symbol: unbounded vector-range slice can read out of bounds (UB) at line 206

items.description: The recursive symbol scan at execute() step 4 returns matches, and the loop iterates over ALL matches without any bound. For a common symbol name (or a wildcard-ish name, or a name that matches many nested scopes), matches can grow large and the loop re-reads the whole file region + builds output for every match with no cap, unbounded output into the LLM context. Also `matches` is collected recursively across the full symbol tree. Recommend capping the number of matches printed (e.g. 10-20 similar to codemap max_items) and truncating output.
items.summary: fs_read_symbol: unbounded matches loop -> unbounded output/context bloat

items.description: `execute()` (line 73) filters compiler diagnostics using substring matching: `err.filepath.find(requested_path_) != npos || safe_path_.find(err.filepath) != npos`. Because both sides use substring semantics (`find(...) != npos`), diagnostics for unrelated files get attributed to the requested file - e.g. requesting `foo.c` would also match `foo.c.orig`, `myfoo.c`, or `foo.cxx`; and because `requested_path_` and `safe_path_` are the same value (per fs_compile_info_security.cpp line 10), the second clause `safe_path_.find(err.filepath)` matches when the diagnostic filename is a substring of the path (e.g. nearly any `main.cpp` diagnostic would match a prompt for `src/main.cpp` whose path happens to contain the error's relative filename). This leaks unrelated compiler errors into the reported table, potentially confusing the agent and, in aggregate, increasing output. Should be an exact normalized path comparison, not two overlapping substring tests.
items.proposed_fix: Normalize `err.filepath` and the requested/safe path (safe_absolute + lexically_normal) and compare them for equality, rather than substring matching. If relative/absolute ambiguity is expected in stored gcc paths, resolve the stored path against the build directory and compare canonical forms.
items.summary: fs_compile_info uses loose bidirectional substring matching to filter diagnostics, leaking unrelated files' errors

items.description: escape_markdown() only escapes the pipe character '|' and strips '\r'/'\n'. All other control characters—notably ESC (0x1b) and other C0 control bytes (0x00-0x1f except those stripped) and DEL (0x7f)—pass through verbatim into the returned Markdown table. The binary guards do not help: both the VFS branch (line 115-121) and disk branch use heuristics that only inspect the first 4KB and explicitly whitelist ESC and tab; a match on a line past the first 4KB that contains ESC can still be emitted. A malicious/edited file can therefore inject terminal escape sequences or markdown/logic-breaking control bytes into the tool result that is rendered to the UI and fed to the LLM. Recommend sanitizing all control characters (not just |, \r, \n) in escape_markdown.
items.summary: fs_regexp_lines: escape_markdown leaves ESC/control bytes unsanitized -> injection into output

items.description: The disk fallback branch (lines 157-189) uses fs_utils::is_binary_file() and a 50MB size check, but never verifies the path is a regular file (S_ISREG). A FIFO or device node with st_size==0 inside the allowlist passes the size guard; is_binary_file() returns false for non-regular files; and the std::getline loop can block indefinitely on a FIFO with no writer or read unboundedly from a pseudo-device. The VFS branch similarly has no special-file notion. Recommend rejecting non-regular files (S_IFMT==S_IFREG) before reading, consistent with other read tools.
items.summary: fs_regexp_lines: no S_ISREG special-file guard on disk branch -> FIFO/device blocking DoS

items.description: In the `tail` branch (lines 196-230) execute() counts lines by opening the file and iterating with std::istreambuf_iterator across the ENTIRE file, with no 50MB size guard, no is_binary_file() check, and no S_ISREG special-file check (unlike read_from_disk which enforces st_size <= 50MB). Consequently passing `tail` on a large file (e.g. a multi-GB log that is nonetheless within the allowlisted workspace) reads the whole file into the counting pass, and on a FIFO/device it can block indefinitely. The same unbounded whole-file line-count pattern also exists in fs_read_symbol::count_total_lines(). Recommend applying the same 50MB/S_ISREG guard (or using the stat-based fast path) before the full-file line-count pass.
items.summary: fs_read_lines tail branch: unbounded full-file read with no 50MB / special-file guard

items.description: validate_access() resolves + canonicalizes the path using std::filesystem::weakly_canonical() and checks the allowlist, but the tools then re-open the returned safe_path by name (stat/open) at execution time. Between validation (Stage 1) and execution (Stage 2) the underlying directory entry can be replaced with a symlink or hardlink pointing outside the allowlist (TOCTOU). Because these tools re-stat and re-open the path without re-verifying canonical form == allowed target at execution time, a race could read a file outside the sandbox. This is a defense-in-depth concern; the canonicalization in the security manager mitigates the common case but does not fully close the TOCTOU window. Recommend re-validating with an openat2/O_NOFOLLOW-style handle or re-running the canonicalization at execution time.
items.summary: All read tools: TOCTOU between validate_access canonicalization and re-open at execute()

items.description: Both fs_file_codemap (line 81) and fs_file_size route user-supplied paths through file_security_manager::validate_access (file_security_manager.cpp:125-144). That function auto-trusts the "file://", "tmp://", and "images://" schemes: it returns `out_resolved_path = requested_path` immediately WITHOUT canonicalization, WITHOUT checking the allowlist/allowlist roots, and WITHOUT applying the hardcoded ignore patterns (e.g. /.ssh, /.env, /.aws, /.gnupg). The path is then reopened through the VFS in execute(). The default "file://" provider is constructed with an empty root_dir_ (virtual_file_system.cpp:217), and file_vfs_provider::parse_uri (virtual_file_system.cpp:719-736) calls weakly_canonical() but imposes NO containment to the project root: an absolute path such as `file:///etc/passwd` or `file:///home/user/.ssh/id_rsa` resolves directly to that file, and a relative `file://../../../../<path>` traversal also normalizes outside the root. Unlike create_file/create_directory (which have explicit escape checks, virtual_file_system.cpp:841, 893), the read paths (read_file at 746, get_file_info at 758) enforce no root containment. Consequence: an LLM can pass `file:///etc/passwd` or `file:///home/user/.ssh/id_rsa` to fs_file_size (returns the file's byte size) and to fs_file_codemap (which reads full file content via VFS read_file in fs_file_codemap_entry.cpp:35 and returns markdown headings / code symbols / line counts), thereby exfiltrating the size and, for readable-format files, content of sensitive files outside the workspace and even defeating the hardcoded /.ssh & /.env ignore protections. Recommends: (1) root the default file:// provider to the project dir and reject absolute/traversal paths outside it (mirror create_file's containment check on ALL read operations), (2) enforce ignore-pattern and allowlist checks on file:///tmp:///images:// URIs before trusting them, or (3) drop the file:// scheme from the auto-trusted list in validate_access.
items.summary: file:// VFS scheme bypasses allowlist, ignore patterns, and root containment → sandbox escape / arbitrary file read

items.description: The `max_symbols` parameter defaults to 0, which the comment and the execute() code (fs_file_codemap_entry.cpp:62-65) treat as "unlimited / no cap", and `full` defaults to true. A large source/header file with tens of thousands of functions/classes will therefore render the ENTIRE codemap table into the tool result with no bound, which can blow out the LLM context window (cost/availability DoS) and cause a huge response. Additionally, execute() reads the full file a first time to compute total_lines (fs_file_codemap_entry.cpp:47-51) and then get_document_codemap_symbols() reads the entire file into memory again via std::istreambuf_iterator (codemap_utils.cpp:298), doubling memory use for huge files. Recommends: (1) enforce a sane default cap on the number of symbols rendered (e.g. 200-500) while still exposing total+omitted counts so the agent can request more explicitly, (2) clamp max_symbols to a hard upper bound, and (3) reuse a single file read for both line count and symbol extraction to avoid the double read.
items.summary: fs_file_codemap defaults to unbounded symbol output → LLM context-window/resource DoS

items.description: Good news: validate_access() uses std::filesystem::weakly_canonical() (file_security_manager.cpp:157) which resolves symlinks and .. before the allowlist check, so a symlink inside the workspace that points outside gets canonicalized to its real target and is then correctly denied by the allowlist — symlink-following into sensitive dirs is mitigated for ordinary (non-URI) paths. However, there is a TOCTOU gap: the canonical absolute path is computed once during validation, stored, and later reopened by path inside execute() (std::filesystem::status/file_size here, std::ifstream in the codemap disk branch). If an attacker with write access to the workspace swaps a path component or the final entry for a symlink between validation and the open, the tool could open a different (out-of-scope) file than the one that was authorized. With malicious local write access this could widen to sensitive files. Recommends re-opening safely (e.g. openat with O_NOFOLLOW / dirfd pinned to the canonical parent, or re-running the security check immediately before open on the same path and using a handle rather than a raw path). Severity low because it requires a concurrent local-write primitive that is outside the normal threat model, and it is mitigated for the static case, but it is worth tightening.
items.summary: TOCTOU: canonicalized path re-opened at execute time without re-validation (symlink swap)

items.description: In validate_access() (file_security_manager.cpp lines 125-144), any path containing '://' whose scheme is one of "file", "tmp", or "images" is accepted immediately and returned as the resolved path WITHOUT running the ignore-pattern check or the allowlist check. This means a request like `file://<abs path>` (or `tmp://...` pointing outside the real workspace) bypasses the .ssh/.env/.aws ignore list and the workspace allowlist entirely. The impact depends on how the mounted virtual_file_system resolves these schemes, but the security manager is the enforcement layer for all fs_* tools, so the scheme whitelist short-circuit is a sandbox-escape concern if any such scheme maps to real local disk paths. Recommend that 'file' (and any local-file-mapping) scheme go through the same canonicalize + ignore + allowlist path rather than short-circuiting, or be removed from the whitelist.
items.summary: file_security_manager: file/tmp/images scheme short-circuit bypasses ignore list + allowlist

items.description:
In fs_file_codemap_tool::execute (fs_file_codemap_entry.cpp:67, 81), the table is rendered with `format_codemap_table(args_.requested_path, ...)`. `requested_path` is the raw, unvalidated user/LLM-supplied string (stored at fs_file_codemap_security.cpp:85 before canonicalization). It is interpolated directly into backtick-delimited triple-backtick headers in the generated Markdown (`### Codemap for \`{display_path}\` ...`) with no escaping. A malicious path containing a newline or backticks (e.g. `foo

# injected heading

\`bar`) can break out of the code span/header and inject arbitrary Markdown into the agent-visible tool result. Severity is low since the result is fed back to the same LLM/agent rather than rendered to a third party, but it can distort the agent's view, cause confusing output, or be used to smuggle misleading content. The symbol `display_name` fields likewise come from file/LSP content and are interpolated raw (codemap_utils.cpp:506) — though that content is already confined to an allowed file. Recommendations: escape backticks, newlines and pipe characters in the display path (and ideally symbol names) before embedding into the Markdown table, or use a sanitized relative display name derived from the canonical path.
items.line_content: std::string table = format_codemap_table(args_.requested_path, symbols, /*rich_format=*/true, total_lines, total_symbols_count, omitted_count, &ctx);
items.summary: Raw requested_path and symbol names interpolated unescaped into generated Markdown (markdown/header injection)

items.description: The `url` argument (agent-controlled) is only checked for non-emptiness in both `validate_args_impl` and `validate_runtime`. It is then passed directly into `a2a::a2a_client::fetch_agent_card()` which constructs `httplib::Client(url_str)` and issues GET requests to `/.well-known/agent-card.json` and `/agent.json`. There is no validation of the URL scheme (only http/https allowed, `file://`/`gopher://` etc. rejected), no host resolution/blocklist (localhost, link-local, private IP ranges, cloud metadata endpoints such as 169.254.169.254), and no redirect confinement. This constitutes a classic Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) primitive: a malicious or compromised agent (or a remote agent card returned by a compromised server) can direct the editor process to probe arbitrary internal network services and metadata endpoints. Because the agent is itself the caller, this primarily matters when an A2A server's advertised card or skills drive the agent into connecting to internal addresses, or when a low-privilege/read-only agent can reach internal network hosts. Recommend validating the scheme to http/https only, rejecting non-public/loopback/private/cloud-metadata hosts unless explicitly allowlisted, and disabling or bounding redirects.
items.summary: A2A connect server URL is not validated against SSRF (no scheme/host allowlist)

items.description: When `persistent` is true, the raw `auth_token` supplied by the agent is stored verbatim via `a2a_server_manager::add_server()` and then `save_project_servers()`, which `save_servers_to_file()` writes in plaintext to `<project_cache_root>/a2a_servers.json` (see src/a2a/a2a_server_manager.cpp:60-85). Bearer tokens / API keys are thus persisted unencrypted on disk in a project-local JSON file, with no file-permission tightening and no obfuscation. Any process or user with read access to the project cache directory can recover the secret. Tokens are also passed over the network embedded in the Authorization header. Recommend encrypting at rest (e.g. OS keyring / platform secure storage), restricting file permissions (0600), or at minimum warning the user that a sensitive token is being persisted in cleartext before committing it.
items.summary: A2A auth_token and server details persisted to disk in plaintext

items.description: The `skills` (and the remote `card->name`) are loaded from the remote server's agent-card JSON — fully untrusted network data retrieved via `fetch_agent_card()`. These values, including free-form `name` fields of skills pulled from the remote JSON (a2a_client.cpp:64-68), are serialized verbatim back into the tool result that is fed into the agent's context. A malicious/buggy A2A server can embed instructions, fake tool descriptions, or markup in skill names / descriptions that get interpreted by the LLM as directives (prompt-injection via the skill-summary dump). The television-style output has no escaping/sanitization. Recommend treating remote card content as untrusted: render it in clearly fenced user-facing form (not agent instructions), strip control characters / instruction-like content, and never feed remote free-form text as authoritative skill guidance.
items.summary: A2A agent-card skills/name reflected unsanitized into agent context (prompt injection channel)

items.description: `apply_text_filter` overrides `is_pure()` to return true (src/tools/apply_text_filter/apply_text_filter.h:44-47), yet its `execute()` has significant side effects: it can read an arbitrary file from disk (via `path`) AND write filtered output to an arbitrary output destination (`output_path`/`safe_output_path`), either through the VFS or via `std::ofstream` directly to the resolved filesystem path (apply_text_filter_entry.cpp:39-62). In `tool_registry::prepare_tool` (src/agentlib/tool_registry.cpp:310) the check `if (ctx.properties.read_only && !validator->is_pure())` blocks only non-pure tools in read-only contexts. Because this tool is flagged pure, a read-only agent is permitted to invoke it and write files to any `output_path` that passes `validate_access` write checks, effectively bypassing the read-only sandbox. Also `is_silent_by_default()` returns `is_pure()`, so these writes happen silently in the UI. Fix: return `false` from `is_pure()` (and do not derive silent-by-default), or gate write capability so that read-only agents can only apply filters to in-memory text without an output path.
items.summary: apply_text_filter marked is_pure() but writes output files -> read-only sandbox bypass

items.description: `activate_skill` returns `is_pure() == true` (activate_skill_security.cpp:21-24) but `execute()` mutates agent state via `ctx.active_agent->add_active_skill(args_.name)` and reads skill content from disk/VFS. Because `prepare_tool` (tool_registry.cpp:310) only blocks state-modifying tools in read-only mode when `is_pure()` is false, a read-only agent is allowed to activate skills, changing the agent's effective capabilities and causing filesystem/VFS reads with no size limits. Marking state-mutating tools as pure is semantically incorrect and undermines the read-only guarantee. Fix: return `false` from `is_pure()`, or move the activation state change to a non-pure path.
items.summary: activate_skill marked is_pure() but mutates agent active-skill state

items.description: `activate_tool_family` returns `is_pure() == true` (activate_tool_family_security.cpp:20-23) but `execute()` mutates agent state via `ctx.active_agent->add_active_tool_family(args_.name)`, granting the agent access to entire tool families (and thus state/data-modifying capabilities) that were previously unavailable. Because `prepare_tool` only blocks non-pure tools in read-only mode (tool_registry.cpp:310), a read-only agent is allowed to activate additional tool families, escalating its own privileges within the session and changing its capability surface. This is stateful/authoritative mutation and should not be flagged `is_pure()`. Fix: return `false` from `is_pure()` (and from silent-by-default), or gate family activation behind a non-read-only context.
items.summary: activate_tool_family marked is_pure() but escalates agent tool-family access

items.description: `apply_text_filter` reads an entire user-supplied `path` file into memory (`std::string((std::istreambuf_iterator<char>(ifs)), std::istreambuf_iterator<char>())`, apply_text_filter_entry.cpp:29) and applies arbitrary registered filters (`markdown_align_tables`, `html_to_markdown`, etc.) with no input size limits. There is no cap on the input file size or on the `text` argument size, no maximum output size, and no re-entrancy/CPU bound on filter execution. A large file (or a filter with super-linear cost such as `markdown_align_tables`) could exhaust memory or block the editor event loop / agent thread indefinitely. Validate_access only confirms the path is readable; it does not bound size. Recommend enforcing a configurable max input size, streaming filter output, and running filters with a timeout/token budget.
items.summary: apply_text_filter reads unbounded file/input sizes into memory with no limits

items.description: No real issue: the auth_token is not included in the returned message (only name/card-name/url/skills are echoed). Token persistence is covered by a separate finding. This item is invalid and removed.
items.line_content: return std::format("Successfully connected to A2A server '{}' ({}) at '{}'.{}", args_.name, card->name, args_.url, skills_summary);
items.summary: Informational note only (no token in response message); covered elsewhere

items.description: The validator (`fs_purge_tmp_security.cpp`) authorizes the operation by calling `ctx.fs_security.validate_access("tmp://", access_type::write, ...)`, which only accepts the `tmp` VFS scheme in `file_security_manager::validate_access` (line 129-131 returns true for scheme 'tmp' regardless of permission). However, `execute()` then ignores the VFS entirely and performs a recursive delete directly on the on-disk directory returned by `fs_utils::get_project_tmp_dir()` via `recursive_directory_iterator` + `std::filesystem::remove`. The execute path never re-validates the disk directory (or any individual deleted path) against the security manager's allowlist. This is an authorization scope mismatch: the tool checks permission on the logical `tmp://` URI but deletes the physical directory directly, bypassing the security manager's per-path authorization checks on the disk location. If the on-disk tmp dir resolution (e.g., testsuite `get_project_dir()/.turbostar_tmp` or `get_project_cache_root()/tmp`) ever diverges from / is symlinked to a location outside the sanctioned scratch space, this tool can delete files never authorized for deletion. It also redundantly requires `get_vfs()` to be present in `validate_runtime` even though the VFS is never used during execution, which obscures the actual deletion target.
items.proposed_fix: Re-validate the physical tmp directory at execute time: resolve `fs_utils::get_project_tmp_dir()` and confirm it is within the security manager's allowed cache/workspace roots before iterating, and/or enumerate deletions through the `tmp://` VFS provider so the same parse_uri/canonicalization/traversal checks apply. Avoid requiring VFS presence when the implementation operates on the disk path directly.
items.summary: fs_purge_tmp: destructive recursion targets on-disk dir without per-path authorization (scope mismatch)

items.description: When `substring_` is empty, the filter condition `substring_.empty() || filename.find(substring_) != npos` matches EVERY entry, so `execute()` recursively deletes all files and directories under the project tmp dir. This is a single-argument destructive operation with no confirmation step. Because the on-disk tmp dir is deleted directly (see the separate scope-mismatch finding), an empty/substring-specified call can wipe the entire scratch space plus any nested data present there. While purging scratch space is by design, given the authorization mismatch on the disk dir and the potential for the tmp dir to contain diagnostics/agent artifacts that a manipulated agent call could destroy, this should be constrained (e.g., require explicit confirmation, enforce a maximum number of deletions, or always operate strictly through a validated VFS path). There is also a logic inconsistency: the filter matches only `entry.path().filename()` while the tool description says "only deletes files/directories whose names contain the substring" and the tool schema mentions "in their name/path".
items.proposed_fix: Operate the delete exclusively through the `tmp://` VFS provider (which applies parse_uri/canonicalization/traversal checks), and consider requiring an explicit non-empty filter or a confirmation flag before allowing a full-recursive purge.
items.summary: fs_purge_tmp: empty substring recursively deletes entire scratch dir (destructive, no safety boundary)

items.description: `execute()` validates the INPUT `args_.path` against the security allowlist, but the RESULT paths returned by the LSP server (`loc.path`, set from `loc.uri.path()` in `lsp_manager::query_definition`/`query_references`) are echoed into the JSON output (`result.push_back({{"path", display_path}, ...})`) without any re-validation or canonicalization against the file security manager's allowlist. An LSP server (which runs in the editor's context, potentially resolving definitions/references from system headers, node_modules, symlinked paths, or externally-downloaded locations) can therefore cause arbitrary absolute filesystem paths outside the workspace to be disclosed to the LLM agent in the tool output. This is an information-disclosure / output-sanitization gap: the tool advertises results for paths the agent has no read authorization for. The comment at lines 27-28 says "Resolve path relative to project root if possible for cleaner output" but no such resolution is implemented; the raw absolute LSP path is used directly.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize each result path before emitting: run it through `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(path, read, ...)` and, if it is not authorized (outside the workspace), either drop the entry, redact/mark it as external, or emit only a relative path confined to the workspace root. Apply the same treatment in `code_get_references`.
items.summary: code_get_definition: LSP output paths are not re-sanitized against workspace allowlist (path disclosure to agent)

items.description: Mirrors the `code_get_definition` finding. `execute()` validates the input path but then emits `loc.path` (absolute LSP-server-controlled path from `loc.uri.path()`) into the JSON output without re-validating against the file security manager. References queries are even more likely to return paths spread across the whole project/include tree, including external/system headers, disclosing filesystem paths outside the agent's authorized workspace to the LLM. No relative-path conversion or workspace confinement is applied to the output.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize each output `loc.path` through `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(..., read)`; drop or redact entries pointing outside the authorized workspace, or emit them relative to the project root (only when they remain inside the root).
items.summary: code_get_references: same missing output path sanitization as code_get_definition

items.description: `fs_mkdir_tool::validate_runtime` only special-cases the `://` VFS path; for the normal disk path it simply `return true;` without re-running `ctx.fs_security.validate_access()` on `safe_path_`. Security currently relies entirely on the construction-time resolution done by `single_file_tool_validator` (which does validate and canonicalize). This is inconsistent with the `code_get_*` tools, whose `validate_runtime` re-validates the resolved path as defense in depth. Because the `fs_mkdir_tool` constructor is public and accepts an arbitrary string, any path that reaches `execute()` without going through the validator (or after a path doubt) will be passed straight to `std::filesystem::create_directories` with no allowlist check at runtime. The public ctor + runtime gap weakens the sandbox boundary if a future code path constructs the tool without the validator.
items.proposed_fix: Re-validate `safe_path_` in `validate_runtime` via `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(safe_path_, access_type::write, ...)` for the disk case (mirroring the code_get_* tools), instead of unconditionally returning true. Make the constructor accept a value already known to be validated, or perform the validation check at execute time as a safety net.
items.summary: fs_mkdir: validate_runtime does not re-validate the resolved disk path (defense-in-depth gap vs code_get_* tools)

items.description: For VFS paths (`safe_path_` containing `://`), `execute()` calls `vfs->create_directory(safe_path_)`. Whether a path-traversal escape is blocked depends entirely on the provider. For `tmp://` and `file://` the `file_vfs_provider::create_directory` does enforce a root-confinement check, but other registered providers derive `create_directory` from the base `vfs_provider` default (returns false) or may implement it without equivalent traversal checks. `fs_mkdir` accepts any scheme (validation in `validate_access` passes `tmp`, `file`, and `images` plus any existing VFS scheme), and `validate_runtime`/`execute` route any `://` path to the provider. The tool does not itself re-confirm the resolved physical path is inside the allowed root before delegating, so the security relies on each provider's best-effort check. Flagging as a defense-in-depth/consistency concern.
items.proposed_fix: Before delegating to the VFS, call `ctx.fs_security.validate_access(safe_path_, access_type::write, ...)` and only invoke `vfs->create_directory()` on the resolved path, so the tool itself enforces the workspace/write boundary regardless of provider implementation.
items.summary: fs_mkdir VFS path: relies on file_vfs_provider create_directory traversal check but only for 'tmp'/'file' providers

items.description: The `a2a_connect_server_tool` validator returns `get_family() == "base|a2a"` (a2a_connect_server_security.cpp:31-34). Since the `base` family is active by default and `prepare_tool` (tool_registry.cpp:291-302) considers a tool usable if ANY of its families is active, the `a2a` family designation provides NO actual access control here — the tool is always permitted regardless of whether the `a2a` tool family was explicitly activated. Combined with the lack of an SSRF allowlist (separate finding), this tool's outbound network capability is effectively always available to any agent role. Recommend gating the tool strictly behind the `a2a` family (removing `base` from its family string) so it is disabled unless the operator explicitly activates the `a2a` tool family, and confirming network-exfiltration/SSRF mitigations are in place since the tool will broadly be callable.
items.summary: a2a_connect_server family 'base|a2a' means it is always active regardless of a2a family gating

items.description: The fs_run_tests validator's validate_args_impl unconditionally returns true, performing no validation of the `timeout` (or `test_names`) arguments. The timeout is passed straight through to runner.set_timeout() and then to command_runner. In command_runner::should_continue(), a timeout_seconds_ of 0 or negative is treated as 'no timeout' (`if (timeout_seconds_ > 0)`), so an agent-supplied value of 0 (or negative) results in an unbounded test run that can only be stopped manually. This is inconsistent with the positive-bound validation done in similar tools (e.g. crashdump_list enforces limit > 0). Recommend validating timeout within an allowed range (e.g. 1..N) in validate_args_impl or create_tool_impl.
items.proposed_fix: In create_tool_impl (or validate_args_impl), clamp/reject timeout values <= 0 (and optionally enforce an upper bound), e.g. `if (timeout < 1) timeout = 300;`. Also consider validating that test_names entries contain only safe characters.
items.summary: fs_run_tests timeout argument is never validated, allowing unbounded execution

items.description: In the cmake build branch, resolved test names are concatenated directly into a ctest `-R "(" ... ")"` regular expression with no regex-escaping (and no shell-escaping, since the regex is quoted but still passed to /bin/sh -c). Although the names originate from the project's available-tests list (resolved via substring expansion), test names that legitimately contain regex metacharacters (e.g. '.', '+', '|', '(') — the code even uses '|' as the separator — can alter the regex semantics, cause a malformed-regex ctest failure, or match an unintended set of tests. The meson branch correctly uses escape_shell_arg() for the arguments. Recommend regex-escaping each name (e.g. std::regex_replace with '\$&') or validating the test-name charset before embedding it into the -R expression.
items.line_content:
for (size_t i = 0; i < resolved.size(); ++i) {
				cmd += resolved[i];
items.proposed_fix: Escape regex metacharacters in each resolved name before building the -R expression (e.g. escape `\^$.|?*+()[]{})`), or constrain test names to an allowed character set.
items.summary: cmake path concatenates test names into ctest -R regex without escaping

items.description: The crash_id validator only rejects empty values; it does not restrict the character set. crash_id flows into two places in the entry code: (1) `fs::path(dump_dir) / ("crash_" + crash_id)` in has_coredump() where a crafted value containing path separators / '..' could traverse to an unexpected directory (mitigated somewhat because has_coredump() is only reached when crash_id matches an entry in the in-memory dump list); and (2) a `coredumpctl --user info {}` subprocess. The shell invocation is escaped via escape_shell_arg(), so command injection is blocked, but the path construction and the subprocess would both benefit from the same alphanumeric/'-'/'_' whitelist already enforced by agent_debug_coredump_validator for the identical crash_id parameter. Recommend applying the same charset validation for consistency and defense-in-depth.
items.proposed_fix: Reject crash_id values containing anything other than [A-Za-z0-9_-] in crashdump_get_info_validator::validate_args_impl, mirroring agent_debug_coredump_validator.
items.summary: crashdump_get_info does not validate crash_id character set (defense-in-depth)

items.description: crashdump_get_info_tool::execute returns dump.raw_info (the full backtrace + memory-map report generated from crash files) with no length cap. A crash dump with a very large memory map or verbose backtrace could produce a multi-megabyte string that is returned directly to the LLM context, unlike fs_run_tests which enforces a 10,000-character cap. This risks blowing out the agent's context window. Recommend truncating output to a sane limit (with a marker) before returning.
items.proposed_fix: Cap result length (e.g. 10,000-50,000 chars) and append a truncation marker, mirroring the fs_run_tests output-cap pattern.
items.summary: crashdump_get_info returns unbounded raw_info without output cap

items.description: crashdump_clear_tool::execute unconditionally calls clear_all(), which performs fs::remove_all() on the entire project dump directory (deleting all crash report directories, including any coredumps that may still be needed for forensics). There is no confirmation step and no scope restriction, and any agent permitted to run this tool can silently destroy all crash evidence. While clear_all() is correctly marked is_pure()==false (so it is blocked in read-only mode), an LLM could invoke it mid-investigation and permanently erase data that cannot be recovered. Recommend adding an explicit confirmation/guard and documenting the irreversibility, or restricting it to an explicit user-approved workflow.
items.proposed_fix: Consider requiring an explicit confirmation argument or user approval before triggering the destructive remove_all, and/or gating this tool behind a higher-privilege role.
items.summary: crashdump_clear is a destructive all-or-nothing deletion invoked without confirmation

items.description: The 'args' parameter is passed verbatim (un-escaped) into a shell command string that editor::start_app (src/editor_events_ui.cpp:1002 non-debugger path, and :946 debugger/gdbserver path) executes with `execl("/bin/bash", "bash", "-c", sandboxed_cmd, ...)` (src/ui/terminal_window.cpp:161). The ONLY defense against shell injection is this blacklist of `; & | \` $ < > ( ) \n \r` characters. Blacklists are fragile and incomplete: single/double quotes, backslash, globs, `~`, `#`, `!`, tabs, and other shell metacharacters are NOT filtered, and the args are concatenated raw into the command string (e.g. `std::format(" {}", args)` at editor_events_ui.cpp:1002 for non-debugger, and `gdbserver_cmd += std::format(" {}", args)` at :946 for the gdbserver path, both of which are later run via bash -c). Any future call path to editor::start_app that bypasses this validator, or any oversight in the blacklist, yields arbitrary command execution in the sandbox. Defense-in-depth requires shell-escaping each argument at command construction time (the code already uses fs_utils::escape_shell_arg for the executable path / fifo path but NOT for args) rather than relying solely on a character blacklist in the validator. Recommended fix: escape args tokens with fs_utils::escape_shell_arg at the call site, or build argv directly without the shell, and keep the blacklist only as a secondary guard.
items.summary: agent_start_app: raw 'args' concatenated into bash -c command; only an incomplete blacklist protects against shell injection

items.description: When the 'output' flag is true, recorded PTY output is accumulated into output_str and returned verbatim to the LLM agent. The recorded data is only sanitized (utf8::sanitize_terminal_output) when the terminal window's sanitize_recorded_data_ flag is enabled — and that flag is only set on "Debugger (GDB)" windows (editor_events_ui.cpp:933, terminal_window.cpp:593-601). For the normal "Run Output" application window (the common case), the raw recorded data, including any terminal control characters / ANSI escape sequences / malicious text emitted by the running (potentially untrusted) program, is returned un-sanitized. This is an output-injection / prompt-injection vector where a compromised or untrusted child process can inject control sequences or textual instructions into the agent's context. Also note the returned value is a raw string (not JSON), so there is no structured escaping. Recommend always sanitizing recorded data before returning it to the agent (or at minimum for the app window too), and capping the returned size.
items.summary: agent_write_to_run: recorded PTY output returned raw (unsanitized) enabling output/prompt injection to the agent

items.description: agent_start_app's wait_for_time is only validated as `>= 0` with no upper bound. In agent_start_app_entry.cpp:33-40, when wait_for_time > 0 the tool synchronously calls ctx.doc_provider->wait_for_app(run_id, "ended", wait_for_time), which blocks on the agent thread for up to wait_for_time seconds looping with only a 50ms sleep (editor_events_ui.cpp:1177-1254). In contrast, the separate agent_wait_for_app tool correctly caps timeout_sec at 300 (agent_wait_for_app_security.cpp:61). An LLM or caller passing a very large wait_for_time (e.g. days/weeks) would block the agent's execution thread for that duration — a self-DoS / availability concern, and an inconsistency with the sibling tool's bound. Recommend adding an upper bound consistent with agent_wait_for_app (e.g. 1..300).
items.summary: agent_start_app: wait_for_time validated only as non-negative (no upper bound) allowing long synchronous blocking / DoS of agent thread

items.description: The screenshot grid (vector of glyph strings read verbatim from the terminal emulator via terminal_window::get_screenshot, terminal_window.cpp:562-583) is placed raw into the JSON response. These glyphs originate from the (potentially untrusted) running program's output and are returned to the LLM agent context without filtering of control characters or validation of UTF-8. Malicious/terminal-emitted content can (a) inject misleading text/prompt-injection data into the agent context, and (b) contain bytes that break JSON serialization or leak control characters. The application-window screenshot path has no sanitization (sanitize_recorded_data_ only applies to recorded data, not get_screenshot). Recommend sanitizing each grid line with the existing utf8::sanitize_terminal_output before embedding in JSON, consistent with the recorded-data path.
items.summary: agent_get_run_screenshot: terminal grid embedded in JSON without control-character / UTF-8 sanitization

items.description: Unlike the other validators in this set (which persist validated values into a member `args_` in validate_args_impl and have create_tool_impl ignore the passed-in json), agent_get_run_screenshot_validator's validate_args_impl validates args but stores nothing, and create_tool_impl re-deserializes directly from the raw `args` json parameter (which may be a different/untracked snapshot than the one validated). This breaks the 'validate-then-reuse-validated-state' invariant used elsewhere and creates a minor TOCTOU / consistency hazard: if create_tool_impl is ever handed different raw args than those validated (e.g. the run_id validation for >=0 still happens in execute(), but `settle` is never validated here), the tool could run with a value that was never validated. Recommend storing validated values into a member and having create_tool_impl use it, matching the sibling validators.
items.summary: agent_get_run_screenshot validator does not persist validated args; create_tool_impl re-reads raw args (TOCTOU/consistency)

items.description: Project rule requires all `#include ""` to be relative to src/ (e.g. "agentlib/tool_registry.h"). agent_start_app_security.cpp, agent_terminate_run_security.cpp, and agent_write_to_run_security.cpp (and their headers) use `../../agentlib/...` relative paths, while agent_wait_for_app_security.cpp, agent_get_run_screenshot_security.cpp and the newer .cpp files consistently use `agentlib/...` / `tools/...` src-relative includes. This inconsistency is a maintainability nit and risks broken or non-portable builds when files/directories are relocated. Recommend normalizing to src-relative includes.
items.summary: Inconsistent include style: several *_security.cpp use ../../agentlib/... instead of src-relative agentlib/...

items.description: The claimed 'stray editor backup file committed' is not accurate. `git ls-files src/tools/agent_write_to_run/` lists only the real .h/.cpp files, and the `*.~` pattern is matched by `.gitignore:3` (`*~`), so `agent_write_to_run_security.cpp~` is NOT tracked in the repository (git status shows it as ignored). While the file does physically exist in the working tree, it is neither committed nor a source of repo pollution, and it cannot be accidentally opened as a wrong file in version control. The finding overstates the severity/impact. (Optionally deleting the local artifact or documenting it could be done, but there is no committed-stray-file defect.)
items.summary: Stray editor backup file committed: agent_write_to_run_security.cpp~

items.description: The validator only rejects an empty 'path'. Any other string (including Windows paths 'C:\\...' or '..' traversal like '../../../../usr/bin/python') is accepted and persisted via config_manager::set_main_executable(), then written to the project/global config by agent_set_application_binary_tool::execute(). This value is later consumed by editor::start_app() (src/editor_events_ui.cpp:888-901) which resolves it -- first under project_root/'build'/exe, then project_root/exe, then the raw string -- and executes it directly (or via gdbserver) through start_process/terminal_window with a shell. Because the resolved path falls back to the raw string, an agent can set the main executable to an arbitrary path on the host and then invoke agent_start_app to execute it, bypassing the intended 'relative to build/ directory' contract and the sandbox's intended working-directory containment. There is no canonicalization, no check that the path stays within the build/ dir or project root, and no enforcement that it is an actually-built target.
items.proposed_fix: Canonicalize and contain the path: reject absolute paths, reject any '.' or '..' components, and require the path (lexically_normal relative to project_root/'build') to resolve to an existing regular file inside the build directory before persisting it. Also validate against executable-name characters (no spaces, no shell metacharacters). Optionally verify it is a known meson executable target before accepting.
items.summary: agent_set_application_binary: no path containment validation on executable path shared to start_app (arbitrary execution / sandbox bypass)**

items.description: When no file_path/function_name filter is supplied, execute() copies ALL of report.top_lines into matched_samples. For each hot line it expands to a +/-2 line window plus the symbol bounds, and embeds the raw source file contents (file_lines[line_num-1]) into the JSON (line 430). There is no cap on the number of samples, files, or total output bytes. A broad profile (or a substring match that over-matches, since match_symbol_string uses substring containment both ways) can produce a very large JSON payload that is returned into the LLM context window, causing context flooding. Broad substring matches also inflate matched_samples significantly. This is an unbounded-output-into-context concern: the tool can be triggered to dump a large amount of source code.
items.proposed_fix: Impose an explicit cap on the number of line entries emitted (e.g. a maximum like 200-500 entries per call), and on total output bytes. Truncate and include a 'truncated' flag when the limit is hit. Consider bounding the +/-2 line expansion and using exact symbol-bound matching rather than bidirectional substring matching by default.
items.summary: agent_get_profile_details: unbounded source-code output into LLM context (no size cap)

items.description: resolve_file_path() lets an absolute input path fall straight through to the candidate list (line 270-271 pushes the raw absolute path) and returns it whenever it exists and is not a directory -- no check that the returned path is inside the project root or the configured build dir. It is then passed to read_file_lines() (line 415) which opens it with std::ifstream and the contents are embedded into the returned JSON. So an attacker/WRIGHT-able profile whose file_path is an absolute path (e.g. '/etc/passwd' or '/home/user/secret') yields an arbitrary-file read whose contents are returned to the LLM. Additionally, the final fallback (lines 294-301) performs a recursive_directory_iterator over the entire project root matching by basename and returns the first match -- it follows directory listings of large trees and does not handle symlinks specially, so a symlink inside the project tree can redirect reads outside the sandbox. There is no symlink-resolution containment (no fs_utils safe_absolute / canonical containment check) applied to the resolved path before opening it.
items.proposed_fix: After resolving the candidate, verify the canonical path (std::filesystem::canonical) stays within the project root (or a configurable allowed set such as the build dir + source dir), and reject results of the recursive scan that escape the tree. Reject absolute input paths that are not inside the project. Resolve symlinks and re-check containment before opening the file. Reuse the existing safe_absolute/equivalent containment helpers in fs_utils.
items.summary: agent_get_profile_details: resolve_file_path permits reading arbitrary files (no containment / symlink handling)

items.description: The validator rejects limit<=0 but imposes no upper bound. An agent can pass a very large 'limit' (e.g. 100000), causing execute() to iterate and emit up to two times 'limit' JSON objects (top_functions + top_lines) from the profile report straight into the LLM context. While the underlying report is finite in size, there is no explicit cap, so combined with the default behavior this permits unbounded expansion of the returned payload relative to what the caller needed.
items.proposed_fix: Clamp limit to a sane maximum (e.g. 100) in the validator, in addition to the existing >0 check.
items.summary: agent_get_profile_summary: 'limit' unbounded on the upper side -> large output / context flood

items.description: execute() spawns a detached std::thread for each call with no upper bound on the number of simultaneous timers or on 'seconds' (validate_runtime only checks seconds > 0; validate_args_impl imposes no limit at all). Each detached thread captures a shared_ptr to the active agent (keeping it alive until the timer fires). An agent could issue many agent_set_timer calls (or one per turn) to spawn unbounded detached threads/sleeps, creating a resource-exhaustion vector and, because threads are detached, providing no lifecycle/join control or shutdown coordination. There is also no cap preventing absurdly long sleeps from pinning the agent's shared_ptr forever. Per the project's thread-lifecycle guidelines, detached, unmanaged threads are discouraged.
items.proposed_fix: Bound the number of pending timers (e.g. allow at most one active timer per agent, or track timers in a manager with a max count) and clamp 'seconds' to an upper limit. Keep the timer handle in a managed structure (not fire-and-forget detach) so it can be cancelled/joined on agent shutdown, and only hold the agent shared_ptr while actually needed.
items.summary: agent_set_timer: unbounded detached threads holding shared_ptr to agent (resource exhaustion / lifetime)

items.description: Both profile tools accept an arbitrary run_id string with no character validation. perf_manager::normalize_run_id() will pass through any arbitrary string unchanged (it only special-cases empty/'editor'/'latest', 'run_' prefix and all-digits). While currently used only as a map key into saved_reports_ (not as a filesystem path here), the permissive normalization means an arbitrary/non-canonical key can be stored (via set_active_profile) and later looked up, which is fragile and, if run_id is ever used to build a file path (e.g. in get_project_perf_dir flows), could contribute to traversal. Recommend validating the charset (alphanumeric/_/-) and rejecting anything else.
items.proposed_fix: Validate run_id in the validators against a safe charset (alphanumeric, '_', '-') and reject anything else, or at least enforce normalization in one place so arbitrary strings cannot become keys/filesystem components.
items.summary: agent_get_profile_details / agent_get_profile_summary: run_id normalized but not validated for dangerous characters

items.description: The `episode_id` argument is fully attacker-controlled (it comes from the LLM toolcall) and `validate_args_impl()` performs NO validation whatsoever: no character whitelist, no rejection of path separators or `..`, no length check. It is passed verbatim into `ai_agent::page_in_context()` -> `set_episode_state()`, which concatenates `history_dir + "/" + episode_id + ".json"` and `history_dir + "/" + episode_id + "_metadata.json"`, checks `std::filesystem::exists()`, opens the file with `ifstream`, and `Episode::deserialize(root)`s the JSON. An episode_id like `../../../../<some_dir>/file` (with the `.json` suffix, so limited to JSON files) escapes the history directory and lets a malicious agent read arbitrary `.json` files from disk and inject their content into the active conversation context (prompt-injection / data-exfiltration path). Even without traversal, episode IDs can contain control characters. Fix: validate episode_id against a strict allowlist (e.g. matching `episode_[0-9]+` or a safe identifier pattern) before use, and reject any `..`, `/`, `\`, or control characters.
items.proposed_fix: Add a strict validation step: reject episode_id unless it matches a safe pattern (^[A-Za-z0-9_:-]+$), does not contain `/`, `\`, `..`, or control chars, and is length-bounded. Alternatively sanitize/normalize the resolved path and enforce it stays under get_project_history_dir (fs_utils already has is_valid_db_name-style allowlist helpers to reuse).
items.summary: Path traversal in agent_restore_context episode_id allows arbitrary JSON file read into LLM context

items.description: agent_restore_context_validator::is_pure() returns true (header line 28), and validate_runtime() here only checks `!ctx.active_agent->is_mutation_possible()` — it does NOT check `ctx.active_agent->is_read_only()` (unlike agent_compress_history, which explicitly checks both). In tool_registry::prepare_tool, the read-only gate is `if (ctx.properties.read_only && !validator->is_pure(args))`, so because this tool claims to be pure, a read-only agent passes the gate, and because validate_runtime never checks read_only, a read-only agent CAN execute agent_restore_context. This pages an entire archived episode (potentially containing attacker-influenced content) into the agent's active LLM context — effectively a read-only-mode bypass and a prompt-injection vector. is_pure()==true is also semantically wrong: this tool mutates agent conversation/context state.
items.proposed_fix: Add an explicit read-only guard in validate_runtime (mirror agent_compress_history): if (ctx.active_agent->is_read_only()) reject. Also reconsider is_pure() returning true for a tool that injects context state; it should return false so the registry-level read-only gate blocks it as well.
items.summary: Read-only sandbox bypass: agent_restore_context marked is_pure and validate_runtime omits is_read_only check

items.description: agent_compress_history_validator claims is_pure()==true (header line 55) and is_silent_by_default() derives from is_pure(). However this tool performs a state-mutating operation: it erases conversation turns and replaces them with a summary pointer, reorganizes episode state, and even spawns an LLM summarization. is_pure() is documented as 'has no persistent side effects on the project codebase' — while paging context is arguably not a 'project codebase' mutation, the is_silent_by_default() side effect means its side effects are hidden from the UI by default, which weakens auditability. More importantly the semantic overlap with the read-only gate (registry allows pure tools in read-only mode) risks this state-mutating tool being runnable by read-only agents. It happens to have an explicit is_read_only() check in validate_runtime which mitigates the read-only path, but the is_pure()/is_silent_by_default() classification is misleading for a compound tool with LLM-triggered summarization side effects.
items.line_content: bool is_pure() const override { return true; }
items.proposed_fix: Reconsider is_pure() for these context-management tools. If a tool should not run under read-only agents, it must return false for is_pure() so the registry-level gate blocks it, rather than relying solely on per-tool runtime checks (which can be omitted, as agent_restore_context demonstrates). At minimum document why context paging is treated as pure.
items.summary: agent_compress_history marked is_pure despite state-mutating side effects; misleading classification weakens auditability

items.description: agent_list_episodes_tool::execute() outputs each episode's `reactivation_hint` verbatim into a markdown table that is returned as the tool result, which is fed straight back into the LLM context (set_success + return res). The reactivation_hint is machine-generated by the background summarizer from archived episode content (ai_agent::summary_worker_loop calls the LLM and stores res.msg.content verbatim via update_episode_hint), and these hints are persisted in metadata files on disk. An archived episode whose content contains prompt-injection instructions can cause the summarizer to emit a malicious 'hint' that is later re-injected into the primary agent's context through this tool (and also through inject_archived_episodes_summary). There is NO sanitization of the hint before it is placed into LLM context: no stripping of control chars, no fence/role-escape handling, and no length cap at output time (the fallback caps at 500 but LLM-generated hints are uncapped). This is a stored/second-order prompt injection channel. Fix: sanitize reactivation_hint before reflection into context (strip control chars, cap length), wrap output in an explicit untrusted-data boundary, and avoid echoing raw LLM-generated hint text into primary context.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize reactivation_hint before including it in output (e.g. reject/strip control characters and ANSI escapes, cap length, replace '|' to avoid table injection). Treat the hint as untrusted data and clearly delimit it in the returned markdown. Consider capping LLM-generated hint length in update_episode_hint as well.
items.summary: agent_list_episodes reflects unsanitized LLM-generated reactivation hints into context (stored prompt injection)

items.description: This tool constructs the input prompt shown to the user and the returned answer is injected back into the LLM context. Issues: (1) The `question` text and the `options` strings are completely attacker-controlled (from the LLM toolcall) and contain NO validation: no control-character/ANSI-escape stripping, no newline-delimiter/UI-spoof sanitization, and no length limits. Since these strings are rendered in a dialog and echoed back into the conversation stream, a malicious agent can embed ANSI escape sequences or spoofed UI text; this is especially relevant because reactivation_hint / episode content are attacker-influenceable. (2) There is an asymmetry/robustness concern: only the FIRST question in the 'questions' array is processed while the schema advertises an arbitrary-length array; any subsequent question is silently dropped, which could lead the agent and user to believe multiple prompts were handled.
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize the question and each option through fs_utils::is_safe_for_ui (or equivalent control-char/ANSI stripping), enforce max length limits on question and options, and either support the full questions array or reject with a clear error when more than one question is supplied.
items.summary: ask_user does not sanitize question/options (control chars, ANSI, length) and silently drops all but the first question

items.description: agent_mark_episode_tool uses raw C++ string concatenation to build the interaction system message: `"Episode Marked: " + args_.title + "\nSummary: " + args_.summary` (entry line 8), and the executor embeds args_.title/summary into the returned result. The security validator enforces only non-empty and length<=500; it does NOT strip control characters, ANSI escapes, or newline tricks. The title/summary are LLM-controlled and persist to episode metadata files and get re-read by load_episode_index and later injected into context (get_memory_index, inject_archived_episodes_summary). Embedding raw LLM text into a system message and into persisted metadata that later gets reflected into context is a prompt-injection/UI-spoofing channel. Also note agent_compress_history_validator DOES call is_safe_for_ui on title and rejects control chars in summary, but agent_mark_episode does NOT apply the same hygiene — an inconsistency that leaves this tool un-hardened.
items.proposed_fix: Apply the same control-character/ANSI sanitization used by agent_compress_history (fs_utils::is_safe_for_ui for title and a multiline-safe check for summary) in the validator, and prefer std::format for building the message. This prevents malicious control sequences from being embedded in persisted metadata that is later reflected into LLM context.
items.summary: agent_mark_episode embeds raw LLM-controlled title/summary into system message and persisted metadata without control-char sanitization

items.description: Two related input-hygiene gaps in agent_compress_history_validator: (1) the `tags` array items are never validated — no per-tag length limit, no control-char/ANSI stripping (loop at lines 61-78 only checks title and summary, not tags). Tags are LLM-controlled and are written into episode metadata files and echoed back into context in page_out_context (pointer_msg "...Tags: [...]") and get_memory_index, so a malicious tag can carry control/ANSI sequences into persisted state and into LLM context. (2) the length checks use `.length()` (byte count, fine for ASCII) but the summary control-char check uses a local lambda rather than the shared fs_utils helper, duplicating logic that can drift — and the title uses is_safe_for_ui which rejects ALL c < 32 including TAB/LF/CR, whereas the summary lambda allows TAB/LF/CR; this is a documented inconsistency but acceptable given one-line vs multiline semantics. The tags omission is the actual gap.
items.proposed_fix: Validate each tag: cap length (e.g. 100), reject control characters/ANSI escapes with is_safe_for_ui, and reject empty tags. This prevents LLM-controlled tags from carrying malicious sequences into persisted metadata and into LLM-reflected context.
items.summary: agent_compress_history tags array is not validated (no length/control-char/ANSI limits) despite being persisted and reflected into context

items.description: agent_restore_context_validator::validate_args_impl does not validate the `compression_level` integer against its documented range (0..3, default 1). The schema says 0=Raw, 1=Think-Free, 2=Terminal Truncated, 3=Highly Aggressive. An out-of-range or negative value is accepted and passed straight to ai_agent::page_in_context -> set_episode_state. While the current set_episode_state only compares against COMPACTION_LEVEL_PAGED_OUT, relying on downstream comparisons means future refactors could misinterpret attacker-controlled out-of-range levels; at minimum it should be range-clamped/rejected at the boundary to keep argument validation complete and consistent with the other tools in this family.
items.proposed_fix: Validate/clamp compression_level to the documented 0..3 range (reject out-of-range values) during arg validation.
items.summary: agent_restore_context does not validate compression_level integer range (0..3)

items.description: The validator declares `is_pure() { return true; }` with the comment that "Subagent orchestration does not modify project codebase". This is incorrect and creates a privilege/scoping bypass: tool_registry::prepare_tool (src/agentlib/tool_registry.cpp:318) only blocks a tool from a read-only agent when `!validator->is_pure(args)`. Because invoke_subagent is reported as pure, a summarizer/read-only agent is permitted to invoke the tool, and the tool then injects a `profile` (arbitrary system-prompt text supplied by the caller) into a newly spawned mutable subagent (invoke_subagent_entry.cpp:95-126). Spawning a full-powered subagent is a state/mutation-capable operation (it can run git, shell, file, and process tools with the profile acting as unvalidated system instructions), so this is not read-only behavior. The allowlist is inverted with respect to the security intent. Either the whole orchestration must be gated on read-only (validate_runtime already attempts this) so that is_pure()=false is correct, and the injected profile must not be treated as trusted system instructions; the current is_pure()=true is inconsistent with the tool's own read-only guards and with the registry's central check. (validate_runtime does return an error for read-only agents at runtime, and the Stage 2 runtime check is also enforced in execute() directly - see line 38-40 - so the practical runtime guard holds; nevertheless, marking it pure defeats the registry-level read-only filter and relies solely on the tool's own runtime check, and the profile-as-system-prompt injection is a prompt-injection amplifier for spawned agents. Recommend is_pure()=false and explicit review of the injected profile handling.)
items.line_content:
return true;
	} // Subagent orchestration does not modify project codebase
items.proposed_fix: Set `is_pure()` to return false, and instead gate spawning on `ctx.active_agent->is_read_only()` (already done in validate_args_impl and validate_runtime). Treat `profile`/`task` as untrusted content that is submitted to the subagent prompt, not as an authoritative expansion, and ensure the spawned subagent's read-only/property constraints are derived from the profile's declared properties only when the caller is privileged.
items.summary: invoke_subagent marked is_pure()=true enables subagent spawn even in read-only agents

items.description: Validation of `subagent_name` (or the fallback `name`) splits on the first ':' to detect remote A2A invocation. However, the schema advertises an `enum` of known local subagent names for `subagent_name`, yet a caller can supply an arbitrary 'server:agent' string that is not in the enum but passes validation (the colon branch only checks that the server exists in the registry). Additionally the `local_only` flag just forbids the colon form; `name` is required in the schema while `subagent_name` is optional, so `name` may carry the remote target instead. This is mostly a UX/consistency issue, but combined with the `profile` injection (which is passed verbatim to a remote A2A agent) it means unvalidated profile content and repository_url/git_ref are forwarded to a remote server selected by a colon-prefixed string. Confirm the colon target and that the `name`-as-target fallback path matches the schema's documented required 'name' semantics; otherwise the effective target selection (entry uses `target_name = subagent_name.empty()? name : subagent_name`) diverges from what the enum implies and could let a caller target a remote server while intending a local profile.
items.proposed_fix: Clarify the schema so the remote ('server:agent') form is intentional (e.g. a separate explicit `server`/`agent` param), and validate that the remote agent name component does not itself contain characters that could alter the prompt sent to the server; document that profile/task are forwarded untrusted to the remote server.
items.summary: subagent_name enum bounds are enforced during validation but remote ('server:agent') form bypasses profile existence check while local_only only checked via colon

items.description: In validate_args_impl() (lines 52-56), ctx.fs_security.validate_access(...) canonicalizes the model-supplied path and returns the fully resolved safe path into the local variable `safe_path` (allowlist + symlink + ignore-pattern enforcement). That validated result is then DISCARDED — it is a local variable never stored into args_ or any member. In create_tool_impl() (lines 61-76) the raw, un-canonicalized `args["path"]` is copied verbatim into `t_args.safe_path` with the comment "We will validate again in execute or just use the filename", but execute() (flag_as_error_entry.cpp) performs NO re-validation and simply uses args_.safe_path. The defense-in-depth boundary computed at validation time is therefore thrown away, so the stored build_error.filepath is the raw relative/symlinked model path rather than the canonical allowed path. This defeats the purpose of validate_access (canonicalization/allowlist-normalization) and can cause the error overlay to be attached to a non-canonical path that editor lookups (build_error_manager::find_error_at compares exact filepath strings) will not match. Fix: store the canonical path (e.g., in the validator args / flags) at validation time and use it in create_tool_impl, or re-run validate_access in execute().
items.line_content: t_args.safe_path = path; // We will validate again in execute or just use the filename
items.proposed_fix: Have validate_args_impl persist the resolved canonical path (e.g., store it into a member/store the returned `safe_path`), and in create_tool_impl() set `t_args.safe_path = <canonical path>` instead of `args["path"]`. Do not rely on "validate again in execute" which is never implemented.
items.summary: Validated canonical path is discarded in flag_as_error; raw untrusted path used in execution

items.description: `args_.error_string` arrives from the untrusted LLM/tool payload and is stored verbatim into build_error.message (line 18), which is subsequently rendered as an error overlay in the editor UI. There is no sanitization of ANSI escape sequences or control characters (unlike create_code_review_item_entry.cpp, which strips C0 controls via sanitize_for_parent_line()), and no length cap. If the UI renders the message without stripping escapes, this is an ANSI/injection surface that could corrupt the terminal or present misleading content. Length is also unbounded, which can bloat the shared build_error_list. Recommend sanitizing/escaping untrusted message content and bounding its length before storage.
items.proposed_fix: Reuse/refactor the sanitize_for_parent_line-style filter (strip C0 control characters and clamp length) on args_.error_string before assigning to err.message, or ensure the render path strips ESC sequences.
items.summary: flag_as_error: model-supplied error_string is not sanitized before display; potential escape/control-char injection and unbounded size

items.description: send_message accepts an arbitrary `id` integer and a free-form `message`. In `execute()` (send_message_entry.cpp) the `id` is matched against `ctx.active_agent->get_subagents()` and the message is delivered via `target_agent->submit_prompt(args_.message)`. Two issues: (1) There is no length/control-character sanitization of the message before it is injected into the subagent's prompt via submit_prompt. The security validator only enforces a max length (100KB) and non-empty; it does not strip control characters/terminal escape sequences (unlike invoke_subagent which at least calls is_safe_multiline and is_safe_for_ui). A prompt containing ANSI escape sequences or control bytes will be echoed back through agent_get_output/UI flows and rendered by the TUI, enabling terminal escape-sequence injection / UI spoofing (prompt injection to the subagent AND terminal injection to the operator). (2) Because messages are submitted via submit_prompt without explicit framing, a message containing its own "instructions" can be interpreted as authoritative commands by the subagent - the sender (which can be a compromised agent) controls exactly what the subagent executes. Recommend explicit framing as untrusted data and control-char sanitization (reuse fs_utils::is_safe_for_ui / an is_safe_multiline helper).
items.proposed_fix: Sanitize the delivered message: reject/strip control characters and ANSI escape sequences (reuse fs_utils::is_safe_for_ui and a multiline-safety check as done in invoke_subagent) and frame the message downstream as untrusted user content rather than an authoritative system instruction.
items.summary: send_message delivers unsanitized message (no control-char/escape filtering) into subagent prompt and terminal output

items.description: send_message_validator has `is_pure() { return true; }`. While enqueueing a prompt to an already-running subagent is not itself a filesystem mutation, it programs the subagent to perform arbitrary work including state-modifying tools. When a read-only (summarizer) agent is in read-only mode and is marked non-pure tools are blocked (tool_registry.cpp:318), send_message would remain permitted and could instruct a mutable subagent to run mutating tools. Also, send_message_validator::validate_args_impl ignores the `ctx` and does not check `ctx.active_agent->is_read_only()`, unlike invoke_subagent and kill_subagent. This is a privilege/scoping inconsistency: a read-only agent can message a mutable subagent and thereby indirectly cause mutations. Additionally validate_runtime only checks for an active agent, not read-only. Recommend either marking send_message as non-pure and adding a read-only guard, or clearly document that messaging a subagent is allowed even from read-only contexts (in which case the spawned subagent must itself enforce its own read-only policy).
items.proposed_fix: Add an explicit `ctx.active_agent->is_read_only()` guard in validate_args_impl (and/or mark is_pure() false) so a read-only agent cannot drive a mutable subagent to perform mutations, unless that is the intended policy.
items.summary: send_message is_pure()=true and lacks a read-only guard, letting a read-only agent drive a mutable subagent

items.description: `wait_for_subagent` performs `target_agent->wait_until_idle()` which is a blocking wait on the agent's status_cv_ (ai_agent.cpp:576-585) and can block indefinitely if the target relies on parent progress, or for as long as the target's blocking tools run. There is no timeout parameter or cancellation. In particular a synchronous agent waiting on a subagent whose run-loop thread is itself blocked inside a synchronously executing tool (e.g. that subagent's own wait_for_subagent/invoke_subagent wait=true) can deadlock: wait_until_idle() on the parent blocks while the subagent's run-loop is blocked waiting on ITS parent (or vice-versa), and the code comment in ai_agent.cpp start_processing explicitly notes agents wait on their own run-loop thread inside blocking tools. Because the tool blocks the agent's run-loop thread while waiting, any prompt queued to the parent cannot be processed to break the cycle (a self-heal path relies on the run-loop resuming after the blocking tool unblocks). At minimum the wait should be bounded/timeout-capable, and cycles (parent waits on child while child waits on parent) should be detected to avoid indefinite hangs / resource exhaustion. Also note wait_for_subagent returns success even though its is_pure() is true and it modifies agent status, which is only a minor inconsistency.
items.proposed_fix: Add an optional timeout to wait_until_idle/wait_for_subagent and detect parent<->child wait cycles to prevent indefinite blocking and DoS of the agent's run-loop thread.
items.summary: wait_for_subagent blocks indefinitely with no timeout and can deadlock in parent/child wait cycles

items.description: In validate_args_impl() (lines 52-71) of create_code_review_item_security.cpp, canceld_path is validated for READ access via validate_access(parsed.path, read, canonical_path, ...). However, the create_code_review_item_tool::execute() then optionally READS the file to auto-fill line_content. The read is performed directly using raw LLM input: for a plain disk path, `std::ifstream f(args_.safe_path)` where args_.safe_path was set to the canonical path returned by validate_access, so the disk-read path is safe. BUT for VFS URIs, execute() uses `ctx.fs_security.get_vfs()->read_file(args_.safe_path)` to read arbitrary file content, which it then echoes back verbatim into the agent's context via `parent->inject_context(...)`?
