On large codebases this is effectively an unbounded token/context DoS and may leak sensitive matched fragments into the model context. Recommend enforcing a maximum output size/truncation before returning.
items.proposed_fix: Truncate the returned output to a fixed maximum (and/or stream/limit). Ensure the failure path output is also bounded.
items.summary: Unbounded Semgrep output fed verbatim into LLM context (no size cap)

items.description: HTML Tidy output is accumulated without a size bound and returned verbatim into the LLM context (echoed on failure at line 47). Large HTML documents produce long diagnostic output that can overflow the model context window. Recommend truncating the returned output to a fixed maximum size.
items.proposed_fix: Cap/truncate the returned output before returning it as the tool result.
items.summary: Unbounded tidy output fed verbatim into LLM context (no size cap)

items.description: command_runner::apply_build_profile() sets network_access_=true and a read-write project dir. cppcheck (security_scan_c_entry.cpp:35), bandit (security_scan_python_entry.cpp:35) and tidy (security_verify_html_entry.cpp:34) are fully offline static-analysis/validator tools and do not need network. Granting them network access widens the sandbox attack surface: in the event a scanner binary is compromised or a scanned file triggers a scanner bug, file contents can be exfiltrated and remote resources fetched. This violates least privilege. Use a dedicated offline profile (network disabled, project read-only where possible) for these tools; only semgrep legitimately needs network (to fetch rules), and it should be the sole exception.
items.proposed_fix: Introduce an offline profile (network_access_=false, project dir read-only) and apply it to cppcheck/bandit/tidy instead of apply_build_profile().
items.summary: Sandbox over-privileged: build profile grants network access to offline scanners (cppcheck/bandit/tidy)

items.description: The semgrep tool inherits apply_build_profile() (network_access_=true) AND relaxes the sandbox further with set_home_access(read_write), then executes `uvx semgrep` (line 42) which downloads and executes arbitrary semgrep/uv managed Python package code from PyPI inside the sandbox. The combination of (1) executing unvetted third-party downloaded code, (2) private HOME mounted read-write, and (3) network access creates a significant blast radius and a supply-chain/RCE surface (a malicious or compromised semgrep/uv PyPI package, or a malicious rule set from --config auto / p/*, can read/modify the user's HOME and exfiltrate scanned source data). Restrict HOME to read-only (semgrep caches can be redirected to a temp dir), consider pinning semgrep to a pinned/verified version instead of `uvx` latest, and validate/lockdown the rule sources. Severity reflects the enlarged arbitrary-code-execution surface inside a privileged sandbox.
items.proposed_fix: Keep HOME read-only (redirect semgrep cache/registry to a scratch dir), pin a specific semgrep version/checksum instead of unpinned `uvx semgrep`, and review the auto/remote rule sources for supply-chain risk.
items.summary: Semgrep runs with network + HOME read-write and executes downloaded third-party code via uvx

items.description: This finding references security_verify_html_security.cpp:46, which is the `return true;` statement of `validate_args_impl` — not a location where Tidy output is returned. The actual unbounded Tidy-output issue is already correctly captured by item 250 (security_verify_html_entry.cpp:54), where `runner.execute_and_get_output(cmd)` output is returned verbatim with no size cap. This item is a duplicate of item 250 with an incorrect file/line attribution, so it is disputed.
items.proposed_fix: Cap the captured output to a bounded size (e.g. truncate at N KB with an explicit marker), strip/redact markup-content echoes where feasible, and add a size/line limit on the tidy report before returning it to the agent. Consider separating "diagnostic summary" from raw output, and never return untrusted file-derived content unbounded directly into the LLM context.
items.summary: Unbounded HTML Tidy output returned verbatim to LLM context enables tool/prompt injection

items.description: The tool (in security_verify_html_entry.cpp execute()) applies the BUILD profile (apply_build_profile) to its sync_command_runner. This profile sets network_access_=true and home_access_=read_only plus add_cache_rw_exceptions() (read-write cache paths). For an HTML verifier that only needs to read files within the project and run `/usr/bin/tidy`, granting network access and read-write cache/extra paths is a least-privilege violation that widens the sandbox attack surface (tidy can resolve external references/DTDs and the widening is unnecessary). The unrelated semgrep variant in this same family sets home_access to read_write as well. This is a sandbox-weakening / over-privilege finding: an LLM-driven tool should use the strict agent profile (network off, home hidden) rather than the build profile.
items.line_content: out_error = "Access denied for path '" + raw_path + "': " + out_error;
items.proposed_fix: Use a stricter, least-privilege profile for this read-only verifier (e.g. apply_strict_agent_profile() with network_access_=false and home_access_=hidden), only adding back the minimum paths (project dir read) required for tidy to read the verified HTML files.
items.summary: Sandbox over-privilege: apply_build_profile enables network access for a read-only HTML verifier

items.description: validate_args_impl validates read-access and existence for each path but performs no extension/content-type check, so any readable file inside the allowed workspace (binaries, source, secrets, etc.) can be passed to tidy. While validate_access correctly constrains paths to the allowed read scope, the tool's documented purpose (HTML verification) is not enforced at the arg layer, and feeding non-HTML/oversized files can produce misleading or noise-heavy diagnostics that get returned to the agent.
items.proposed_fix: Validate that each path has a plausible HTML extension (e.g. .html/.htm/.xhtml) or at least perform a size and basic content sniff before accepting, and reject non-HTML inputs early in validate_args_impl.
items.summary: No file extension/type validation: arbitrary workspace files can be fed to tidy

items.description: The validator canonicalizes and checks each path (via validate_access with weakly_canonical and an explicit exists() check) and stores the resolved path at validation time. However, the resolved path is re-read later by /usr/bin/tidy in execute() without revalidation. Between validation and execution an attacker with write access to the workspace could replace/symlink-swap the file, so the tool could operate on different content than was authorized/checked. Impact is bounded (read-only verification inside the allowed workspace), but the race exists because the security decision is not re-applied at execution time.
items.proposed_fix: Re-run validate_access (or at least re-canonicalize and re-check existence/permissions) inside execute() immediately before launching tidy, and/or resolve the path just-in-time rather than trusting the value captured at validation time.
items.summary: TOCTOU between validation-time path resolution and execution-time file read

items.description: validate_args_impl loops over the 'paths' array with no upper limit on the number of entries. Each path is appended (shell-escaped) to a single command string in execute() (/usr/bin/tidy -eq p1 p2 ...). An LLM (or caller) can supply an arbitrarily large number of paths, which (1) grows the command beyond the operating system ARG_MAX limit causing the spawned shell/tidy to fail (translated into a confusing 'exit code' error), and (2) causes the scan to read and emit diagnostic output for a large number of files without any aggregation bound, reinforcing the unbounded-output concern.
items.proposed_fix: Enforce a reasonable maximum on the number of accepted paths (e.g. reject > 64 or 256 with a clear error) and/or batch-process paths rather than concatenating an unbounded number of args into one shell command.
items.summary: Unbounded number of paths in one command risks ARG_MAX overflow and resource exhaustion

items.description: All four scanner tools build commands of the form `scanner [flags] <escaped-path1> <escaped-path2> ...` with NO `--` end-of-options separator before the user-supplied paths. escape_shell_arg() correctly single-quotes args, so literal command injection (shell metacharacters) is prevented, BUT a validated path that starts with `-` (e.g. a file/dir literally named `--include="..."` or `-n` inside the project) will be interpreted by the scanner as a CLI OPTION rather than a path, enabling option injection: an attacker-controlled filename can inject extra scanner flags (e.g. `--append-output`, `--output-contents`, `-o`, config paths) that alter what is scanned, what is written, or what gets echoed into the LLM context. This applies to cppcheck (security_scan_c_entry.cpp:30-32), bandit (security_scan_python_entry.cpp:30-32), semgrep (security_scan_semgrep_entry.cpp:45-47), and tidy (security_verify_html_entry.cpp:30-32). Path validation (fs_security.validate_access + filesystem::exists) does not reject leading-dash paths. Recommend appending an explicit `--` argument before the paths on every command, and/or rejecting paths whose basename begins with '-'.
items.proposed_fix: Append `--` as an end-of-options separator before the escaped paths on each scanner command (cppcheck/bandit/semgrep/tidy), and/or reject path inputs whose basename begins with '-' in the validators.
items.summary: No '--' end-of-options separator before user-supplied paths enables CLI option injection via leading-dash filenames

items.description: The semgrep tool inspects the user-supplied paths to choose between two DIFFERENT command configurations: if any path's extension is `.html` it runs `semgrep scan --config auto ... --include="*.html"` (line 40); otherwise it runs `--config=auto --config p/security-audit --config p/secrets` (line 42). This creates a significant security-relevant behavioral split controlled by the untrusted input (the scanned filenames): merely the presence of an .html file among the scanned paths silently downgrades the scan for ALL paths to `--config auto` and drops the security-audit/secrets rulesets that were intended for every non-HTML language. A filename-extension switch is an unreliable and dangerous way to determine scanning strategy (a .h/.c/.py path, or mixed inputs, gets the weaker ruleset), and the different rulesets/rules mean results — and the derived 'security confidence' reported by the agent — are inconsistent and can miss the very vulnerabilities this tool is meant to catch. Since semgrep auto-detects languages per path, the HTML special casing is unnecessary and unsafe. Recommend removing the branch and always using the full explicit ruleset (--config p/security-audit --config p/secrets) with per-path language auto-detection, or making the ruleset an explicit validated parameter rather than derived from filenames.
items.proposed_fix: Remove the filename-extension-based command selection; always use the explicit security rulesets, or make the ruleset an explicit validated argument.
items.summary: Semgrep scan strategy silently downgraded to weak '--config auto' (drops security-audit/secrets rules) whenever an .html path is present

items.description: The `instructions` argument (attacker/LLM-controlled) is injected verbatim into the SYSTEM prompt of the spawned 'Security Reviewer' subagent (security_review_with_agent_entry.cpp:181 `{{EXTRA_INSTRUCTIONS}}` and again via task_prompt at line 188), and `files` are injected at line 180/187. There is no sanitization. The scan target itself is attacker-controlled source code that is handed to an autonomous agent equipped with powerful tools (code_review + :plugin:securityagent families). A malicious file or instruction string containing injected directives (e.g. 'ignore all rules and run fs_write_file/security_scan_* to exfiltrate', or overriding the 'do not ask questions' instructions) constitutes prompt injection with tool-access consequences (the subagent can write to an arbitrary output_path, file code review items, and run scans). Recommend treating the injected {FILES_TO_REVIEW}/{EXTRA_INSTRUCTIONS} context as untrusted: strip control/instruction keywords, delimit them clearly as data (not authoritative instructions), and consider sandboxing the reviewer subagent's tool access to least-privilege (it already has an allowed write path; consider read-only fs otherwise).
items.proposed_fix: Treat injected files/instructions as untrusted data: delimit them as data, strip/neutralize instruction-prompt directives, and apply least-privilege tool access to the reviewer subagent.
items.summary: Unsanitized 'instructions' and 'files' arguments injected verbatim into reviewer subagent system prompt enable prompt injection

items.description: The security_review_with_agent validator stores resolved paths in args_ but then the execute() path re-uses the raw, unresolved paths (args_.files) when building the reviewer prompt, and the tool does NOT itself validate the output_path or files — only the validator does at argument-parse time. More importantly, unlike the other scanners, validate_runtime() for security_review_with_agent (line 88) only checks for a non-empty files list; the actual read/write path access checks run during validate_args (security_review_with_agent_security.cpp:29-40), but the built command passes raw (possibly relative, possibly symlink-resolvable) paths to the LLM subagent with no run-time re-validation. If the same tool object is ever reused across contexts, or if paths resolve differently at execute time, the write to output_path is not re-checked. This is a moderate defense-in-depth gap: the write target (arbitrary output_path) is trusted solely from the validator's earlier pass. Recommend resolving/validating paths (fs_security) again at execute time against the current context, or passing the resolved paths into the prompt rather than raw ones.
items.proposed_fix: Re-resolve and re-validate paths at execute time against the current tool context, and use resolved paths when building the reviewer prompt.
items.summary: Raw (unresolved) paths passed to reviewer agent; write target not re-validated at execute time

items.description: The three getter/setter security validator implementations (security_scan_c_security.cpp, security_scan_python_security.cpp, security_scan_semgrep_security.cpp) are byte-for-byte duplicated logic, and the four scanner entry files duplicate the same command-construction pattern. Beyond maintenance duplication, each validator validates read access and existence but the resolved path returned by fs_security.validate_access is stored and later re-escaped. This is consistent across the three, which is at least a low-severity DRY/architecture concern flagged because divergence (e.g. one scanner gaining a stricter/different validation than another) creates inconsistent security posture. Consider a shared helper for path validation and command construction.
items.proposed_fix: Factor the duplicated cmd/path-validation logscanner logic into a shared helper to guarantee a consistent security posture across all scanned tools.
items.summary: Duplicated path-validation and command-construction logic across the scanner/validator files risks inconsistent security posture

items.description: performance/robustness nit: On the semgrep command (security_scan_semgrep_entry.cpp:42) the flags mix styles (`--config=auto` inline-arg with `--config "p/security-audit"` escaped-string) and the command appends ` 2>/dev/null` (line 48). Redirecting stderr is fine (command_runner executes via `sh -c` and appends `2>&1` only when no `2>`/`>&` present), but because the HTML branch (line 40) uses `--include=\"*.html\"` the quotes must survive bash correctly — escape_shell_arg is NOT used for the `--include` value, so if special characters were interpolated they could break out. In the current code the value is a literal constant so this is not exploitable, but the inconsistent quoting styles plus discovery that an HTML-screen-path triggers completely different flag sets (see the separate medium finding) warrant a single consistent, explicitly-quoted command builder. Flagged here only as a low/nit for maintainability and to ensure the `--include` value is properly quoted if ever parameterized.
items.proposed_fix: Use a consistent, explicitly-quoted command builder for the semgrep command instead of mixing quoting styles and manually embedding flag values.
items.summary: Inconsistent flag quoting styles in semgrep command construction

items.description: command_runner::timeout_seconds_ defaults to 0 (no timeout; should_continue only enforces when timeout_seconds_ > 0). None of the four scanner tools call set_timeout(). Combined with unbounded output accumulation and, for semgrep, network fetch of rules, a scanner can run indefinitely (e.g., semgrep pulling/updating large rule sets while the network is up, or a scanner hanging on a pathological input), hanging the agent's synchronous execute() (the tool waits for full subprocess completion before returning) and wasting resources/tokens. Recommend setting an explicit, generous timeout on each scanner run (e.g. set_timeout) so runaway scans are bounded.
items.proposed_fix: Set an explicit timeout (runner.set_timeout(...)) for each scanner invocation to bound execution time.
items.summary: Scanner subprocesses run with no timeout (default 0 = unlimited), enabling hang/DoS

items.description: The spawned reviewer (line 283) and background verifier (line 108) agents are assigned agent_role::reviewer / agent_role::verifier via set_role(), but ai_agent::set_role() only sets properties_.read_only = true for agent_role::summarizer (see src/agentlib/ai_agent.cpp:3297). Consequently these subagents are NOT read-only. In ai_agent::start_processing (src/agentlib/ai_agent.cpp:1234-1236), since !is_read_only() is true, the tool context grants ctx.fs_security.add_allowed_root(workspace_root, access_type::write) — i.e. WRITE access to the entire project workspace. Combined with the base+git families the role setup auto-activates (ai_agent.cpp:3301-3306), a reviewer can call write-capable base tools (fs_write_file, fs_replace_content, fs_replace_lines, fs_mkdir, run_python, run_shell_command) and git-mutating tools (git_commit, git_push, git_restore). This directly contradicts the injected system prompt's claim that 'your execution context is read-only', and renders the set_allowed_write_file(args_.result_file) restriction (lines 291-293) essentially meaningless (set_allowed_write_file only narrows write scope when read_only is true). Because the review task feeds untrusted file contents into the reviewer's LLM context, prompt injection in a reviewed file could induce the reviewer to modify/commit source or run shell commands. Fix: call reviewer_agent->set_read_only(true) (and for the verifier) when spawning, so write access is only granted to the explicitly allowed result_file. Note the sibling tool security_review_with_agent also sets role reviewer, but should be audited likewise.
items.proposed_fix: After setting the role, explicitly mark the subagent read-only: reviewer_agent->set_read_only(true); and verifier_agent->set_read_only(true); so that start_processing does NOT add a workspace-root write allowlist, leaving only the explicitly granted result_file write (via set_allowed_write_file + add_allowed_file at ai_agent.cpp:1229-1232).
items.summary: Reviewer/verifier subagents are not enforced read-only and get full workspace write access + shell/git tools

items.description: The validator only checks that parsed.files is non-empty; it imposes no upper bound on the number of entries. execute() then groups the files (10 per group / 1500 lines per group) and spawns a code-reviewer ai_agent for EVERY group (perform_code_review_entry.cpp:268-359), plus a detached background verifier thread. An LLM call (or a hijacked/compromised subagent call) that lists hundreds or thousands of files forces the spawning of a matching number of subagents and LLM chat sessions, each consuming threads, memory, and API budget — a denial-of-service / resource-exhaustion vector. Other orchestration tools (e.g. invoke_subagent) bound their inputs; this one does not. Recommend capping the number of files (and/or total reviewers) and rejecting oversized requests.
items.proposed_fix: Add a hard limit on parsed.files.size() (e.g. reject if > some N like 100 or 500) and/or cap the number of reviewer groups spawned concurrently, returning a validation error when exceeded. Document the limit in get_parameters_schema().
items.summary: Unbounded 'files' argument allows unbounded subagent/thread spawning (resource exhaustion)

items.description: The validator copies parsed.instructions, parsed.result_file, and parsed.files verbatim into args_ with no length caps and no sanitization (unlike invoke_subagent_security.cpp which caps profile/task at 10000 chars and runs is_safe_for_ui/is_safe_multiline checks). The instructions string is injected verbatim into both the reviewer's system_prompt and task_prompt (perform_code_review_entry.cpp:335-348, 352-355); an oversized or control-character-laden string expands prompt/API usage, enables terminal/UI corruption via injected escape sequences (when the toolcall result is rendered), and broadens prompt-injection surface area. The unbounded instructions can also inflate the reviewer/verifier task prompts unboundedly.
items.proposed_fix: Enforce maximum lengths for instructions (and result_file / each file path), reject control characters / escape sequences via fs_utils::is_safe_for_ui on the instructions string and file paths, mirroring the invoke_subagent validator's checks.
items.summary: 'instructions', 'result_file', and file path strings are length-unbounded and not control-character-sanitized

items.description: validate_args_impl resolves each file through ctx.fs_security.validate_access() which canonicalizes against the security manager's cwd_ and re-checks ignore lists/allowlists, but the resolved canonical paths are DISCARDED. execute() then independently recomputes each path as workspace_root / f (is_file_reviewable at line 213 and grouping at line 233) using project_manager::get_instance().get_project_root(). If the fs_security cwd_ differs from the project root, or if the filesystem changes between validation and execution (e.g. a symlink swapped in), the file actually reviewed may differ from the one validated, potentially reading a file that was not access-checked (or was validated against a different path). The downstream subagents also re-resolve relative paths against the workspace root in start_processing. Recommend threading the canonical resolved path from validation into the tool/execute path (store resolved paths in args_) rather than re-deriving them, eliminating the stale-path/TOCTOU window.
items.proposed_fix: Store the canonical resolved path returned by validate_access (out_resolved_path) in perform_code_review_args and use it in execute()/is_file_reviewable() and in the subagent file listing instead of re-reconstructing workspace_root / f. This keeps validation and execution on the identical resolved path.
items.summary: TOCTOU / stale-path hazard: validation canonicalizes paths but execute re-resolves workspace_root/f
